What I want is, that you should write to your sisters and tell them of the fortune that has accrued to them.”

33.124.oldText: “I have intimated my view of the case: I am incapable of taking any other. I am not brutally selfish, blindly unjust, or fiendishly ungrateful. Besides, I am resolved I will have a home and connections. I like Moor House, and I will live at Moor House; I like Diana and Mary, and I will attach myself for life to Diana and Mary. It would please and benefit me to have five thousand pounds; it would torment and oppress me to have twenty thousand; which, moreover, could never be mine in justice, though it might in law. I abandon to you, then, what is absolutely superfluous to me. Let there be no opposition, and no discussion about it; let us agree amongst each other, and decide the point at once.”

33.125.oldText: “This is acting on first impulses; you must take days to consider such a matter, ere your word can be regarded as valid.”

33.126.oldText: “Oh! if all you doubt is my sincerity, I am easy: you see the justice of the case?”

33.127.oldText: “I _do_ see a certain justice; but it is contrary to all custom. Besides, the entire fortune is your right: my uncle gained it by his own efforts; he was free to leave it to whom he would: he left it to you. After all, justice permits you to keep it: you may, with a clear conscience, consider it absolutely your own.”

33.128.oldText: “With me,” said I, “it is fully as much a matter of feeling as of conscience: I must indulge my feelings; I so seldom have had an opportunity of doing so. Were you to argue, object, and annoy me for a year, I could not forego the delicious pleasure of which I have caught a glimpse—that of repaying, in part, a mighty obligation, and winning to myself lifelong friends.”

33.129.oldText: “You think so now,” rejoined St. John, “because you do not know what it is to possess, nor consequently to enjoy wealth: you cannot form a notion of the importance twenty thousand pounds would give you; of the place it would enable you to take in society; of the prospects it would open to you: you cannot—”

33.130.oldText: “And you,” I interrupted, “cannot at all imagine the craving I have for fraternal and sisterly love. I never had a home, I never had brothers or sisters; I must and will have them now: you are not reluctant to admit me and own me, are you?”

33.131.oldText: “Jane, I will be your brother—my sisters will be your sisters—without stipulating for this sacrifice of your just rights.”

33.132.oldText: “Brother? Yes; at the distance of a thousand leagues! Sisters? Yes; slaving amongst strangers! I, wealthy—gorged with gold I never earned and do not merit! You, penniless! Famous equality and fraternisation! Close union! Intimate attachment!”

33.133.oldText: “But, Jane, your aspirations after family ties and domestic happiness may be realised otherwise than by the means you contemplate: you may marry.”

33.134.oldText: “Nonsense, again! Marry! I don’t want to marry, and never shall marry.”

33.135.oldText: “That is saying too much: such hazardous affirmations are a proof of the excitement under which you labour.”

33.136.oldText: “It is not saying too much: I know what I feel, and how averse are my inclinations to the bare thought of marriage. No one would take me for love; and I will not be regarded in the light of a mere money speculation. And I do not want a stranger—unsympathising, alien, different from me; I want my kindred: those with whom I have full fellow-feeling. Say again you will be my brother: when you uttered the words I was satisfied, happy; repeat them, if you can, repeat them sincerely.”

33.137.oldText: “I think I can. I know I have always loved my own sisters; and I know on what my affection for them is grounded,—respect for their worth and admiration of their talents. You too have principle and mind: your tastes and habits resemble Diana’s and Mary’s; your presence is always agreeable to me; in your conversation I have already for some time found a salutary solace. I feel I can easily and naturally make room in my heart for you, as my third and youngest sister.”

33.138.oldText: “Thank you: that contents me for to-night. Now you had better go; for if you stay longer, you will perhaps irritate me afresh by some mistrustful scruple.”

33.139.oldText: “And the school, Miss Eyre? It must now be shut up, I suppose?”

33.140.oldText: “No. I will retain my post of mistress till you get a substitute.”

33.141.oldText: He smiled approbation: we shook hands, and he took leave.

33.142.oldText: I need not narrate in detail the further struggles I had, and arguments I used, to get matters regarding the legacy settled as I wished. My task was a very hard one; but, as I was absolutely resolved—as my cousins saw at length that my mind was really and immutably fixed on making a just division of the property—as they must in their own hearts have felt the equity of the intention; and must, besides, have been innately conscious that in my place they would have done precisely what I wished to do—they yielded at length so far as to consent to put the affair to arbitration. The judges chosen were Mr. Oliver and an able lawyer: both coincided in my opinion: I carried my point. The instruments of transfer were drawn out: St. John, Diana, Mary, and I, each became possessed of a competency.

34.114.oldText: He threw himself down on a swell of heath, and there lay still

34.115.oldText: “I _can_ do what he wants me to do: I am forced to see and acknowledge that,” I meditated,—“that is, if life be spared me. But I feel mine is not the existence to be long protracted under an Indian sun. What then? He does not care for that: when my time came to die, he would resign me, in all serenity and sanctity, to the God who gave me. The case is very plain before me. In leaving England, I should leave a loved but empty land—Mr. Rochester is not there; and if he were, what is, what can that ever be to me? My business is to live without him now: nothing so absurd, so weak as to drag on from day to day, as if I were waiting some impossible change in circumstances, which might reunite me to him. Of course (as St. John once said) I must seek another interest in life to replace the one lost: is not the occupation he now offers me truly the most glorious man can adopt or God assign? Is it not, by its noble cares and sublime results, the one best calculated to fill the void left by uptorn affections and demolished hopes? I believe I must say, Yes—and yet I shudder. Alas! If I join St. John, I abandon half myself: if I go to India, I go to premature death. And how will the interval between leaving England for India, and India for the grave, be filled? Oh, I know well! That, too, is very clear to my vision. By straining to satisfy St. John till my sinews ache, I _shall_ satisfy him—to the finest central point and farthest outward circle of his expectations. If I _do_ go with him—if I _do_ make the sacrifice he urges, I will make it absolutely: I will throw all on the altar—heart, vitals, the entire victim. He will never love me; but he shall approve me; I will show him energies he has not yet seen, resources he has never suspected. Yes, I can work as hard as he can, and with as little grudging.

34.116.oldText: “Consent, then, to his demand is possible: but for one item—one dreadful item. It is—that he asks me to be his wife, and has no more of a husband’s heart for me than that frowning giant of a rock, down which the stream is foaming in yonder gorge. He prizes me as a soldier would a good weapon; and that is all. Unmarried to him, this would never grieve me; but can I let him complete his calculations—coolly put into practice his plans—go through the wedding ceremony? Can I receive from him the bridal ring, endure all the forms of love (which I doubt not he would scrupulously observe) and know that the spirit was quite absent? Can I bear the consciousness that every endearment he bestows is a sacrifice made on principle? No: such a martyrdom would be monstrous. I will never undergo it. As his sister, I might accompany him—not as his wife: I will tell him so.”

34.117.oldText: I looked towards the knoll: there he lay, still as a prostrate column; his face turned to me: his eye beaming watchful and keen. He started to his feet and approached me.

34.118.oldText: “I am ready to go to India, if I may go free.”

34.119.oldText: “Your answer requires a commentary,” he said; “it is not clear.”

34.120.oldText: “You have hitherto been my adopted brother—I, your adopted sister: let us continue as such: you and I had better not marry.”

34.121.oldText: He shook his head. “Adopted fraternity will not do in this case. If you were my real sister it would be different: I should take you, and seek no wife. But as it is, either our union must be consecrated and sealed by marriage, or it cannot exist: practical obstacles oppose themselves to any other plan. Do you not see it, Jane? Consider a moment—your strong sense will guide you.”

34.122.oldText: I did consider; and still my sense, such as it was, directed me only to the fact that we did not love each other as man and wife should: and therefore it inferred we ought not to marry. I said so. “St. John,” I returned, “I regard you as a brother—you, me as a sister: so let us continue.”

34.123.oldText: “We cannot—we cannot,” he answered, with short, sharp determination: “it would not do. You have said you will go with me to India: remember—you have said that.”

34.125.oldText: “Well—well. To the main point—the departure with me from England, the co-operation with me in my future labours—you do not object. You have already as good as put your hand to the plough: you are too consistent to withdraw it. You have but one end to keep in view—how the work you have undertaken can best be done. Simplify your complicated interests, feelings, thoughts, wishes, aims; merge all considerations in one purpose: that of fulfilling with effect—with power—the mission of your great Master. To do so, you must have a coadjutor: not a brother—that is a loose tie—but a husband. I, too, do not want a sister: a sister might any day be taken from me. I want a wife: the sole helpmeet I can influence efficiently in life, and retain absolutely till death.”

34.126.oldText: I shuddered as he spoke: I felt his influence in my marrow—his hold on my limbs.

34.127.oldText: “Seek one elsewhere than in me, St. John: seek one fitted to you.”

34.128.oldText: “One fitted to my purpose, you mean—fitted to my vocation. Again I tell you it is not the insignificant private individual—the mere man, with the man’s selfish senses—I wish to mate: it is the missionary.”

34.129.oldText: “And I will give the missionary my energies—it is all he wants—but not myself: that would be only adding the husk and shell to the kernel. For them he has no use: I retain them.”

34.130.oldText: “You cannot—you ought not. Do you think God will be satisfied with half an oblation? Will He accept a mutilated sacrifice? It is the cause of God I advocate: it is under His standard I enlist you. I cannot accept on His behalf a divided allegiance: it must be entire.”

34.131.oldText: “Oh! I will give my heart to God,” I said. “_You_ do not want it.”

34.132.oldText: I will not swear, reader, that there was not something of repressed sarcasm both in the tone in which I uttered this sentence, and in the feeling that accompanied it. I had silently feared St. John till now, because I had not understood him. He had held me in awe, because he had held me in doubt. How much of him was saint, how much mortal, I could not heretofore tell: but revelations were being made in this conference: the analysis of his nature was proceeding before my eyes. I saw his fallibilities: I comprehended them. I understood that, sitting there where I did, on the bank of heath, and with that handsome form before me, I sat at the feet of a man, erring as I. The veil fell from his hardness and despotism. Having felt in him the presence of these qualities, I felt his imperfection and took courage. I was with an equal—one with whom I might argue—one whom, if I saw good, I might resist.

34.133.oldText: He was silent after I had uttered the last sentence, and I presently risked an upward glance at his countenance. His eye, bent on me, expressed at once stern surprise and keen inquiry. “Is she sarcastic, and sarcastic to _me!_” it seemed to say. “What does this signify?”

34.134.oldText: “Do not let us forget that this is a solemn matter,” he said ere long; “one of which we may neither think nor talk lightly without sin. I trust, Jane, you are in earnest when you say you will serve your heart to God: it is all I want. Once wrench your heart from man, and fix it on your Maker, the advancement of that Maker’s spiritual kingdom on earth will be your chief delight and endeavour; you will be ready to do at once whatever furthers that end. You will see what impetus would be given to your efforts and mine by our physical and mental union in marriage: the only union that gives a character of permanent conformity to the destinies and designs of human beings; and, passing over all minor caprices—all trivial difficulties and delicacies of feeling—all scruple about the degree, kind, strength or tenderness of mere personal inclination—you will hasten to enter into that union at once.”

34.135.oldText: “Shall I?” I said briefly; and I looked at his features, beautiful in their harmony, but strangely formidable in their still severity; at his brow, commanding but not open; at his eyes, bright and deep and searching, but never soft; at his tall imposing figure; and fancied myself in idea _his wife_. Oh! it would never do! As his curate, his comrade, all would be right: I would cross oceans with him in that capacity; toil under Eastern suns, in Asian deserts with him in that office; admire and emulate his courage and devotion and vigour; accommodate quietly to his masterhood; smile undisturbed at his ineradicable ambition; discriminate the Christian from the man: profoundly esteem the one, and freely forgive the other. I should suffer often, no doubt, attached to him only in this capacity: my body would be under rather a stringent yoke, but my heart and mind would be free. I should still have my unblighted self to turn to: my natural unenslaved feelings with which to communicate in moments of loneliness. There would be recesses in my mind which would be only mine, to which he never came, and sentiments growing there fresh and sheltered which his austerity could never blight, nor his measured warrior-march trample down: but as his wife—at his side always, and always restrained, and always checked—forced to keep the fire of my nature continually low, to compel it to burn inwardly and never utter a cry, though the imprisoned flame consumed vital after vital—_this_ would be unendurable.

34.136.oldText: “St. John!” I exclaimed, when I had got so far in my meditation.

34.138.oldText: “I repeat I freely consent to go with you as your fellow-missionary, but not as your wife; I cannot marry you and become part of you.”

34.139.oldText: “A part of me you must become,” he answered steadily; “otherwise the whole bargain is void. How can I, a man not yet thirty, take out with me to India a girl of nineteen, unless she be married to me? How can we be for ever together—sometimes in solitudes, sometimes amidst savage tribes—and unwed?”

34.140.oldText: “Very well,” I said shortly; “under the circumstances, quite as well as if I were either your real sister, or a man and a clergyman like yourself.”

34.141.oldText: “It is known that you are not my sister; I cannot introduce you as such: to attempt it would be to fasten injurious suspicions on us both. And for the rest, though you have a man’s vigorous brain, you have a woman’s heart and—it would not do.”

34.142.oldText: “It would do,” I affirmed with some disdain, “perfectly well. I have a woman’s heart, but not where you are concerned; for you I have only a comrade’s constancy; a fellow-soldier’s frankness, fidelity, fraternity, if you like; a neophyte’s respect and submission to his hierophant: nothing more—don’t fear.”

34.143.oldText: “It is what I want,” he said, speaking to himself; “it is just what I want. And there are obstacles in the way: they must be hewn down. Jane, you would not repent marrying me—be certain of that; we _must_ be married. I repeat it: there is no other way; and undoubtedly enough of love would follow upon marriage to render the union right even in your eyes.”

34.144.oldText: “I scorn your idea of love,” I could not help saying, as I rose up and stood before him, leaning my back against the rock. “I scorn the counterfeit sentiment you offer: yes, St. John, and I scorn you when you offer it.”

34.145.oldText: He looked at me fixedly, compressing his well-cut lips while he did so. Whether he was incensed or surprised, or what, it was not easy to tell: he could command his countenance thoroughly.

34.146.oldText: “I scarcely expected to hear that expression from you,” he said: “I think I have done and uttered nothing to deserve scorn.”

34.147.oldText: I was touched by his gentle tone, and overawed by his high, calm mien.

34.148.oldText: “Forgive me the words, St. John; but it is your own fault that I have been roused to speak so unguardedly. You have introduced a topic on which our natures are at variance—a topic we should never discuss: the very name of love is an apple of discord between us. If the reality were required, what should we do? How should we feel? My dear cousin, abandon your scheme of marriage—forget it.”

34.149.oldText: “No,” said he; “it is a long-cherished scheme, and the only one which can secure my great end: but I shall urge you no further at present. To-morrow, I leave home for Cambridge: I have many friends there to whom I should wish to say farewell. I shall be absent a fortnight—take that space of time to consider my offer: and do not forget that if you reject it, it is not me you deny, but God. Through my means, He opens to you a noble career; as my wife only can you enter upon it. Refuse to be my wife, and you limit yourself for ever to a track of selfish ease and barren obscurity. Tremble lest in that case you should be numbered with those who have denied the faith, and are worse than infidels!”

34.150.oldText: He had done. Turning from me, he once more

34.152.oldText: But this time his feelings were all pent in his heart: I was not worthy to hear them uttered. As I walked by his side homeward, I read well in his iron silence all he felt towards me: the disappointment of an austere and despotic nature, which has met resistance where it expected submission—the disapprobation of a cool, inflexible judgment, which has detected in another feelings and views in which it has no power to sympathise: in short, as a man, he would have wished to coerce me into obedience: it was only as a sincere Christian he bore so patiently with my perversity, and allowed so long a space for reflection and repentance.

34.153.oldText: That night, after he had kissed his sisters, he thought proper to forget even to shake hands with me, but left the room in silence. I—who, though I had no love, had much friendship for him—was hurt by the marked omission: so much hurt that tears started to my eyes.

34.154.oldText: “I see you and St. John have been quarrelling, Jane,” said Diana, “during your walk on the moor. But go after him; he is now lingering in the passage expecting you—he will make it up.”

34.155.oldText: I have not much pride under such circumstances: I would always rather be happy than dignified; and I ran after him—he stood at the foot of the stairs.

34.159.oldText: What a cold, loose touch, he impressed on my fingers! He was deeply displeased by what had occurred that day; cordiality would not warm, nor tears move him. No happy reconciliation was to be had with him—no cheering smile or generous word: but still the Christian was patient and placid; and when I asked him if he forgave me, he answered that he was not in the habit of cherishing the remembrance of vexation; that he had nothing to forgive, not having been offended.

34.160.oldText: And with that answer he left me. I would much rather he had knocked me down.

36.53.oldText: The next minute she lay smashed on the pavement

36.55.oldText: “Dead! Ay, dead as the stones on which her brains and blood were scattered.”

36.57.oldText: “You may well say so, ma’am: it was frightful!”

36.60.oldText: “Well, ma’am, afterwards the house was burnt to the ground: there are only some bits of walls standing now.”

36.62.oldText: “No—perhaps it would have been better if there had.”

36.64.oldText: “Poor Mr. Edward!” he ejaculated, “I little thought ever to have seen it! Some say it was a just judgment on him for keeping his first marriage secret, and wanting to take another wife while he had one living: but I pity him, for my part.”

36.65.oldText: “You said he was alive?” I exclaimed.

36.66.oldText: “Yes, yes: he is alive; but many think he had better be dead.”

36.67.oldText: “Why? How?” My blood was again running cold. “Where is he?” I demanded. “Is he in England?”

36.68.oldText: “Ay—ay—he’s in England; he can’t get out of England, I fancy—he’s a fixture now.”

36.69.oldText: What agony was this! And the man seemed resolved to protract it.

36.70.oldText: “He is stone-blind,” he said at last. “Yes, he is stone-blind, is Mr. Edward.”

36.71.oldText: I had dreaded worse. I had dreaded he was mad. I summoned strength to ask what had caused this calamity.

36.72.oldText: “It was all his own courage, and a body may say, his kindness, in a way, ma’am: he wouldn’t leave the house till every one else was out before him. As he came down the great staircase at last, after Mrs. Rochester had flung herself from the battlements, there was a great crash—all fell. He was taken out from under the ruins, alive, but sadly hurt: a beam had fallen in such a way as to protect him partly; but one eye was knocked out, and one hand so crushed that Mr. Carter, the surgeon, had to amputate it directly. The other eye inflamed: he lost the sight of that also. He is now helpless, indeed—blind and a cripple.”

36.73.oldText: “Where is he? Where does he now live?”

36.74.oldText: “At Ferndean, a manor-house on a farm he has, about thirty miles off: quite a desolate spot.”

36.76.oldText: “Old John and his wife: he would have none else. He is quite broken down, they say.”

36.78.oldText: “We have a chaise, ma’am, a very handsome chaise.”

36.79.oldText: “Let it be got ready instantly; and if your post-boy can drive me to Ferndean before dark this day, I’ll pay both you and him twice the hire you usually demand.”

38.17.oldText: And have you a pale blue dress on?

38.18.oldText: I had. He informed me then, that for some time he had fancied the obscurity clouding one eye was becoming less dense; and that now he was sure of it.

38.19.oldText: He and I went up to London. He had the advice of an eminent oculist; and he eventually recovered the sight of that one eye. He cannot now see very distinctly: he cannot read or write much; but he can find his way without being led by the hand: the sky is no longer a blank to him—the earth no longer a void. When his first-born was put into his arms, he could see that the boy had inherited his own eyes, as they once were—large, brilliant, and black. On that occasion, he again, with a full heart, acknowledged that God had tempered judgment with mercy.

38.20.oldText: My Edward and I, then, are happy: and the more so, because those we most love are happy likewise. Diana and Mary Rivers are both married: alternately, once every year, they come to see us, and we go to see them. Diana’s husband is a captain in the navy, a gallant officer and a good man. Mary’s is a clergyman, a college friend of her brother’s, and, from his attainments and principles, worthy of the connection. Both Captain Fitzjames and Mr. Wharton love their wives, and are loved by them.

38.21.oldText: As to St. John Rivers, he left England: he went to India. He entered on the path he had marked for himself; he pursues it still. A more resolute, indefatigable pioneer never wrought amidst rocks and dangers. Firm, faithful, and devoted, full of energy, and zeal, and truth, he labours for his race; he clears their painful way to improvement; he hews down like a giant the prejudices of creed and caste that encumber it. He may be stern; he may be exacting; he may be ambitious yet; but his is the sternness of the warrior Greatheart, who guards his pilgrim convoy from the onslaught of Apollyon. His is the exaction of the apostle, who speaks but for Christ, when he says—“Whosoever will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross and follow me.” His is the ambition of the high master-spirit, which aims to fill a place in the first rank of those who are redeemed from the earth—who stand without fault before the throne of God, who share the last mighty victories of the Lamb, who are called, and chosen, and faithful.

38.22.oldText: St. John is unmarried: he never will marry now. Himself has hitherto sufficed to the toil, and the toil draws near its close: his glorious sun hastens to its setting. The last letter I received from him drew from my eyes human tears, and yet filled my heart with divine joy: he anticipated his sure reward, his incorruptible crown. I know that a stranger’s hand will write to me next, to say that the good and faithful servant has been called at length into the joy of his Lord. And why weep for this? No fear of death will darken St. John’s last hour: his mind will be unclouded, his heart will be undaunted, his hope will be sure, his faith steadfast. His own words are a pledge of this—

38.23.oldText: “My Master,” he says, “has forewarned me. Daily He announces more distinctly,—‘Surely I come quickly!’ and hourly I more eagerly respond,—‘Amen; even so come, Lord Jesus!’”

1.0.oldText: There was no chance of going for a walk that day. We had wandered through the bare shrubbery for an hour that morning, but since lunch (Mrs. Reed dined early when there were no guests), the cold winter wind had brought such dark clouds and such relentless rain that any further time outdoors was out of the question.

1.2.oldText: Eliza, John, and Georgiana were now gathered around their mama in the drawing room. She lay on a sofa by the fire, and with her darlings around her (for the moment neither fighting nor crying), she looked perfectly content. She had excused me from joining the group, saying that she regretted having to keep me at a distance, but that until she heard from Bessie, and could see for herself, that I was genuinely trying to develop a more sociable and childlike nature, a more appealing and lively manner—something lighter, more open, more natural—she really had to exclude me from privileges meant only for happy, well-behaved little children.

1.5.oldText: A breakfast room adjoined the drawing room, and I slipped in there. It had a bookcase, and I quickly grabbed a book, making sure it was one full of pictures. I climbed into the window seat, tucked my feet up, and sat cross-legged. Having pulled the red curtain nearly shut, I was hidden away in double seclusion.

1.6.oldText: Folds of scarlet fabric blocked my view to the right. To the left were the clear glass panes, shielding me from but not hiding the dreary November day. Now and then, while turning the pages of my book, I studied the winter afternoon. In the distance, there was nothing but a pale blur of mist and cloud. Nearby, a scene of wet lawn and battered shrubs, with endless rain sweeping wildly before a long, mournful wind.

1.7.oldText: I went back to my book—Bewick's History of British Birds. I didn't care much for the text itself, generally speaking, but there were certain introductory pages that, young as I was, I couldn't simply skip over. They described the haunts of seabirds, the solitary rocks and headlands where only they lived, the coast of Norway dotted with islands from its southern tip, the Lindeness or Naze, all the way to the North Cape—

1.9.oldText: I was equally struck by the descriptions of the bleak shores of Lapland, Siberia, Spitzbergen, Nova Zembla, Iceland, Greenland, with "the vast sweep of the Arctic Zone, and those desolate regions of barren space—that reservoir of frost and snow, where solid fields of ice, built up over centuries of winters, rising to alpine heights above heights, surround the pole and concentrate the extreme cold." Of these death-white realms I formed my own idea: shadowy, like all the half-understood notions that drift through children's minds, but strangely powerful. The words in those introductory pages connected themselves to the illustrations that followed, and gave meaning to the rock standing alone in a sea of waves and spray, to the wrecked boat stranded on a desolate coast, to the cold and ghostly moon glancing through bars of cloud at a ship just sinking.

1.23.oldText: John Reed was a schoolboy of fourteen, four years older than me—I was only ten. He was big and heavy for his age, with a dull, unhealthy complexion, coarse features in a broad face, thick limbs, and large hands and feet. He constantly stuffed himself at meals, which left him with a sluggish look, bleary eyes, and flabby cheeks. He should have been at school, but his mama had brought him home for a month or two on account of his "delicate health." Mr. Miles, the headmaster, said he would do perfectly well if fewer cakes and sweets were sent from home. But his mother rejected such a harsh opinion and preferred the more flattering idea that John's sallowness was due to too much studying and, perhaps, homesickness.

1.24.oldText: John didn't have much affection for his mother and sisters, and he actively disliked me. He bullied and hurt me—not two or three times a week, not once or twice a day, but constantly. Every nerve in my body feared him, and every bit of me shrank when he came near. There were moments when his cruelty left me stunned, because I had no defense against his threats or his violence. The servants didn't want to upset their young master by taking my side, and Mrs. Reed was blind and deaf to it all. She never saw him hit me or heard him insult me, though he did both in her very presence from time to time—more often, though, behind her back.

1.25.oldText: As usual, I obeyed John and came up to his chair. He spent about three minutes sticking his tongue out at me as far as it would go. I knew he would hit me soon, and while dreading the blow, I studied the disgusting, ugly face of the person about to deliver it. I wonder if he saw that thought in my expression, because without a word, he suddenly struck me, hard. I staggered, and once I regained my balance, I stepped back a pace or two from his chair.

1.38.oldText: "Goodness! What a terror, to attack Master John like that!"

2.4.oldText: "No, you are less than a servant, because you do nothing to earn your keep. Now sit down and think about what you've done."

2.18.oldText: "Besides," said Miss Abbot, "God will punish her. He might strike her dead in the middle of one of her tantrums, and then where would she go? Come, Bessie, let's leave her. I wouldn't have her heart for anything. Say your prayers, Miss Eyre, when you're alone. If you don't repent, something terrible might come down the chimney and carry you off."

2.21.oldText: The room was cold, because it rarely had a fire. It was silent, because it was far from the nursery and kitchen. It was solemn, because everyone knew how rarely it was entered. Only the housemaid came here on Saturdays to dust the mirrors and furniture. And Mrs. Reed herself, at long intervals, visited it to check the contents of a secret drawer in the wardrobe, where she kept various documents, her jewelry box, and a portrait of her dead husband. In those last words lies the secret of the red room—the reason it remained so lonely despite its grandeur.

2.25.oldText: All of John Reed's violent cruelties, all his sisters' cold indifference, all his mother's hostility, all the servants' favoritism—it all churned up in my troubled mind like dark sediment in a stirred well. Why was I always suffering, always put down, always blamed, forever condemned? Why could I never please anyone? Why was it pointless even to try? Eliza, who was stubborn and selfish, was respected. Georgiana, who had a spoiled temper, a sharp spite, and a rude, arrogant manner, was indulged by everyone. Her beauty, her pink cheeks and golden curls, seemed to enchant everyone who saw her, and to buy forgiveness for every fault. No one crossed John, let alone punished him, though he wrung the necks of pigeons, killed baby peacocks, set the dogs on the sheep, stripped the greenhouse vines of their fruit, and broke the buds off the finest plants in the conservatory. He called his mother "old girl," mocked her for her dark skin (which matched his own), blatantly ignored her wishes, and regularly tore and ruined her silk clothes—and he was still "her darling." I dared not make a single mistake. I tried to do everything right. And still I was called naughty and tiresome, sulky and sneaky, from morning to noon and from noon to night.

2.29.oldText: I was a misfit at Gateshead Hall. I was unlike anyone there. I had nothing in common with Mrs. Reed or her children or her chosen household. If they didn't love me, I loved them just as little. They had no reason to feel affection for someone who couldn't relate to any of them—an outsider, different in temperament, ability, and inclination. A useless thing, unable to serve their interests or add to their pleasure. A troublesome thing, harboring the seeds of resentment at their treatment and contempt for their judgment. I know that if I had been a cheerful, bright, carefree, bold, and pretty child—though equally dependent and friendless—Mrs. Reed would have tolerated my presence more easily. Her children would have felt more warmth toward me. The servants would have been less inclined to make me the nursery scapegoat.

2.31.oldText: A strange idea occurred to me. I had never doubted that if Mr. Reed had been alive, he would have treated me kindly. And now, as I sat staring at the white bed and shadowed walls—glancing now and then at the dimly glinting mirror—I began to recall what I'd heard about dead men, disturbed in their graves when their last wishes were violated, returning to earth to punish oath-breakers and protect the wronged. I imagined Mr. Reed's spirit, troubled by the suffering of his sister's child, might leave its resting place—whether in the church vault or wherever the dead go—and appear before me in this room. I wiped my tears and stifled my sobs, afraid that any sign of violent grief might summon a supernatural voice to comfort me, or draw from the shadows some glowing face bending over me with unearthly pity. This idea, comforting in theory, would have been terrifying in reality, and I tried with all my strength to suppress it. I tried to be brave. Shaking my hair from my eyes, I raised my head and forced myself to look boldly around the dark room. At that moment, a light gleamed on the wall. Was it, I wondered, a ray of moonlight coming through a gap in the blind? No—moonlight would be steady, and this was moving. As I watched, it glided up to the ceiling and flickered above my head. I can easily guess now that the light was probably from a lantern carried by someone crossing the lawn. But at the time, with my mind primed for horror and my nerves shattered, I thought the darting beam was a sign of some approaching vision from another world. My heart pounded, my head burned. A sound filled my ears that I took for the rushing of wings. Something seemed near me. I felt crushed, suffocated. My endurance broke. I rushed to the door and shook the lock in desperate effort. Footsteps came running along the hallway outside. The key turned. Bessie and Abbot entered.

2.42.oldText: "Silence! This behavior is utterly revolting." And no doubt she believed it. In her eyes, I was a dramatic little actress. She genuinely saw me as a bundle of violent passions, petty spirit, and dangerous deceit.

3.12.oldText: "You fainted, I suppose, in the red room from all the crying. You'll be better soon, I'm sure."

3.14.oldText: "Sarah, come sleep with me in the nursery. I'm terrified to be alone with that poor child tonight. She could die. It's so strange that she had that fit. The Missus was rather too hard on her."

3.18.oldText: No serious or lasting physical illness followed the red room incident. It only gave my nerves a shock whose aftershocks I feel to this day. Yes, Mrs. Reed, I owe you some terrible moments of mental anguish. But I should forgive you, because you didn't know what you were doing. While you were tearing my heart apart, you thought you were only correcting my bad tendencies.

3.20.oldText: Bessie had been down to the kitchen and brought back a tart on a certain brightly painted china plate, whose bird of paradise nestled in a wreath of flowers. That plate had always stirred in me a rush of admiration, and I had often begged to be allowed to hold it and examine it up close, but had always been considered unworthy of such a privilege. Now this precious dish was placed on my knee, and I was warmly invited to eat the ring of delicate pastry on it. But it was no use. Like most long-awaited favors, it came too late. I couldn't eat the tart, and the plumage of the bird, the colors of the flowers, seemed strangely faded. I pushed both plate and tart away. Bessie asked if I wanted a book. The word book acted as a brief spark, and I asked her to fetch Gulliver's Travels from the library. I had read that book again and again with delight. I considered it a true account and found in it a deeper interest than fairy tales offered. As for elves, having searched for them in vain among foxglove leaves and bells, under mushrooms, and beneath the ivy on old walls, I had finally accepted the sad truth that they had all left England for some wild country where the forests were thicker and the people fewer. But Lilliput and Brobdingnag, I firmly believed, were real places on the earth's surface, and I had no doubt that someday, by taking a long voyage, I would see with my own eyes the tiny fields, houses, and trees, the miniature people, the little cows, sheep, and birds of one realm, and the towering crops, the enormous dogs, the monstrous cats, and the giant men and women of the other. Yet now, when this beloved book was placed in my hands—when I turned its pages and looked for the magic in its wonderful pictures that had never failed me before—everything was eerie and bleak. The giants were gaunt goblins, the little people were sinister imps, and Gulliver was the loneliest wanderer in the most terrifying of lands. I closed the book, afraid to keep reading, and put it on the table beside the untouched tart.

3.31.oldText: Bessie said I was doing well enough.

3.40.oldText: The kind apothecary looked a little puzzled. I was standing before him, and he studied me steadily. His eyes were small and gray, not especially bright, but I think now they were quite shrewd. He had a rough-featured but kind-looking face. After considering me for a moment, he said—

3.45.oldText: As he tucked the box back into his waistcoat pocket, a loud bell rang for the servants' dinner. He knew what it was. "That's for you, nurse," he said. "You can go down. I'll have a talk with Miss Jane while you're gone."

3.75.oldText: "I can't say. Aunt Reed says if I have any, they must be a wretched lot. I wouldn't want to go begging."

3.77.oldText: I thought again. I barely knew what school was. Bessie sometimes described it as a place where young ladies sat on hard benches, wore stiff boards strapped to their backs for posture, and were expected to be extremely refined and proper. John Reed hated his school and complained about his teachers—but John Reed's tastes were no guide for mine. And if Bessie's accounts of school discipline (gathered from the young ladies of a family where she had worked before Gateshead) were somewhat alarming, her descriptions of the skills those same young ladies had acquired were, I thought, equally appealing. She boasted of beautiful landscape and flower paintings they had done, songs they could sing and pieces they could play, purses they could knit, French books they could translate. My spirit stirred with ambition as I listened. Besides, school would be a complete change. It would mean a long journey, a total separation from Gateshead, and entry into a new life.

3.82.oldText: Bessie invited him into the breakfast room and led the way out. In the conversation that followed between him and Mrs. Reed, I gathered from what happened afterward that the apothecary suggested I be sent to school. The suggestion was no doubt eagerly accepted, because as Abbot said when discussing it with Bessie one night while they sewed in the nursery—after I was in bed and, they assumed, asleep—"The Missus was glad enough to get rid of such a tiresome, ill-natured child, who was always watching everybody and scheming behind their backs." Abbot, I think, gave me credit for being a sort of infant Guy Fawkes.

3.85.oldText: "Yes," Abbot replied. "If she were a nice, pretty child, you might feel sorry for her being alone in the world. But you really can't care much about such an ugly little creature."

3.86.oldText: "Not a great deal, I suppose," Bessie agreed. "At any rate, a beauty like Miss Georgiana would stir more sympathy in the same situation."

4.0.oldText: From my conversation with Mr. Lloyd and from the discussion between Bessie and Abbot that I overheard, I gathered enough hope to keep me going while I waited to get well. A change seemed near, and I longed for it in silence. But it was slow in coming. Days and weeks passed. I regained my normal health, but no one mentioned the subject I was constantly thinking about. Mrs. Reed watched me sometimes with a stern eye but rarely spoke to me. Since my illness, she had drawn an even sharper line between me and her own children, giving me a small closet to sleep in alone, making me eat my meals by myself, and spending all my time in the nursery while my cousins stayed in the drawing room. She dropped no hint about sending me to school, yet I felt instinctively certain she wouldn't keep me under her roof much longer. Her glance, more than ever, expressed a deep and fixed aversion when it fell on me.

4.1.oldText: Eliza and Georgiana, clearly following orders, spoke to me as little as possible. John stuck his tongue in his cheek whenever he saw me and once tried to hit me. But when I instantly turned on him, driven by the same deep fury and desperate defiance that had flared up before, he decided it was better to back off. He ran from me, cursing and swearing I had broken his nose. I had indeed aimed the hardest blow my fist could deliver right at that prominent feature, and when I saw that either the punch or my expression scared him, I was strongly tempted to press my advantage. But he was already running to his mama. I heard him blubbering out the tale of how "that awful Jane Eyre" had attacked him like a wild cat. He was cut off rather sharply—

4.5.oldText: Mrs. Reed was a fairly stout woman, but on hearing this brazen declaration, she ran nimbly up the stairs, swept me like a whirlwind into the nursery, and, crushing me down on the edge of my crib, dared me in a fierce voice to get up or say one more word for the rest of the day.

4.9.oldText: Mrs. Reed quickly recovered herself. She shook me hard, boxed both my ears, and left without a word. Bessie filled the gap with an hour-long lecture, proving beyond doubt that I was the most wicked and abandoned child ever raised under a roof. I half believed her, because all I could feel were dark emotions surging inside me.

4.10.oldText: November, December, and half of January passed. Christmas and New Year had been celebrated at Gateshead with the usual festivities—presents exchanged, dinners and parties given. I was excluded from all of it, of course. My share of the celebrations consisted of watching Eliza and Georgiana get dressed in their thin muslin frocks and red sashes, their hair elaborately curled, and seeing them go down to the drawing room. After that, I listened to the sounds of piano or harp playing below, to the footsteps of the butler and footman, to the clinking of glass and china as refreshments were served, and to the muffled hum of conversation whenever the drawing room door opened and closed. When I tired of this, I retreated from the top of the stairs to the lonely, silent nursery. There, though somewhat sad, I wasn't miserable. To tell the truth, I had no desire to join the company—when I was among people, I was almost never noticed. If Bessie had only been kind and companionable, I would have considered it a treat to spend the evenings quietly with her instead of enduring the formidable gaze of Mrs. Reed in a room full of guests. But as soon as Bessie had dressed the young ladies, she took herself off to the lively kitchen and housekeeper's room, usually taking the candle with her. I would sit with my doll on my knee until the fire burned low, glancing around now and then to make sure nothing worse than myself haunted the shadowy room. When the embers faded to a dull red, I undressed quickly, struggling with knots and buttons as best I could, and sought shelter from the cold and darkness in my crib. I always took my doll to bed with me. Human beings need to love something, and with nothing worthier to love, I managed to find pleasure in loving and cherishing a faded little figure, shabby as a miniature scarecrow. It puzzles me now to remember with what absurd devotion I doted on this toy, half-imagining it was alive and could feel. I couldn't sleep unless it was tucked inside my nightgown, and when it lay there safe and warm, I was relatively happy, believing it was happy too.

4.11.oldText: The hours dragged while I waited for the guests to leave, listening for Bessie's step on the stairs. Sometimes she would come up between events to fetch her thimble or scissors, or perhaps to bring me something for supper—a bun or a small cake. Then she would sit on the bed while I ate, and when I finished, she would tuck the covers around me. Twice she kissed me and said, "Good night, Miss Jane." When she was gentle like this, Bessie seemed to me the best, prettiest, kindest person in the world, and I desperately wished she would always be so pleasant and never push me around or scold me or make unreasonable demands, as she too often did. Bessie Lee must have been a girl of real natural ability, because she was sharp in everything she did and had a remarkable gift for storytelling—at least, that's how I judge it from the impression her nursery tales made on me. She was pretty too, if I remember her face and figure correctly. I recall her as a slim young woman with black hair, dark eyes, very nice features, and a clear complexion. But she had a changeable and hasty temper, and vague ideas about fairness or justice. Still, such as she was, I preferred her to anyone else at Gateshead Hall.

4.13.oldText: Georgiana sat on a high stool at the mirror, doing her hair and weaving in artificial flowers and faded feathers she'd found in an attic drawer. I was making my bed, under strict orders from Bessie to have it done before she came back (for Bessie now often used me as a sort of assistant nursemaid, to tidy the room, dust the furniture, and so on). After spreading the quilt and folding my nightgown, I went to the window seat to straighten some picture books and dollhouse furniture scattered there. An abrupt command from Georgiana to leave her things alone (the tiny chairs and mirrors, the fairy plates and cups were hers) stopped me. With nothing else to do, I breathed on the frost patterns on the window, melting enough of the silvery-white designs to clear a space through which I could look out at the grounds, where everything lay still and frozen under a hard frost.

4.14.oldText: From this window I could see the porter's lodge and the carriage road. Just as I had melted enough frost to peer through, I saw the gates thrown open and a carriage roll through. I watched it come up the drive without much interest—carriages often came to Gateshead, but none ever brought visitors who mattered to me. It stopped in front of the house. The doorbell rang loudly. The newcomer was let in. Since none of this concerned me, my idle attention soon found a livelier attraction in a little hungry robin that came chirping on the bare branches of a cherry tree nailed against the wall near my window. The remains of my bread and milk breakfast sat on the table. I crumbled a bit of roll and was tugging at the window sash to put the crumbs on the sill when Bessie came rushing upstairs into the nursery.

4.20.oldText: I now stood in the empty hall. Before me was the breakfast room door, and I stopped, intimidated and trembling. What a miserable little coward fear and unjust punishment had made of me in those days! I was afraid to go back to the nursery and afraid to go forward to the parlor. For ten minutes I stood in anxious indecision. The fierce ringing of the breakfast room bell decided it—I had to go in.

4.21.oldText: "Who could want me?" I asked myself, as I turned the stiff door handle with both hands. It resisted for a second or two. "What will I see besides Aunt Reed in there? A man or a woman?" The handle turned, the door opened, and passing through with a low curtsy, I looked up at—a black pillar! That, at least, was what it looked like at first glance: a straight, narrow, black-clad shape standing stiffly on the rug. The grim face at the top was like a carved mask placed above a column.

4.52.oldText: "No? Oh, shocking! I have a little boy, younger than you, who knows six Psalms by heart. And when you ask him which he'd rather have, a gingerbread biscuit to eat or a verse of a Psalm to learn, he says: 'Oh, the verse of a Psalm! Angels sing Psalms,' says he. 'I wish to be a little angel here below.' And then he gets two biscuits as a reward for his goodness."

4.57.oldText: I had every right to dread Mrs. Reed and every reason to dislike her, because it was in her nature to wound me cruelly. I was never happy in her presence. No matter how carefully I obeyed or how hard I tried to please her, my efforts were always rejected and repaid with words like these. Now, spoken in front of a stranger, the accusation cut me to the heart. I dimly sensed that she was already destroying hope in the new life she was sending me to. I felt, though I couldn't have put it into words, that she was planting hatred and suspicion along my future path. I could see myself being transformed in Mr. Brocklehurst's eyes into a cunning, dangerous child. And what could I do to undo the damage?

4.65.oldText: "You may, madam. She shall be placed in that nursery of chosen plants, and I trust she will show herself grateful for the precious privilege of being admitted."

4.70.oldText: With these words, Mr. Brocklehurst put a thin pamphlet into my hand, rang for his carriage, and left.

4.82.oldText: "How dare I, Mrs. Reed? How dare I? Because it is the truth. You think I have no feelings and that I can survive without a single bit of love or kindness. But I cannot live like that, and you have no pity. I will remember how you shoved me back—roughly and violently shoved me back—into the red room and locked me in there, until my dying day. Even though I was in agony. Even though I cried out, while choking with distress, 'Have mercy! Have mercy, Aunt Reed!' And that punishment you gave me because your wicked boy hit me—knocked me down for nothing. I will tell anyone who asks the exact truth. People think you're a good woman, but you are bad and hard-hearted. You are the deceitful one!"

4.83.oldText: How dare I, Mrs. Reed? How dare I? Because it is the truth.

4.84.oldText: Before I had even finished, my soul began to expand and soar with the strangest sense of freedom and triumph I had ever felt. It was as if an invisible chain had snapped and I had broken through into an undreamed-of liberty. Mrs. Reed looked frightened. Her sewing had slipped from her lap. She was lifting her hands, rocking back and forth, and even twisting her face as if she might cry.

4.85.oldText: "Jane, you're mistaken. What's the matter with you? Why are you trembling so violently? Would you like a glass of water?"

4.87.oldText: "Is there anything else you want, Jane? I assure you, I want to be your friend."

4.88.oldText: "Not you. You told Mr. Brocklehurst I had a bad character, a deceitful nature. And I'll let everyone at Lowood know what you are and what you've done."

4.89.oldText: "Jane, you don't understand these things. Children must be corrected for their faults."

4.90.oldText: "Deceit is not my fault!" I cried out in a fierce, high voice.

4.91.oldText: "But you are passionate, Jane—you must admit that. Now go back to the nursery—there's a dear—and lie down for a bit."

4.92.oldText: "I am not your dear. I cannot lie down. Send me to school soon, Mrs. Reed, because I hate living here."

4.93.oldText: "I will indeed send her to school soon," murmured Mrs. Reed under her breath. And gathering up her work, she abruptly left the room.

4.94.oldText: I was left alone—the winner of the battle. It was the hardest fight I had ever fought and the first victory I had ever won. I stood for a while on the rug where Mr. Brocklehurst had stood, savoring my triumph. First I smiled to myself and felt elated. But this fierce pleasure faded as quickly as my racing pulse slowed. A child cannot fight with her elders as I had done, cannot let her furious feelings run wild as I had let mine, without suffering the sting of remorse and the chill of reaction afterward. A line of burning heath, alive with leaping, devouring flame, would have been the right image for my mind when I accused and threatened Mrs. Reed. That same line, blackened and dead after the fire burns out, would have perfectly captured my state half an hour later, when silence and reflection had shown me the madness of what I'd done and the bleakness of my hated, hating situation.

4.95.oldText: I had tasted revenge for the first time. Going down, it felt like rich wine—warm and heady. But the aftertaste was metallic and corrosive, as if I'd swallowed poison. I would gladly have gone and begged Mrs. Reed's forgiveness now, but I knew, partly from experience and partly from instinct, that this would only make her reject me with doubled scorn, reigniting every turbulent impulse in my nature.

4.96.oldText: I wished I could use some better ability than savage speaking, and find nourishment for some less dark feeling than bitter resentment. I picked up a book—some Arabian tales—and sat down, trying to read. But the words made no sense; my own thoughts kept swimming between me and the page. I opened the glass door to the breakfast room. The shrubbery was perfectly still, gripped by black frost with no sun or breeze to break it. I wrapped my head and arms in the skirt of my dress and went out to walk in a secluded part of the grounds. But I found no pleasure in the silent trees, the falling pine cones, or the frozen relics of autumn—russet leaves swept into piles by past winds, now stiff and stuck together. I leaned against a gate and looked into an empty field where no sheep grazed, where the short grass was bitten down and bleached. It was a very gray day, the sky completely overcast and threatening snow. Flakes fell now and then, settling on the hard path and the frosty meadow without melting. I stood there, wretched child that I was, whispering to myself over and over, "What shall I do? What shall I do?"

4.97.oldText: Suddenly I heard a clear voice call, "Miss Jane! Where are you? Come to lunch!"

4.98.oldText: It was Bessie—I knew her voice well—but I didn't move. Her light step came tripping down the path.

4.99.oldText: "You naughty little thing!" she said. "Why don't you come when you're called?"

4.100.oldText: Bessie's presence, compared with the dark thoughts I'd been brooding over, seemed cheerful—even though, as usual, she was a bit cross. The fact is, after my battle with and victory over Mrs. Reed, I wasn't inclined to worry about the nursemaid's passing irritation. And I was inclined to enjoy her youthful lightness of spirit. I just wrapped my arms around her and said, "Come on, Bessie, don't scold."

4.101.oldText: This was a bolder and more open gesture than I usually allowed myself, and it seemed to please her.

4.102.oldText: "You are a strange child, Miss Jane," she said, looking down at me. "A little wandering, solitary thing. And you're going to school, I suppose?"

4.104.oldText: "And won't you be sorry to leave poor Bessie?"

4.105.oldText: "What does Bessie care about me? She's always scolding me."

4.106.oldText: "Because you're such a strange, frightened, shy little thing. You should be bolder."

4.107.oldText: "What, so I can get knocked around more?"

4.108.oldText: "Nonsense! But you do get pushed around, that's for certain. My mother said, when she came to see me last week, that she wouldn't want one of her own children in your position. Now come inside—I have some good news for you."

4.110.oldText: "Child! What do you mean? What sad eyes you're fixing on me! Well, the Missus and the young ladies and Master John are going out for tea this afternoon, and you can have tea with me. I'll ask the cook to bake you a little cake, and then you can help me go through your drawers—I'll need to pack your trunk soon. The Missus plans to send you away from Gateshead in a day or two, and you can choose which toys you'd like to take with you."

4.111.oldText: "Bessie, you must promise not to scold me anymore before I go."

4.112.oldText: "All right, I will. But you must be very good, and don't be afraid of me. Don't flinch when I happen to speak a bit sharply—it's so annoying."

4.113.oldText: "I don't think I'll ever be afraid of you again, Bessie, because I've gotten used to you, and I'll soon have a whole new set of people to fear."

4.114.oldText: "If you fear them, they'll dislike you."

4.116.oldText: "I don't dislike you, Miss. I think I'm fonder of you than of any of the others."

4.118.oldText: "You sharp little thing! You've got a whole new way of talking. What's made you so bold?"

4.119.oldText: "Well, I'll be leaving soon, and besides—" I was about to say something about what had passed between me and Mrs. Reed, but on second thought I decided it was better to keep quiet about that.

4.121.oldText: "Not at all, Bessie. Actually, right now I'm rather sorry."

4.122.oldText: "Right now! And rather! How coolly my little lady says it! I bet if I asked you for a kiss, you wouldn't give me one—you'd say you'd rather not."

4.123.oldText: "I'll kiss you gladly—bend your head down." Bessie stooped. We hugged each other, and I followed her into the house feeling quite comforted. That afternoon passed in peace and harmony, and in the evening Bessie told me some of her most enchanting stories and sang some of her sweetest songs. Even for me, life had its moments of sunshine.

5.0.oldText: It was barely five o'clock on the morning of January nineteenth when Bessie brought a candle into my closet and found me already up and nearly dressed. I had risen half an hour before she came in and had washed my face and put on my clothes by the light of a half-moon just setting, its rays streaming through the narrow window near my crib. I was to leave Gateshead that day on a coach that passed the lodge gates at six in the morning. Bessie was the only person up yet. She had lit a fire in the nursery and now set about making my breakfast. Few children can eat when excited about a journey, and I was no exception. After Bessie pressed me in vain to take a few spoonfuls of the boiled milk and bread she'd prepared, she wrapped some biscuits in paper and put them in my bag. Then she helped me into my coat and bonnet, wrapped herself in a shawl, and together we left the nursery. As we passed Mrs. Reed's bedroom, she asked, "Will you go in and say good-bye to the Missus?"

5.1.oldText: "No, Bessie. She came to my crib last night when you were down at supper and said I needn't disturb her in the morning, or my cousins either. She told me to remember that she had always been my best friend and to speak well of her and be grateful to her."

5.17.oldText: I remember little of the journey. I only know the day seemed supernaturally long, and that we appeared to travel over hundreds of miles. We passed through several towns. In one very large one, the coach stopped. The horses were changed and the passengers got out to eat. I was carried into an inn where the guard wanted me to have some dinner, but since I had no appetite, he left me in an enormous room with a fireplace at each end, a chandelier hanging from the ceiling, and a small red gallery high on the wall filled with musical instruments. I wandered around this room for a long time, feeling very strange and desperately afraid someone might come in and kidnap me—for I believed in kidnappers, whose exploits featured regularly in Bessie's fireside stories. At last the guard returned. I was packed back into the coach, my protector climbed to his seat, sounded his horn, and off we rattled.

5.40.oldText: Lessons began. The day's prayer was recited, then certain Bible verses, followed by a long reading of Scripture chapters that lasted an hour. By the time that was over, full daylight had come. The tireless bell rang for the fourth time. The classes formed up and marched to another room for breakfast. How glad I was at the prospect of eating! I was nearly faint with hunger, having eaten so little the day before.

5.49.oldText: Order was restored. Within five minutes the confused crowd had arranged itself, and relative quiet replaced the chaos. The senior teachers promptly returned to their posts, but still, everyone seemed to be waiting. Sitting on benches along the sides of the room, the eighty girls sat motionless and upright—a quaint sight, all with plain hair combed back from their faces, not a curl in sight, wearing brown dresses buttoned high with a narrow band at the throat, and small linen pockets (shaped something like a Highland sporran) pinned to the front of their frocks to hold their sewing things. They all wore woolen stockings and country-made shoes with brass buckles. More than twenty of them were full-grown young women, and the uniform suited them badly, giving an air of oddness even to the prettiest.

5.51.oldText: What was happening? I had heard no command given and was confused. Before I could gather my wits, the classes had sat down again. But since all eyes were now turned in one direction, mine followed, and I saw the woman who had received me the night before. She stood at the far end of the long room by the fireplace (there was one at each end) and surveyed the two rows of girls in silence. Miss Miller went up to her, seemed to ask a question, received an answer, returned to her place, and announced—

5.53.oldText: While this was carried out, the lady moved slowly up the room. I must have a strong instinct for reverence, because I still remember the admiring awe with which I watched her. Seen now in full daylight, she was tall, fair, and well-proportioned. Brown eyes with a kindly light and a fine fringe of long lashes softened the whiteness of her broad forehead. Her hair, very dark brown, was arranged in round curls at each temple, in the fashion of the time, when neither smooth bands nor long ringlets were in style. Her dress, also fashionable, was purple cloth trimmed with a sort of Spanish pattern in black velvet. A gold watch (watches were less common then) shone at her waist. Add to this picture refined features, a complexion pale but clear, and a stately bearing, and you will have a fair idea of the appearance of Miss Temple—Maria Temple, as I later saw the name written in a prayer book I was given to carry to church.

5.97.oldText: "The one with red cheeks is Miss Smith. She oversees the needlework and cutting-out—we make our own clothes, our dresses and coats and everything. The small one with black hair is Miss Scatcherd. She teaches history and grammar and hears the second class recitations. And the one who wears a shawl with a handkerchief tied to her side with a yellow ribbon is Madame Pierrot. She comes from Lille in France and teaches French."

5.110.oldText: But at that moment the bell rang for dinner. Everyone went back inside. The smell that now filled the dining hall was scarcely more appetizing than what had greeted us at breakfast. Dinner was served in two huge tin-plated vessels, from which rose a strong steam reeking of rancid fat. The food turned out to be mediocre potatoes and strange shreds of gristly meat, mixed and cooked together. Each girl received a fairly generous plate of it. I ate what I could and wondered if every day's food would be like this.

6.2.oldText: During the course of the day I was enrolled in the fourth class and given regular lessons and tasks. Until now I had only been a spectator at Lowood; I was about to become a participant. At first, being unaccustomed to learning things by heart, the lessons seemed both long and difficult. The constant switching from one subject to another bewildered me, and I was glad when, around three in the afternoon, Miss Smith put a two-yard strip of muslin into my hands along with a needle and thimble and sent me to sit in a quiet corner of the schoolroom to hem it. At that hour most of the others were sewing too. But one class still stood around Miss Scatcherd's chair, reading aloud. Since everything was quiet, I could hear the subject of their lesson and how each girl performed, along with Miss Scatcherd's criticisms or occasional praise. It was English history. Among the readers I noticed my new acquaintance from the garden. At the start of the lesson, she'd been at the top of the class, but for some error of pronunciation or lapse in attention, she was suddenly sent to the very bottom. Even in that lowly position, Miss Scatcherd continued to single her out, constantly directing remarks at her such as—

6.8.oldText: My attention was then diverted by Miss Smith, who asked me to hold a skein of thread while she wound it. As she worked, she chatted with me, asking whether I'd been to school before, whether I could do marking, stitching, knitting, and so on. By the time she dismissed me, I had lost track of Miss Scatcherd. When I returned to my seat, that teacher was just giving an order I didn't catch. But Burns immediately left the class, went into the small inner room where the books were kept, and came back carrying a bundle of twigs tied together at one end. She presented this ominous tool to Miss Scatcherd with a respectful curtsy. Then quietly, without being told, she loosened her pinafore, and the teacher instantly struck her a dozen sharp blows on the neck with the bunch of twigs. Not a tear rose to Burns's eye. And while I froze in my sewing, my fingers trembling with helpless, impotent anger at the spectacle, not a feature of her thoughtful face changed its ordinary expression.

6.29.oldText: "If I were in your place, I'd hate her. I'd fight back. If she hit me with that rod, I'd grab it out of her hand. I'd break it right in front of her."

6.41.oldText: "For you, I'm sure it is. I watched you in class this morning and saw how closely you paid attention. Your mind never seemed to wander while Miss Miller explained the lesson and questioned you. But mine constantly drifts. When I should be listening to Miss Scatcherd and absorbing every word, I often lose the very sound of her voice. I fall into a kind of dream. Sometimes I imagine I'm back in Northumberland, and the noises around me are the bubbling of a little brook that runs through Deepden, near our house. Then when it's my turn to answer, I have to be woken up, and having heard nothing of what was read, I have nothing to say."

6.49.oldText: "There's a great deal of it. You're good to those who are good to you. That's all I ever want to be. If people were always kind and obedient to those who are cruel and unjust, the wicked would have everything their way. They'd never feel afraid, so they'd never change—they'd just get worse and worse. When someone hits us for no reason, we should hit back, and hard—hard enough to teach them never to do it again."

6.63.oldText: "She has been unkind to you, no doubt, because she dislikes your personality—just as Miss Scatcherd dislikes mine. But how precisely you remember everything she has done and said to you! What a remarkably deep impression her injustice has made on your heart! No ill-treatment leaves such a record on my feelings. Wouldn't you be happier if you tried to forget her cruelty, along with the angry emotions it stirred up? Life seems too short to me to be spent nursing grudges or cataloguing wrongs. We are all burdened with faults in this world, every one of us. But the time will come, I trust, when we shed those faults along with our perishable bodies—when sin and degradation fall away with this heavy frame of flesh, and only the spark of the spirit remains, the intangible essence of light and thought, as pure as when it left the Creator to give life to the creature. Where it came from, it will return—perhaps to be given to some being higher than us, perhaps to pass through levels of glory, from the pale human soul brightening to the radiance of an angel! Surely it will never be allowed to degrade from human to demon? No, I cannot believe that. I hold a different belief, one no one ever taught me, one I rarely speak of, but which gives me joy and which I cling to—because it offers hope to everyone. It makes Eternity a place of rest, a great home, not a terror and an abyss. And with this belief, I can clearly separate the wrongdoer from the wrong. I can sincerely forgive the person while hating the act. With this belief, revenge never torments my heart, degradation never crushes me too deeply, injustice never brings me too low. I live in peace, looking toward the end."

6.64.oldText: Helen's head, always drooping a little, sank lower as she finished. I could see she no longer wished to talk to me but would rather be alone with her own thoughts. She wasn't given much time to reflect, though. A monitor—a big, rough girl—came up and exclaimed in a strong northern accent—

7.6.oldText: A small consolation came at teatime: a double ration of bread—a whole slice instead of half—with the glorious addition of a thin scraping of butter. This was the weekly treat we all looked forward to from one Sunday to the next. I usually managed to save some of this feast for myself, but the rest I was invariably forced to give away.

7.7.oldText: Sunday evenings were spent reciting the Church Catechism and chapters five, six, and seven of St. Matthew by heart, and listening to a long sermon read by Miss Miller, whose irrepressible yawns revealed her boredom. A frequent interruption was the spectacle of half a dozen small girls, overwhelmed by sleep, toppling off the fourth bench like so many Eutychuses. The remedy was to push them into the center of the schoolroom and make them stand until the sermon was done. Sometimes their legs gave out and they collapsed in a heap. Then they were propped up with the monitors' tall stools.

7.8.oldText: I haven't mentioned the visits of Mr. Brocklehurst yet. In fact, that gentleman was away from home for most of the first month after my arrival, presumably lingering with his friend the Archdeacon. His absence was a relief to me. I need not explain that I had my own reasons for dreading his appearance. But appear he did, at last.

7.10.oldText: I had my own reasons to be alarmed by this appearance. I remembered all too well Mrs. Reed's treacherous hints about my character, and Mr. Brocklehurst's promise to warn Miss Temple and the teachers about my wicked nature. All along, I had been dreading the fulfillment of that promise—watching daily for the arrival of this man, whose report about my past was going to brand me as a bad child forever. And now here he was.

7.20.oldText: "Madam, allow me a moment. You are aware that my purpose in educating these girls is not to accustom them to luxury and indulgence, but to make them hardy, patient, and self-denying. If some small disappointment of appetite occurs, such as a spoiled meal or an under- or over-cooked dish, the proper response is not to replace it with something finer, thereby pampering the body and undermining the purpose of this institution. Rather, the incident should be used for the spiritual improvement of the pupils, by encouraging them to show courage in the face of temporary deprivation. A brief talk on such occasions would be perfectly appropriate, in which a wise teacher might refer to the sufferings of the early Christians, to the torments of martyrs, to the exhortations of our blessed Lord Himself, calling upon His disciples to take up their cross and follow Him—to His warnings that man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of God—to His divine comfort: 'If you suffer hunger or thirst for My sake, blessed are you.' Oh, madam, when you put bread and cheese instead of burned porridge into these children's mouths, you may indeed feed their worthless bodies, but you little realize how you starve their immortal souls!"

7.28.oldText: Miss Temple passed her handkerchief across her lips, as if smoothing away an involuntary smile. She gave the order, though, and when the first class understood what was being asked, they obeyed. Leaning back on my bench a little, I could see the looks and grimaces they exchanged. It was a pity Mr. Brocklehurst couldn't see them too—he might have realized that however much he controlled the outside of the cup, the inside was far beyond his reach.

7.29.oldText: He examined the backs of their heads for about five minutes, then delivered his verdict. The words fell like a death sentence—

7.48.oldText: A pause—during which I began to steady my shaking nerves and felt that the worst had happened and could no longer be avoided. It must be faced.

7.55.oldText: There I was, raised up high—I, who had said I couldn't bear the shame of standing on my own feet in the middle of the room, was now displayed on a pedestal of disgrace for everyone to see. What I felt, no words can describe. But just as all those feelings rose, choking me and closing my throat, a girl walked past. As she passed, she raised her eyes. What a strange light filled them! What an extraordinary feeling that glance sent through me! How it lifted me up! It was as if a hero had walked past a slave and passed on strength just by being near. I mastered the rising hysteria, raised my head, and stood firm on the stool. Helen Burns asked Miss Smith some trivial question about her work, was scolded for bothering her, returned to her place, and smiled at me as she went by. What a smile! I remember it now, and I know it was the expression of a fine mind and real courage. It lit up her plain features, her thin face, her sunken gray eyes, like the reflection of an angel. Yet at that very moment, Helen Burns wore the "untidy" badge on her arm. Barely an hour ago, I had heard Miss Scatcherd sentence her to a dinner of bread and water the next day for blotting a copying exercise. Such is the imperfect nature of humanity! Such spots exist on the surface of the brightest star—and eyes like Miss Scatcherd's can only see those tiny flaws, blind to the full brilliance of the whole.

8.0.oldText: Before the half hour was up, five o'clock struck. School was dismissed and everyone went to the dining hall for tea. I dared to climb down from the stool. It was deep dusk. I retreated to a corner and sat on the floor. The spell that had sustained me began to dissolve. Reaction set in, and soon the grief that seized me was so overwhelming that I collapsed face-down on the floor. Now I cried. Helen Burns wasn't there. Nothing held me up. Left to myself, I gave in completely, and my tears soaked the floorboards. I had meant to be so good, and to do so much at Lowood—to make friends, earn respect, and win affection. That very morning I had already made real progress: I'd reached the head of my class. Miss Miller had praised me warmly. Miss Temple had smiled with approval and promised to teach me drawing and let me start French if I kept improving for another two months. I had been welcomed by my fellow students—treated as an equal by those my age, and left alone by everyone else. And now here I was, crushed and trampled again. Would I ever be able to rise?

8.12.oldText: "Hush, Jane! You care too much about human love. You are too passionate, too intense. The hand that made you and gave you life has provided you with other resources besides your own frail self, or other frail creatures like you. Beyond this earth and the human race, there is an invisible world and a kingdom of spirits. That world surrounds us, for it is everywhere. Those spirits watch over us, for they are charged with guarding us. And if we were dying in pain and shame, if scorn attacked us from all sides and hatred crushed us, angels would see our suffering, recognize our innocence (if innocent we are, as I know you are of this charge Mr. Brocklehurst has pompously repeated secondhand from Mrs. Reed—for I read a sincere nature in your passionate eyes and clear face), and God waits only for the spirit to leave the body to crown us with a full reward. Why, then, should we ever sink into despair, when life is so soon over and death is so certain a gateway to happiness—to glory?"

8.26.oldText: "No, ma'am. She resented having to do it. But my uncle, as I often heard the servants say, made her promise before he died that she would always keep me."

8.28.oldText: I resolved with all my heart to be careful and fair. After thinking for a few minutes to organize what I had to say, I told her the whole story of my unhappy childhood. Drained by emotion, my language was calmer than it usually was when I talked about that sad subject. And remembering Helen's warnings against giving in to resentment, I put far less bitterness into the account than usual. Restrained and simplified like this, it sounded more believable. I could feel as I went on that Miss Temple fully believed me.

8.48.oldText: We feasted that evening like gods. And the greatest pleasure of the meal was the smile of satisfaction on our hostess's face as she watched us satisfy our starving appetites with the fine food she so generously provided.

8.50.oldText: Miss Temple always carried an air of calm dignity, of refined propriety in her speech, that kept any conversation from becoming too heated or emotional. There was something about her that tempered the pleasure of watching and listening with a restraining sense of awe—and that was what I felt now. But as for Helen Burns, I was struck with amazement.

8.51.oldText: The good food, the warm fire, the presence and kindness of her beloved teacher, or perhaps more than all of these, something in her own extraordinary mind, had awakened her powers.
