They stirred, they caught fire: first glowing in the bright flush of her cheek, which until this hour I had only ever seen pale and bloodless; then shining in the liquid brilliance of her eyes, which had suddenly acquired a beauty more striking than Miss Temple's—a beauty not of fine color or long lashes or sculpted brows, but of meaning, of animation, of radiance. Then her soul sat on her lips, and words flowed from a source I cannot name. Does a fourteen-year-old girl have a heart large enough, strong enough, to hold the swelling spring of pure, passionate eloquence? That was the nature of Helen's speech on that memorable evening. Her spirit seemed to be racing to live as much in a brief span as many live in a long lifetime.

8.57.oldText: The next morning, Miss Scatcherd wrote the word "SLATTERN" in large letters on a piece of cardboard and tied it like a crown of thorns around Helen's large, gentle, intelligent, kind-looking forehead. She wore it all day, patient and uncomplaining, accepting it as a deserved punishment. The moment Miss Scatcherd left after afternoon classes, I ran to Helen, tore it off, and threw it in the fire. The fury that Helen was incapable of feeling had been burning in my soul all day, and tears—hot, large tears—had been scalding my cheeks continuously, because the sight of her quiet resignation caused me unbearable pain.

8.59.oldText: Freed from that crushing weight, I set to work again from that hour, determined to push through every difficulty. I worked hard, and my success matched my effort. My memory, not naturally strong, improved with practice. Exercise sharpened my mind. Within a few weeks I was promoted to a higher class. In less than two months I was allowed to start French and drawing. I learned the first two tenses of the verb etre and sketched my first cottage (whose walls, I should mention, rivaled the leaning tower of Pisa in their slope) on the same day. That night, going to bed, I forgot to fantasize about the imaginary feast of hot roast potatoes or fresh bread and milk that I usually conjured to comfort my hunger. Instead I feasted on visions of ideal drawings, all created by my own hands—freely sketched houses and trees, picturesque rocks and ruins, groups of cattle like something from a Dutch painting, lovely paintings of butterflies hovering over rosebuds, birds picking ripe cherries, wren's nests holding pearl-like eggs wreathed in young ivy. I also pondered whether I would ever be able to translate a certain little French story that Madame Pierrot had shown me that day. That problem was not solved to my satisfaction before I fell sweetly asleep.

8.60.oldText: Solomon was right: "Better a dinner of herbs where love is, than a fattened calf with hatred."

9.0.oldText: But the hardships of Lowood eased. Spring arrived—she was already here, in fact. The frosts of winter had ended, the snows had melted, the cutting winds had softened. My wretched feet, raw and swollen to the point of lameness from the sharp January air, began to heal and recover under the gentler breath of April. The nights and mornings no longer froze the blood in our veins with their arctic cold. We could now enjoy the play hour in the garden. Sometimes on a sunny day it even began to feel pleasant, and a green tinge spread over those brown beds, freshening daily, suggesting that Hope had walked through them in the night and left brighter traces of her steps each morning. Flowers peeked out among the leaves: snowdrops, crocuses, purple auriculas, and golden-eyed pansies. On Thursday afternoons, which were half-holidays, we now went on walks and found still sweeter flowers opening along the roadsides and under the hedges.

9.1.oldText: I also discovered that a great pleasure—a joy bounded only by the horizon—lay beyond the high, spike-topped walls of our garden. This pleasure was the view: noble summits encircling a great green valley, and a bright stream full of dark stones and sparkling eddies. How different this scene had looked when I first saw it under the iron winter sky, frozen stiff, shrouded in snow! When mists as cold as death drifted along those purple peaks and rolled down into the hollows until they merged with the frozen fog of the stream! That stream had been a torrent then, muddy and wild, tearing through the woods and sending a roaring sound through the air, often thickened with driving rain or whirling sleet. And the forest on its banks had shown only ranks of bare skeletons.

9.2.oldText: April gave way to May—a bright, clear May of blue skies, calm sunshine, and soft western breezes that filled its days from start to finish. The greenery surged with new life. Lowood shook out its foliage. It became all green, all flowers. Its great elms, ashes, and oaks, which had been mere skeletons, were restored to majestic life. Woodland plants sprang up thickly in every hollow. Countless varieties of moss filled the shadowy places, and the wild primroses made a strange ground-level sunshine with their pale gold gleam. I have seen them shining in overshadowed spots like scatterings of the gentlest light. All this I enjoyed often and freely, unwatched and nearly alone. For this unusual freedom, there was a cause, which I must now explain.

9.8.oldText: My favorite seat was a smooth, broad stone rising white and dry from the very middle of the stream, reachable only by wading through the water—a feat I accomplished barefoot. The stone was just wide enough for me and one other girl, my chosen companion at that time: Mary Ann Wilson. She was a shrewd, observant person whose company I enjoyed, partly because she was witty and original, and partly because she had a manner that put me at ease. Several years older than me, she knew more of the world and could tell me many things I liked hearing. She satisfied my curiosity. She was also tolerant of my faults, never curbing or censoring anything I said. She had a talent for telling stories; I had a talent for asking questions. So we got along wonderfully together, drawing much entertainment, if not much improvement, from each other's company.

9.9.oldText: And where, meanwhile, was Helen Burns? Why didn't I spend these sweet, free days with her? Had I forgotten her? Or was I so fickle that I'd grown tired of her pure company? Surely the Mary Ann Wilson I've mentioned was inferior to my first friend. She could only tell me amusing stories and trade sharp gossip with me, while Helen, if I've spoken truly of her, was able to give anyone who shared her conversation a taste of far higher things.

9.12.oldText: One evening, in early June, I had stayed out very late with Mary Ann in the woods. We had separated from the others as usual and wandered so far that we got lost and had to ask directions at a lonely cottage where a man and woman lived, tending a herd of half-wild pigs that fed on acorns in the forest. When we got back, the moon had risen. A pony we recognized as the surgeon's was standing at the garden door. Mary Ann remarked that someone must be very ill if Mr. Bates had been sent for at that hour. She went inside. I stayed behind a few minutes to plant some roots I'd dug up in the forest and was afraid would wilt if I left them until morning. That done, I lingered a little longer. The flowers smelled so sweet as the dew fell. It was such a pleasant evening—so calm, so warm. The still-glowing west promised another fine day tomorrow. The moon rose with such majesty in the solemn east. I was noticing all these things and enjoying them as a child does, when a thought entered my mind that had never come before—

9.27.oldText: Down a staircase, through part of the ground floor, opening and closing two doors without a sound, I reached another flight of steps. I climbed them, and directly opposite was Miss Temple's room. A light shone through the keyhole and under the door. A profound stillness filled the hallway. Drawing near, I found the door slightly ajar—probably to let fresh air into the close, sickly room. Unwilling to hesitate, full of urgent impulse, my soul and senses trembling with sharp feeling, I pushed the door open and looked in. My eyes searched for Helen, afraid of what they might find.

9.42.oldText: "I am very happy, Jane. And when you hear that I'm dead, you must promise not to grieve. There is nothing to grieve about. We all must die someday, and the illness that is taking me away is not painful. It's gentle and gradual. My mind is at peace. I leave no one who will miss me much. I have only a father, and he has recently remarried. He won't miss me. By dying young, I'll be spared great suffering. I didn't have the qualities or talents to do well in the world. I would always have been making mistakes."

9.59.oldText: When I woke, it was daylight. An unusual movement roused me. I looked up. I was in someone's arms—the nurse was carrying me through the corridor back to the dormitory. I was not scolded for leaving my bed; people had other things on their minds. No one answered my many questions at the time. But a day or two later I learned that Miss Temple, returning to her room at dawn, had found me in the little crib, my face against Helen Burns's shoulder, my arms around her neck. I was asleep, and Helen was dead.

9.60.oldText: Her grave is in Brocklebridge churchyard. For fifteen years after her death, it was marked only by a grassy mound. But now a gray marble tablet stands there, inscribed with her name and the single word: Resurgam.

10.0.oldText: Until now I have recorded the events of my insignificant life in detail, devoting almost as many chapters to the first ten years as they deserve. But this is not meant to be a full autobiography. I need only call on memory where her answers will hold some interest. So I now skip over a space of eight years almost in silence. A few lines will suffice to keep the thread connected.

10.3.oldText: During those eight years my life was routine but not unhappy, because it was not idle. I had access to an excellent education. A love for some of my subjects, a desire to excel in all, and a deep pleasure in pleasing my teachers—especially those I loved—drove me forward. I made full use of every opportunity. In time I rose to become the top student in the top class. Then I was appointed teacher, a role I filled with enthusiasm for two years. But at the end of that time, something changed.

10.5.oldText: From the day she left, I was no longer the same person. With her went every settled feeling, every connection that had made Lowood something of a home. I had absorbed much from her nature and her habits: more balanced thoughts, more regulated emotions had taken up residence in my mind. I had pledged myself to duty and order. I was quiet. I believed I was content. To others, and usually even to myself, I appeared disciplined and subdued.

10.6.oldText: But fate, in the form of the Reverend Mr. Nasmyth, came between me and Miss Temple. I watched her step into a carriage in her traveling clothes, shortly after the wedding ceremony. I watched the carriage climb the hill and disappear over the top. Then I returned to my room and spent most of the half-day holiday alone.

10.8.oldText: I went to my window, opened it, and looked out. There were the two wings of the building. There was the garden. There were the edges of Lowood. There was the hilly horizon. My eye passed over everything else to rest on the most distant objects—the blue peaks. Those were what I longed to reach. Everything within their boundary of rock and heath felt like a prison. I traced the white road winding around the base of one mountain and vanishing into a pass between two others. How I longed to follow it! I remembered the time I had traveled that very road in a coach, descending that hill at twilight. It felt like a lifetime ago since the day that first brought me to Lowood, and I had never left since. All my holidays had been spent at school. Mrs. Reed had never sent for me. Neither she nor any of her family had ever visited. I had had no contact with the outside world—no letters, no messages. School rules, school duties, school habits and ideas, and voices and faces and phrases and uniforms and preferences and grudges—that was all I knew of existence. And now I felt it wasn't enough. I grew tired of eight years of routine in a single afternoon. I wanted freedom. I gasped for freedom. I said a prayer for freedom, and it seemed to scatter on the faint breeze. I gave that up and made a humbler plea—for change, for stimulus. That prayer too seemed to dissolve into emptiness. "Then," I cried, half-desperate, "grant me at least a new servitude!"

10.33.oldText: I studied the letter for a long time. The handwriting was old-fashioned and a bit shaky, like an elderly lady's. This was reassuring. A private fear had nagged me that in acting on my own, without guidance, I might get into some kind of trouble. Above all, I wanted the outcome to be respectable and proper. Now I felt that an elderly lady was a comforting element. Mrs. Fairfax! I pictured her in a black dress and widow's cap—perhaps a bit stiff, but perfectly civil. A model of elderly English respectability. Thornfield! That was obviously the name of her house. I imagined a neat, orderly place, though I couldn't form a clear picture of it. Millcote, ——shire—I refreshed my memory of the map of England. Yes, I found it. The county was seventy miles closer to London than the remote region where I lived now. That appealed to me. I longed to go somewhere with life and movement. Millcote was a large manufacturing town on the banks of a river—a busy place, no doubt. All the better. It would be a complete change, at least. Not that I was particularly attracted to the idea of factory chimneys and smoke—"but," I told myself, "Thornfield is probably a good distance from the town."

10.45.oldText: "That's my little boy," said Bessie proudly.

10.49.oldText: "I live at the lodge. The old porter has left."

10.55.oldText: "Oh, he's not doing as well as his mama hoped. He went to university and failed—got expelled, I think they call it. Then his uncles wanted him to become a lawyer, but he's such a wild young man that I don't think they'll make much of him."

10.82.oldText: "Yes. He only stayed a few minutes. The Missus was very cold to him. Afterward she called him a 'sneaky tradesman.' My Robert thinks he was a wine merchant."

11.1.oldText: Reader, though I look comfortably settled, my mind is far from calm. I expected someone to meet me when the coach stopped here. I looked around anxiously as I stepped down, expecting to hear my name called and to see a carriage waiting to take me to Thornfield. There was nothing. When I asked a waiter if anyone had inquired for a Miss Eyre, the answer was no. So I had no choice but to ask for a private room, and here I sit waiting, while all kinds of doubts and fears trouble my thoughts.

11.26.oldText: "Oh, it's no trouble. I'm sure your hands are nearly frozen. Leah, make a little hot toddy and cut a sandwich or two. Here are the keys to the storeroom."

11.43.oldText: I thanked her for the thoughtful choice, and since I truly was worn out from the journey, I said I was ready to go up. She took her candle, and I followed her out of the room. First she checked that the front door was locked, then she led me upstairs. The steps and banisters were oak. The staircase window was tall and latticed. Both the window and the long gallery where the bedroom doors opened looked as though they belonged in a church rather than a house. A cold, vault-like air filled the stairs and gallery, creating a bleak sense of space and solitude. I was glad, when finally shown into my room, to find it small and furnished in a plain, modern style.

11.44.oldText: After Mrs. Fairfax bid me a kind good night, I locked my door and looked around the room at a leisurely pace. The cheerful appearance of my little room gradually erased the eerie impression left by that wide hall, that dark and cavernous staircase, and that long, cold gallery. I remembered that after a day of physical exhaustion and mental worry, I was at last in a safe harbor. Gratitude swelled my heart. I knelt by the bedside and gave thanks where thanks were due, not forgetting to ask for guidance on the road ahead, and for the strength to deserve the kindness so freely offered before I had earned it. My bed held no thorns that night, and my solitary room held no fears. Weary and content at once, I slept quickly and deeply. When I woke, it was broad daylight.

11.46.oldText: I got up and dressed with care. I was obliged to dress plainly—every article of clothing I owned was made with extreme simplicity—but I was by nature careful about my appearance. It wasn't my habit to be careless about how I looked or the impression I made. On the contrary, I always wanted to look as well as I could, and to please as much as my lack of beauty would allow. I sometimes regretted that I wasn't prettier. I sometimes wished for rosy cheeks, a straight nose, and a small, shapely mouth. I wished I were tall, stately, and well-proportioned. I felt it was a misfortune to be so small, so pale, and to have such irregular, striking features. And why did I have these wishes and regrets? It would be hard to say—I couldn't clearly explain it to myself at the time, though I had a reason, a logical, natural one. In any case, once I had brushed my hair very smooth and put on my black dress—which, Quaker-like as it was, at least had the virtue of fitting perfectly—and straightened my clean white collar, I thought I would look respectable enough for Mrs. Fairfax, and that my new pupil wouldn't shrink from me in horror. Having opened my window and checked that everything on the dressing table was neat and tidy, I ventured out.

11.61.oldText: "C'est la ma gouvernante!" she said, pointing at me and speaking to her nurse, who answered—

11.72.oldText: "Adele," I asked, "who did you live with when you were in that pretty, clean town you mentioned?"

11.76.oldText: Adele sang the little song tunefully enough, with the innocence of her age. When she finished, she hopped off my knee and said, "Now, Mademoiselle, I will recite some poetry for you."

11.81.oldText: "With Madame Frederic and her husband. She looked after me, but she's no relation. I think she's poor, because her house wasn't as nice as Mama's. I wasn't there long. Mr. Rochester asked if I'd like to go and live with him in England, and I said yes, because I knew Mr. Rochester from before I knew Madame Frederic, and he was always kind to me and gave me pretty dresses and toys. But he hasn't kept his word—he brought me to England and then went away again, and I never see him."

11.82.oldText: After breakfast, Adele and I went to the library, which Mr. Rochester had designated as the schoolroom. Most of the books were locked behind glass doors, but one bookcase stood open, containing all the elementary works needed, plus several volumes of lighter reading—poetry, biography, travel books, a few novels, and so on. He had probably decided that these were all a governess would need for her own reading, and indeed they more than satisfied me for now. Compared to the meager pickings I had occasionally managed at Lowood, they seemed a rich harvest of entertainment and knowledge. The room also held a cabinet piano, brand new and of excellent quality, as well as an easel for painting and a pair of globes.

11.83.oldText: I found my pupil cooperative enough, though reluctant to concentrate. She hadn't been accustomed to any kind of regular work. I felt it would be unwise to push her too hard at first. So after talking to her a great deal and getting her to learn a little, when mid-morning came I let her go back to her nurse. I then planned to spend the time before dinner making some sketches for her to use.

11.84.oldText: As I was going upstairs to fetch my portfolio and pencils, Mrs. Fairfax called to me. "Your morning lessons are finished now, I suppose?" She was in a room whose folding doors stood open. I stepped in when she spoke. It was a large, stately room with purple chairs and curtains, a Turkish carpet, walnut-paneled walls, one magnificent window rich in stained glass, and a high, beautifully molded ceiling. Mrs. Fairfax was dusting some vases of fine purple stone that stood on a sideboard.

11.101.oldText: When we left the dining room, she offered to show me the rest of the house. I followed her up and down, admiring everything. It was all well arranged and handsome. The large front bedrooms struck me as especially grand. And some of the third-floor rooms, though dark and low-ceilinged, were fascinating in their antiquity. Furniture once used in the main rooms had been moved up here as fashions changed. In the dim light coming through narrow windows, I saw bedsteads a hundred years old, oak and walnut chests carved with palm branches and cherubs' heads that looked like miniature arks, rows of venerable high-backed chairs, and even older stools whose cushions still showed traces of half-faded embroidery, worked by hands that had been dust for two generations. These relics gave the third floor of Thornfield Hall the feel of a museum of the past—a shrine of memory. I liked the hush, the gloom, the quaintness of these rooms in daylight. But I certainly didn't want to sleep in one of those wide, heavy beds—some enclosed behind oak doors, others curtained with ancient English tapestries crusted with thick needlework depicting strange flowers, even stranger birds, and the strangest human figures. All of which would have looked eerie indeed in pale moonlight.

11.109.oldText: "Up to the roof—would you like to come and see the view?" I followed her up a very narrow staircase to the attics, then up a ladder and through a trapdoor to the roof. I was now level with the rooks' colony and could peer into their nests. Leaning over the battlements and looking far down, I surveyed the grounds spread out like a map: the bright, velvety lawn closely circling the gray base of the house; the park-like field dotted with ancient trees; the woods, brown and dry, divided by a path more green with moss than the trees were with leaves; the church at the gates; the road; the peaceful hills—all basking in the autumn sunshine. The horizon was bounded by a clear sky, blue marbled with pearly white. Nothing in the scene was extraordinary, but everything was lovely. When I turned away and went back through the trapdoor, I could barely see my way down the ladder. The attic seemed pitch-black compared to the arch of blue sky I'd been gazing at, and the sunlit scene of grove, meadow, and green hills over which the hall presided.

11.113.oldText: "One of the servants, most likely," she answered. "Probably Grace Poole."

11.118.oldText: I truly hadn't expected anyone called Grace to appear, because the laugh had been as eerie and unnatural as any I'd ever heard. If it hadn't been broad noon, with nothing ghostly about the circumstances—if neither the place nor the time encouraged fear—I would have been superstitious enough to be frightened. But what happened next showed me I was foolish to feel even surprise.

11.119.oldText: The nearest door opened and a servant came out—a woman of about thirty-five, with a stocky, square build, red hair, and a hard, plain face. A less romantic or less ghostly apparition could hardly be imagined.

11.122.oldText: The conversation turned to Adele and continued until we reached the bright, cheerful lower floor. Adele came running to meet us in the hall, calling out—

11.123.oldText: "Mesdames, vous etes servies!" adding, "J'ai bien faim, moi!"

12.1.oldText: This, as an aside, will strike some as cold language—people who hold solemn beliefs about the angelic nature of children and the duty of their teachers to worship them with blind devotion. But I am not writing to flatter parental vanity, to echo platitudes, or to prop up pretense. I am simply telling the truth. I felt a genuine concern for Adele's welfare and progress, and a quiet liking for the child herself—just as I felt toward Mrs. Fairfax a gratitude for her kindness and a pleasure in her company proportional to the calm regard she had for me and the moderation of her mind and character.

12.2.oldText: Anyone who wants to can blame me when I add that, now and then, when I walked alone in the grounds, or went down to the gates and looked along the road, or when, while Adele played with her nurse and Mrs. Fairfax made preserves in the storeroom, I climbed the three staircases, pushed open the attic trapdoor, and stood on the roof looking out over the secluded fields, the hills, and the dim horizon—that then I longed for a power of vision that could reach beyond that boundary, that could see the busy world, the towns, the regions full of life I had heard of but never witnessed. That then I craved more practical experience than I possessed, more contact with my fellow human beings, more acquaintance with the variety of human character than was within my reach here. I valued what was good in Mrs. Fairfax and in Adele, but I believed in the existence of other, more vivid kinds of goodness, and I wanted to see what I believed in.

12.7.oldText: October, November, and December passed. One afternoon in January, Mrs. Fairfax had requested a holiday for Adele because she had a cold. Since Adele backed the request with an enthusiasm that reminded me how precious holidays had been in my own childhood, I agreed, thinking it right to be flexible. It was a fine, calm day, though very cold. I was tired of sitting still in the library all morning. Mrs. Fairfax had just written a letter that needed posting, so I put on my bonnet and cloak and volunteered to carry it to Hay—a pleasant two-mile walk on a winter afternoon. After settling Adele comfortably in her little chair by Mrs. Fairfax's fire, giving her the best wax doll (which I usually kept wrapped in silver paper in a drawer) and a storybook for variety, and answering her "Come back soon, my dear friend, my darling Mademoiselle Jeannette" with a kiss, I set out.

12.8.oldText: The ground was hard, the air was still, the road was deserted. I walked fast until I was warm, then slowed to enjoy and savor the particular pleasure the hour and the setting offered me. It was three o'clock. The church bell tolled as I passed beneath the tower. The charm of the hour lay in the approaching dusk, in the low, pale sun sliding down the sky. I was a mile from Thornfield, in a lane known for wild roses in summer, for nuts and blackberries in autumn, and even now adorned with a few bright red hips and haws. But its greatest winter beauty was its total solitude and bare stillness. If any breeze stirred, it made no sound here—there was no holly, no evergreen to rustle. The stripped hawthorn and hazel bushes were as motionless as the white, worn stones that paved the middle of the path. On either side, far and wide, there were only fields with no grazing cattle, and the small brown birds that occasionally stirred in the hedge looked like single russet leaves that had forgotten to fall.

12.11.oldText: A harsh noise broke through these delicate sounds—suddenly, clearly: a definite tramp, tramp, a metallic clattering that drowned out the soft whispering, the way a solid crag or the rough trunk of a great oak in the foreground of a painting blots out the pale distance of blue hills, sunlit horizon, and melting clouds.

12.12.oldText: The noise was on the path: a horse was approaching. The bends of the lane still hid it, but it was coming closer. I was just leaving the stile, but since the path was narrow, I sat back down to let it pass. In those days I was young, and all kinds of bright and dark fancies filled my mind. Among them were memories of nursery tales, and now that I was older, they had a force and vividness that childhood could never have given them. As this horse drew near and I watched for it to appear through the dusk, I remembered certain of Bessie's stories featuring a North of England spirit called a Gytrash—which, in the form of a horse, mule, or large dog, haunted lonely roads and sometimes appeared to travelers caught out after dark, as this horse was now appearing to me.

12.37.oldText: "You're not a servant at the hall, obviously. You are—" He stopped, running his eye over my clothes, which as usual were plain: a black wool cloak, a black bonnet—neither fine enough for a lady's maid. He seemed puzzled about what I was. I helped him.

12.46.oldText: I was terrified of its stamping front hooves.

12.47.oldText: "I see," he said, "the mountain won't come to Mohammed, so all you can do is help Mohammed get to the mountain. I'll have to ask you to come here."

12.48.oldText: I came. "Excuse me," he went on, "necessity forces me to make use of you." He laid a heavy hand on my shoulder, and leaning on me with considerable weight, limped to his horse. Once he had the bridle, he mastered the animal immediately and swung up into the saddle, grimacing at the pain it caused his sprain.

12.49.oldText: "Now," he said, releasing his lip from a hard bite, "just hand me my riding crop. It's there under the hedge."

12.50.oldText: I found it and brought it to him.

12.51.oldText: "Thank you. Now hurry with that letter to Hay, and get back as fast as you can."

12.52.oldText: A touch of his spurred heel made the horse start, rear, and then bound away. The dog raced after them. All three vanished—

12.53.oldText: "Like heath that, in the wilderness, the wild wind whirls away."

12.54.oldText: I picked up my muff and walked on. The incident had happened and was gone. It was nothing special, really—no drama, no romance, no particular interest. Yet it marked a change in one single hour of a monotonous life. My help had been needed and asked for. I had given it. I was pleased to have done something—trivial and fleeting as it was, it had been an act, and I was tired of a purely passive existence. The new face, too, was like a new picture added to the gallery of my memory, and it was unlike any of the others hanging there. First, because it was male. And second, because it was dark, strong, and stern. I still had it before me when I reached Hay and slipped the letter into the post office. I saw it as I walked fast downhill all the way home. When I reached the stile, I paused, looked around, and listened, half-expecting to hear a horse's hooves ring on the path again, and to see a cloaked rider and a Gytrash-like Newfoundland dog appear once more. I saw only the hedge and a pollard willow before me, standing still and straight against the moonlight. I heard only the faintest breath of wind stirring fitfully among the trees around Thornfield, a mile away. And when I glanced toward the sound, my eye caught a light kindling in a window of the hall. It reminded me I was late, and I hurried on.

12.55.oldText: I didn't want to go back inside Thornfield. To cross its threshold was to return to stagnation. To pass through the silent hall, climb the dark staircase, find my lonely little room, and then sit with tranquil Mrs. Fairfax through the long winter evening—hers the only company—was to completely extinguish the faint excitement my walk had kindled. To slip back into the invisible chains of a routine too still and too unchanging—a life whose very privileges of safety and ease I was becoming unable to appreciate. What good it would have done me then to be tossed in the storms of an uncertain, struggling life, to learn from rough and bitter experience to long for the calm I now found stifling! Yes—exactly as much good as it does a man tired of sitting in a too-comfortable chair to take a long walk. And the wish to move was just as natural in my circumstances as it would be in his.

12.56.oldText: I lingered at the gates. I lingered on the lawn. I paced back and forth on the path. The shutters of the glass door were closed; I couldn't see inside. Both my eyes and my spirit seemed pulled away from the gloomy house—from the gray hollow of dark, lifeless rooms it seemed to be—toward the sky spread before me: a blue sea without a cloud. The moon climbing in solemn procession, her globe seeming to look upward as she left the hilltops far below and aspired to the zenith, midnight-dark in its fathomless depth and limitless distance. And the trembling stars that followed in her path—they made my heart tremble and my blood glow when I gazed at them. Small things call us back to earth. The clock struck in the hall. That was enough. I turned from moon and stars, opened a side door, and went in.

12.57.oldText: The hall was neither dark nor fully lit—only the high-hung bronze lamp illuminated it, plus a warm glow that suffused both the hall and the lower steps of the oak staircase. This ruddy light came from the great dining room, whose double doors stood open, showing a cheerful fire in the grate gleaming on the marble hearth and brass fire tools and casting the most pleasant radiance over the purple curtains and polished furniture. It also revealed a group near the mantelpiece. I had barely glimpsed them, and barely registered a cheerful mix of voices among which I thought I heard Adele's, when the door was closed.

12.58.oldText: I hurried to Mrs. Fairfax's room. There was a fire there too, but no candle and no Mrs. Fairfax. Instead, sitting bolt upright on the rug and gazing solemnly at the flames, I saw a great black and white long-haired dog—exactly like the Gytrash from the lane. It was so like it that I walked up and said "Pilot." The creature got up, came to me, and sniffed my hand. I petted him and he wagged his huge tail. But he looked like an eerie companion to be left alone with, and I couldn't figure out where he'd come from. I rang the bell, wanting a candle and wanting an explanation for this visitor. Leah came in.

12.62.oldText: "With the master—Mr. Rochester. He's just arrived."

12.63.oldText: "Really! And is Mrs. Fairfax with him?"

12.64.oldText: "Yes, and Miss Adele. They're in the dining room. John has gone for the surgeon—the master has had an accident. His horse fell and his ankle is sprained."

12.65.oldText: "Did the horse fall on Hay Lane?"

12.66.oldText: "Yes, coming downhill. It slipped on the ice."

12.67.oldText: "Ah! Bring me a candle, will you, Leah?"

12.68.oldText: Leah brought it. She came in followed by Mrs. Fairfax, who repeated the news, adding that Mr. Carter the surgeon had arrived and was now with Mr. Rochester. Then she hurried out to arrange tea, and I went upstairs to take off my outdoor things.

13.13.oldText: Two wax candles stood lit on the table and two on the mantelpiece. Basking in the light and heat of a magnificent fire lay Pilot, with Adèle kneeling beside him. Half reclined on a couch was Mr. Rochester, his foot propped on a cushion. He was watching Adèle and the dog, the firelight full on his face. I recognized my traveller with his broad, dark eyebrows, his square forehead made squarer by the straight sweep of his black hair. I recognized his decisive nose, more notable for character than beauty, his full nostrils suggesting a quick temper, his stern mouth, chin, and jaw—yes, all three were very stern, no mistake about it. His build, now free of its cloak, matched the squareness of his features. I suppose it was a good figure in the athletic sense—broad-chested and lean-flanked, though neither tall nor graceful.

13.20.oldText: "Will you hand Mr. Rochester his cup?" Mrs. Fairfax said to me. "Adèle might spill it."

13.29.oldText: "Oh, don't retreat into false modesty! I have examined Adèle and find you have taken great pains with her. She is not bright, she has no talents; yet in a short time she has made real improvement."

13.45.oldText: "For the fairies. It was a perfect moonlit evening for them. Did I break through one of your rings, and you spread that cursed ice on the road?"

13.46.oldText: I shook my head. "The fairies all left England a hundred years ago," I said, speaking as seriously as he had. "And not even in Hay Lane, or the fields around it, could you find a trace of them. I don't think summer, harvest, or winter moon will ever shine on their revels again."

13.74.oldText: "And was that the worst of his offences?" demanded Mr. Rochester.

13.91.oldText: "Bring it to the table," he said, and I wheeled it to his couch. Adèle and Mrs. Fairfax came closer to see the pictures.

13.106.oldText: The pictures were watercolours. The first showed clouds, low and dark, rolling over a swollen sea. Everything was in shadow—distance and foreground alike, for there was no land. One gleam of light fell on a half-submerged mast, on which perched a cormorant, dark and large, its wings flecked with foam. Its beak held a gold bracelet set with gems, which I had painted in the most brilliant tints my palette could yield, with as much glittering detail as my brush could manage. Below the bird and mast, a drowned body was visible through the green water—a fair arm the only limb clearly seen, from which the bracelet had been washed or torn.

13.107.oldText: The second picture showed only the dim peak of a hill in the foreground, with grass and leaves slanting as if blown by a breeze. Beyond and above spread a vast sky, dark blue as at twilight. Rising into the sky was a woman's shape, visible to the bust, painted in tints as dusky and soft as I could blend. The shadowy forehead was crowned with a star; the features below were seen as through a veil of vapour; the eyes shone dark and wild; the hair streamed like a cloud torn by storm or lightning. On the neck lay a pale glow like moonlight; the same faint gleam touched the trail of thin clouds from which this vision of the Evening Star rose and bowed.

13.108.oldText: The third showed the peak of an iceberg piercing a polar winter sky. A line of northern lights raised their dim lances along the horizon. In the foreground, dwarfing these into distance, rose a colossal head tilted toward the iceberg and resting against it. Two thin hands, clasped beneath the forehead and propping it up, drew a black veil over the lower features. Only a bloodless brow, white as bone, and an eye—hollow and fixed, blank except for the glassiness of despair—were visible. Above the temples, amid folds of black cloth as vague and shapeless as cloud, gleamed a ring of white flame studded with darker, more ominous sparks. This pale crescent was "the likeness of a kingly crown;" what it crowned was "the shape which shape had none."

13.115.oldText: "Not completely: you've caught the shadow of your thought, but no more, probably. You lacked enough of the artist's skill and knowledge to give it full life. Yet the drawings are, for a schoolgirl, extraordinary. As for the ideas behind them—they are otherworldly. Those eyes in the Evening Star you must have seen in a dream. How did you make them look so clear yet not at all bright? The planet above dims their light. And what meaning lies in their solemn depth? And who taught you to paint wind? There's a fierce gale in that sky and on that hilltop. Where did you see Latmos? For that is Latmos. There—put the drawings away!"

13.118.oldText: Adèle went to kiss him before leaving the room. He endured the embrace but barely seemed to enjoy it more than Pilot would have—and perhaps less.

14.8.oldText: "Ah! Well, come forward; sit down here." He drew a chair near his own. "I am not fond of children's chatter," he continued. "As the old bachelor I am, I have no pleasant associations with their prattle. It would be intolerable to spend an entire evening alone with a child. Don't pull that chair farther away, Miss Eyre; sit down exactly where I placed it—if you please, that is. Confound these courtesies! I keep forgetting them. Nor do I particularly enjoy the company of simple-minded elderly ladies. By the way, I must be mindful of mine; it won't do to neglect her. She is a Fairfax, or married to one, and blood is said to be thicker than water."

14.19.oldText: "Ah! My word! There is something unusual about you," he said. "You have the air of a little nun—quaint, quiet, serious, and simple, sitting there with your hands folded and your eyes generally cast down to the carpet (except, that is, when they are aimed piercingly at my face, as just now). And when someone asks you a question or makes a remark you must reply to, you come out with a blunt answer that is, if not exactly rude, at least brusque. What do you mean by it?"

14.24.oldText: He lifted the dark waves of hair that lay across his brow, revealing a solid enough mass of intellectual development, but a notable deficiency where the gentle curve of benevolence should have risen.

14.27.oldText: "There again! Another jab of the penknife when she pretended to pat my head. And that is because I said I did not like the company of children and old women (said quietly!). No, young lady, I am not a general philanthropist; but I do have a conscience"—he pointed to the bumps on his skull said to indicate that quality, which were, fortunately for him, quite prominent, giving a marked breadth to the upper part of his head—"and besides, I once had a kind of rough tenderness of heart. When I was your age, I was a feeling sort of fellow, partial to the young, the unprotected, and the unlucky. But Fortune has knocked me around since then: she has even kneaded me with her knuckles, and now I flatter myself I am hard and tough as a rubber ball—with a crack or two still open, though, and one sensitive point in the middle. Yes—does that leave hope for me?"

14.32.oldText: With this announcement he rose from his chair and stood leaning his arm on the marble mantelpiece. In that posture his build was plainly visible as well as his face—the unusual breadth of his chest, almost out of proportion with the length of his limbs. I am sure most people would have called him an ugly man. Yet there was so much unconscious pride in his bearing, so much ease in his manner, such complete indifference to his own appearance, so haughty a faith in the power of other qualities—inherent or acquired—to make up for the lack of mere good looks, that in watching him, you inevitably shared his indifference and, even in some blind, instinctive way, trusted his confidence.

14.41.oldText: "Stubborn?" he said. "And irritated. Ah! That is consistent. I put my request in an absurd, almost rude form. Miss Eyre, I apologize. The fact is, once and for all, I don't wish to treat you as an inferior. That is"—he corrected himself—"I claim only the advantage that must come from twenty years' difference in age and a century's advance in experience. This is fair, et j'y tiens, as Adèle would say. And it is by virtue of this advantage, and this alone, that I ask you to be good enough to talk to me a little now and distract my thoughts, which are raw from dwelling on one point—festering like a rusty nail."

14.44.oldText: "Then, first of all, do you agree that I have some right to be a little commanding, abrupt, perhaps demanding, on the grounds I stated—namely, that I am old enough to be your father, and that I have fought through a wide experience with many men of many nations and roamed over half the globe, while you have lived quietly with one group of people in one house?"

14.47.oldText: "I don't think, sir, that you have a right to command me merely because you are older than I, or because you have seen more of the world. Your claim to authority depends on the use you have made of your time and experience."

14.48.oldText: "Humph! Bluntly spoken. But I won't accept that, seeing as it would never suit my case—I have made a poor, not to say bad, use of both advantages. Setting authority aside, then, you must still agree to take my orders now and then without being stung or hurt by the commanding tone. Will you?"

14.55.oldText: "I am sure, sir, I would never mistake informality for rudeness. One I rather like; the other, no one with any self-respect would endure, even for a salary."

14.56.oldText: "Nonsense! Most people with self-respect will endure anything for a salary. So keep your opinions to yourself and don't venture into generalizations you are wholly ignorant about. However, I mentally shake your hand for that answer, inaccurate as it is—as much for the way it was said as for its substance. The manner was frank and sincere; one does not often encounter such a manner. No, on the contrary, affectation, or coldness, or stupid, thick-headed misunderstanding of one's meaning are the usual rewards of candour. Not three in three thousand inexperienced school-girl governesses would have answered me as you just did. But I don't mean to flatter you. If you are made from a different mould than the majority, it is no credit to you—Nature did it. And after all, I go too fast in my conclusions. For all I know yet, you may be no better than the rest; you may have intolerable flaws to offset your few good points."

14.58.oldText: "Yes, yes, you are right," he said. "I have plenty of faults of my own—I know it, and I don't wish to minimize them. God knows I don't need to be harsh about other people when I have so much to answer for myself. I have a past—a series of actions, a pattern of living—that I could contemplate in my own breast, which might well redirect my sneers and judgments from my neighbours to myself. I was set on a wrong course—or rather, like other wrongdoers, I prefer to blame bad luck and circumstances—I was pushed onto a wrong path at the age of twenty-one, and I have never found my way back since. But I might have been very different. I might have been as good as you—wiser—nearly as untainted. I envy you your peace of mind, your clean conscience, your unspoiled memory. Little girl, a memory without stain or corruption must be an exquisite treasure—an inexhaustible source of pure refreshment. Isn't it?"

14.60.oldText: "Perfectly clear then—clean and healthy. No flood of foul water had turned it into a poisoned pool. I was your equal at eighteen—quite your equal. Nature meant me to be, on the whole, a good man, Miss Eyre—one of the better kind. And you see I am not. You would say you don't see it; at least I flatter myself I read that much in your eye (beware, by the way, what you express with that eye of yours; I am quick at reading its language). Then take my word for it—I am not a villain. You are not to think that, not to attribute any such deep wickedness to me. But, owing I truly believe to circumstances rather than my natural inclination, I am an ordinary, commonplace sinner, worn out by all the petty vices that the rich and worthless use to pass the time. Does it surprise you that I confess this to you? Know that in the course of your future life you will often find yourself elected the unwilling keeper of other people's secrets. They will instinctively discover, as I have done, that it is not your way to talk about yourself, but to listen while others speak of themselves. They will feel, too, that you listen without malicious scorn at their indiscretion, but with a kind of natural sympathy—all the more comforting because it is so quietly given."

14.62.oldText: "I know it well; and so I speak almost as freely as if I were writing my thoughts in a diary. You would say I should have been stronger than my circumstances; and I should have—I should have. But I was not. When fate wronged me, I lacked the wisdom to stay calm. I turned desperate; then I degenerated. Now, when some shallow fool disgusts me with his cheap depravity, I cannot flatter myself that I am better than he is. I am forced to admit that he and I are on the same level. I wish I had stood firm—God knows I do! Dread remorse when you are tempted to stray, Miss Eyre. Remorse is the poison of life."

14.78.oldText: "Well thought; well said, Miss Eyre. And at this very moment, I am paving the road to hell with good intentions."

14.80.oldText: "I am laying down intentions I believe to be as solid as flint. My companions and pursuits shall certainly be different than they have been."

14.91.oldText: "The power of declaring any strange, unsanctioned course of action to be right."

14.100.oldText: "If you did, you would say it in such a grave, quiet way that I'd mistake it for wisdom. Do you never laugh, Miss Eyre? Don't bother answering—I can see you rarely laugh. But you can laugh very merrily: believe me, you are not naturally solemn any more than I am naturally wicked. The Lowood restraint still clings to you, controlling your features, muffling your voice, restricting your movements. In the presence of a man—brother, father, master, whatever you wish to call me—you are afraid to smile too freely, speak too openly, or move too easily. But in time, I think you will learn to be natural with me, as I find it impossible to be conventional with you. And then your looks and movements will have more life and variety than they dare to show now. I see, at intervals, the glance of a strange sort of bird through the bars of a cage: a vivid, restless, resolute captive is in there; if it were free, it would soar to the clouds. You are still set on going?"

14.102.oldText: "Never mind—wait a moment. Adèle is not ready for bed yet. My position, Miss Eyre, with my back to the fire and my face to the room, gives me a good view. While talking to you, I have also been watching Adèle from time to time (I have my own reasons for finding her a curious study—reasons I may, indeed shall, share with you someday). She pulled from her box, about ten minutes ago, a little pink silk dress. Rapture lit her face as she unfolded it. Vanity runs in her blood, blends with her mind, and seasons her very bones. 'Il faut que je l'essaie!' she cried, 'et à l'instant même!' and she rushed from the room. She is now with Sophie, being dressed up. In a few minutes she will come back, and I know what I shall see—a miniature of Céline Varens, as she used to appear on stage at the rise of—but never mind that. My tenderest feelings are about to receive a shock—such is my feeling. Stay now and see whether it comes true."

14.107.oldText: "Pre-cise-ly!" was the answer. "And 'just like that,' she charmed my English gold out of my British pockets. I have been green, too, Miss Eyre—oh, green as grass: no fresher shade colours you now than once coloured me. My Spring is gone, however, but it has left me this French flower on my hands, which, in some moods, I would gladly be rid of. Not valuing now the root it sprang from—having found it was a sort that nothing but gold dust could nourish—I have only half a fondness for the blossom, especially when it looks as artificial as it does just now. I keep it and raise it on the Roman Catholic principle of atoning for many sins, great or small, by one good deed. I'll explain all this someday. Goodnight."

15.2.oldText: "And, Miss Eyre, I was so flattered by this French nymph's preference for her British gnome that I set her up in a hotel, gave her a full household of servants, a carriage, cashmeres, diamonds, lace, and the rest. In short, I began the standard process of ruining myself, like any other lovesick fool. I lacked, it seems, the originality to blaze a new trail to shame and destruction, and walked the old path with stupid precision, never straying an inch from the beaten centre. I had—as I deserved—the fate of all such fools. Happening to call one evening when Céline wasn't expecting me, I found her out. But it was a warm night and I was tired from wandering through Paris, so I sat down in her boudoir, happy to breathe the air she had so recently inhabited. No—I exaggerate. I never believed there was anything sacred about her. It was more like a lingering perfume she had left—a scent of musk and amber rather than the fragrance of holiness. I was just beginning to choke on the fumes of hothouse flowers and sprinkled essences when I thought to open the window and step out onto the balcony. It was moonlit and gaslit besides, and very still and calm. The balcony had a chair or two; I sat down and took out a cigar—I will take one now, if you'll excuse me."

15.4.oldText: "I liked sweets too in those days, Miss Eyre, and I was crunching chocolate bonbons and smoking by turns, watching the carriages roll along the fashionable streets toward the nearby opera house, when in an elegant closed carriage drawn by a beautiful pair of English horses, clearly visible in the brilliant city night, I recognized the carriage I had given Céline. She was returning: of course my heart pounded against the iron railing I leaned on. The carriage stopped, as I expected, at the hotel door; my flame (the very word for an opera mistress) stepped out. Though wrapped in a cloak—an unnecessary covering on so warm a June evening—I knew her instantly by her little foot, visible beneath the hem of her dress as she hopped from the carriage step. Leaning over the balcony, I was about to murmur 'Mon ange'—in a tone, naturally, meant only for the ears of love—when a figure jumped from the carriage after her, also cloaked. But that was a spurred heel that rang on the pavement, and that was a hatted head that now passed under the arched entrance of the hotel.

15.7.oldText: He clenched his teeth and stopped. He halted mid-step and struck his boot against the hard ground. Some hated thought seemed to grip him and hold him so tightly he could not move forward.

15.8.oldText: We were climbing the avenue when he paused like this; the hall was before us. Lifting his eyes to its battlements, he cast over them a look such as I had never seen before or since. Pain, shame, fury, disgust, loathing, seemed to wage a trembling war in the wide pupil beneath his dark eyebrow. Fierce was the struggle for dominance; but another feeling rose and conquered: something hard and cynical, self-willed and resolute. It settled his passion and turned his face to stone. He went on—

15.11.oldText: Adèle ran up to him with her shuttlecock. "Away!" he cried harshly. "Keep your distance, child; or go in to Sophie!" Then, continuing his walk in silence, I ventured to bring him back to the point from which he had abruptly wandered—

15.13.oldText: I half expected a rebuff for this poorly timed question, but on the contrary, shaking off his scowling reverie, he turned his eyes toward me and the shadow seemed to lift from his brow. "Oh, I had forgotten Céline! Well, to continue. When I saw my darling arrive accompanied by a gentleman, I seemed to hear a hiss, and the green snake of jealousy, rising on undulating coils from the moonlit balcony, slid inside my waistcoat and in two minutes had eaten its way to my heart. Strange!" he exclaimed, suddenly starting off on another tangent. "Strange that I should choose you as my confidante for all this, young lady—passing strange that you should sit and listen so calmly, as if it were the most natural thing in the world for a man like me to tell stories of his former mistresses to a quiet, inexperienced girl like you! But the last oddity explains the first, as I hinted before: you, with your gravity, thoughtfulness, and caution, were made to be the keeper of secrets. Besides, I know the kind of mind I have opened a channel to: I know it will not be infected. It is a peculiar mind—a unique one. Luckily I do not mean to harm it; but if I did, it would take no harm from me. The more you and I talk, the better: while I cannot damage you, you may refresh me." After this digression, he went on—

15.22.oldText: It was not until I had withdrawn to my own room for the night that I steadily reviewed the tale Mr. Rochester had told me. As he had said, there was probably nothing extraordinary in the story itself: a wealthy Englishman's passion for a French dancer, and her betrayal—these were everyday matters in society. But there was something decidedly strange in the storm of emotion that had suddenly seized him just as he was expressing contentment with his present mood, and his renewed pleasure in the old hall and its surroundings. I thought about this puzzling moment; but gradually letting it go, since I could not explain it, I turned to considering my master's manner toward me. The trust he had chosen to place in me seemed like a tribute to my discretion, and I regarded and accepted it as such. His behaviour toward me had been steadier for some weeks now than at first. I never seemed to be in his way; he no longer had spells of chilling haughtiness. When he met me unexpectedly, the encounter seemed welcome; he always had a word and sometimes a smile for me. When formally invited to his presence, I was received with a warmth that made me feel I genuinely had the power to entertain him, and that these evening conversations were sought as much for his pleasure as for my benefit.

15.32.oldText: Something gurgled and moaned. Soon footsteps retreated along the gallery toward the third-floor staircase. A door that had recently been installed to close off that staircase—I heard it open and close, and then all was still.

15.35.oldText: "Wake! Wake!" I cried. I shook him, but he only muttered and turned. The smoke had stupefied him. Not a moment could be lost: the very sheets were starting to catch fire. I ran to his basin and pitcher; luckily, one was wide and the other deep, and both were full of water. I heaved them up and drenched the bed and its occupant, flew back to my own room, brought my own water jug, doused the bed again, and, by God's aid, succeeded in putting out the flames that were devouring it.

15.41.oldText: "There! I am up now. But at your peril, don't fetch a candle yet. Wait two minutes until I get into some dry clothes, if any are dry—yes, here is my dressing gown. Now run!"

15.45.oldText: "What is it and who did it?" he asked.

15.46.oldText: He listened very seriously. His face, as I went on, showed more concern than surprise. He did not speak right away when I had finished.

15.47.oldText: "Shall I call Mrs. Fairfax?" I asked.

15.48.oldText: "Mrs. Fairfax? No—what on earth would you call her for? What can she do? Let her sleep undisturbed."

15.49.oldText: "Then I will fetch Leah and wake John and his wife."

15.50.oldText: "Not at all. Just stay still. You have a shawl on. If you're not warm enough, take my cloak over there; wrap it around you and sit in the armchair. There—I will put it on for you. Now put your feet on the stool, to keep them out of the wet. I am going to leave you for a few minutes. I will take the candle. Stay where you are until I return. Be as still as a mouse. I must visit the second floor. Don't move, remember, or call anyone."

15.51.oldText: He left. I watched the light recede. He passed along the gallery very softly, opened the staircase door with barely a sound, closed it behind him, and the last glow vanished. I was left in total darkness. I listened for any noise but heard nothing. A very long time passed. I grew weary; it was cold despite the cloak; and I could not see the point of staying if I was not to rouse the house. I was on the verge of disobeying Mr. Rochester's orders when the light gleamed dimly on the gallery wall once more, and I heard his stockinged feet on the matting. "I hope it is him," I thought, "and not something worse."

15.52.oldText: He came back in, pale and very grim. "I have found it all out," he said, setting his candle on the washstand. "It is as I thought."

15.54.oldText: He made no reply but stood with his arms folded, staring at the floor. After a few minutes he asked, in a rather odd tone—

15.55.oldText: "I forget whether you said you saw anything when you opened your bedroom door."

15.56.oldText: "No, sir, only the candlestick on the ground."

15.57.oldText: "But you heard a strange laugh? You have heard that laugh before, I imagine, or something like it?"

15.58.oldText: "Yes, sir. There is a woman who sews here, called Grace Poole. She laughs like that. She is a very odd person."

15.59.oldText: "Just so. Grace Poole—you've guessed it. She is, as you say, odd—very. Well, I shall think about it. Meanwhile, I am glad you are the only person besides myself who knows the full details of tonight's incident. You are not a gossip—say nothing about it. I will account for the state of things"—he pointed to the bed—"and now go back to your own room. I shall do well enough on the library sofa for the rest of the night. It is nearly four; in two hours the servants will be up."

15.60.oldText: "Goodnight then, sir," I said, turning to leave.

15.61.oldText: He seemed surprised—very oddly so, since he had just told me to go.

15.62.oldText: "What!" he exclaimed. "Are you leaving me already, and like that?"

15.64.oldText: "But not without a farewell—not without a word or two of thanks and goodwill. Not so quick and cold. Why, you have saved my life! Snatched me from a horrible and agonizing death! And you walk past me as if we were strangers! At least shake hands."

15.65.oldText: He held out his hand; I gave him mine. He took it first in one, then in both of his.

15.66.oldText: "You have saved my life. I have a pleasure in owing you so great a debt. I cannot say more. Nothing else in the world would have been bearable to me as a creditor for such an obligation—but you: it is different. I feel your kindness no burden, Jane."

15.67.oldText: He paused, gazing at me. Words nearly visible trembled on his lips—but his voice was checked.

15.68.oldText: "Goodnight again, sir. There is no debt, burden, or obligation in the case."

15.69.oldText: "I knew," he continued, "you would do me good in some way, at some time. I saw it in your eyes when I first looked at you: their expression and smile did not"—he stopped again—"did not"—he rushed on—"strike delight to my very heart for nothing. People talk of natural sympathies; I have heard of guardian spirits. There are grains of truth in the wildest fairy tales. My dear preserver, goodnight!"

15.70.oldText: Strange energy was in his voice, strange fire in his look.

15.71.oldText: "I am glad I happened to be awake," I said, and then I was going.

15.74.oldText: "Cold? Yes—and standing in a puddle! Go, then, Jane—go!" But he still held my hand, and I could not free it. I thought of an excuse.

15.75.oldText: "I think I hear Mrs. Fairfax moving, sir," I said.

15.76.oldText: "Well, leave me." He released his fingers, and I was gone.

15.77.oldText: I reached my bed but never thought of sleep. Until morning dawned, I was tossed on a buoyant but restless sea, where waves of trouble rolled under swells of joy. Sometimes I thought I glimpsed beyond those wild waters a shore as sweet as the hills of Beulah; now and then a freshening wind, stirred by hope, carried my spirit triumphantly toward that distant land. But I could not reach it, even in fancy—an opposing breeze blew off shore and continually drove me back. Reason would resist delusion; judgment would warn passion. Too feverish to rest, I rose as soon as daylight broke.

16.1.oldText: But the morning passed as usual: nothing interrupted the quiet course of Adèle's lessons. Soon after breakfast, though, I heard some commotion near Mr. Rochester's room—Mrs. Fairfax's voice, and Leah's, and the cook's (that is, John's wife), and even John's own gruff tones. There were exclamations: "What a mercy the master wasn't burned in his bed!" "It's always dangerous to keep a candle lit at night." "How lucky he had the sense to think of the water jug!" "I wonder he didn't wake anyone!" "Let's hope he won't catch cold from sleeping on the library sofa." And so on.

16.20.oldText: "Fiend! She wants to know my habits, so she can plan accordingly!" Indignation overwhelmed caution. I replied sharply, "Until now I have often forgotten to fasten the bolt. I did not think it necessary. I was not aware there was any danger to be feared at Thornfield Hall. But in future"—and I stressed the words—"I shall take care to make everything secure before I go to sleep."

16.30.oldText: I barely heard Mrs. Fairfax's account of the curtain fire over dinner, so preoccupied was I with puzzling over Grace Poole's enigmatic character, and even more with the question of her position at Thornfield and why she had not been handed over to the authorities that morning—or at the very least dismissed from service. Mr. Rochester had practically declared his conviction of her guilt last night. What mysterious reason held him back from accusing her? Why had he ordered me to keep silent too? It was strange: a bold, proud, assertive gentleman seemed somehow in the power of one of the lowliest of his dependents—so much in her power that even when she raised her hand against his life, he dared not openly charge her with it, let alone punish her.

16.75.oldText: I kept my word. An hour or two was enough to sketch my own portrait in chalk, and in less than two weeks I had completed an ivory miniature of an imaginary Blanche Ingram. It was a lovely face, and when set beside the real head in chalk, the contrast was as stark as self-control could wish. I benefited from the exercise: it had kept my head and hands busy, and had driven home the new truths I wished to stamp permanently on my heart.

16.76.oldText: Before long, I had reason to be glad of the harsh discipline I had forced upon my feelings. Thanks to it, I was able to meet what came next with a composure that, had it caught me unprepared, I probably could not have maintained even on the surface.

17.0.oldText: A week passed with no news of Mr. Rochester; ten days, and still he did not come. Mrs. Fairfax said she would not be surprised if he went straight from the Leas to London and from there to the Continent, not showing his face at Thornfield again for a year. He had left just as abruptly and unexpectedly before. When I heard this, I felt a strange chill and sinking at the heart. I was actually letting myself feel a sickening sense of disappointment. But rallying my wits and remembering my principles, I called my emotions to order at once—and it was remarkable how quickly I got over the blunder of supposing Mr. Rochester's movements were something I had any reason to care about. Not that I humbled myself with some slavish sense of inferiority; on the contrary, I simply said—

17.1.oldText: "You have nothing to do with the master of Thornfield beyond receiving the salary he pays you for teaching his ward, and being grateful for whatever respectful and kind treatment you have a right to expect if you do your duty. That is the only connection he seriously recognizes between you and him. So don't make him the object of your fine feelings, your raptures and agonies. He is not of your class: keep to your own, and be too self-respecting to pour out the love of your whole heart and soul where such a gift is not wanted and would be despised."

17.11.oldText: The party was expected to arrive on Thursday afternoon, in time for dinner at six. During the wait, I had no time to nurse fantasies, and I believe I was as active and cheerful as anyone—except Adèle. Still, now and then, something dampened my spirits and threw me back, despite myself, into the territory of doubt and dark speculation. This happened when I chanced to see the third-floor staircase door (which lately had always been kept locked) open slowly and give passage to Grace Poole, in her neat cap, white apron, and handkerchief. I watched her glide along the gallery, her quiet step muffled in a cloth slipper; I saw her look into the busy, upside-down bedrooms, perhaps say a word to the charwoman about the proper way to polish a grate, clean a marble mantelpiece, or remove stains from wallpaper, and then move on. She would descend to the kitchen once a day, eat her dinner, smoke a moderate pipe by the hearth, and go back, carrying her pot of porter for her own private comfort to her gloomy upper rooms. Only one hour out of twenty-four did she spend with the other servants below; the rest of her time was spent in some low-ceilinged, oak-panelled room on the second floor. There she sat and sewed—and probably laughed bleakly to herself—as solitary as a prisoner in a dungeon.

17.22.oldText: Afternoon arrived. Mrs. Fairfax put on her best black satin dress, her gloves, and her gold watch, since it was her role to receive the company and show the ladies to their rooms. Adèle, too, was to be dressed, though I thought she had little chance of being introduced to the party that day. Still, to please her, I let Sophie put her in one of her short, full muslin frocks. For myself, I needed no change; I would not be called from my sanctuary of the schoolroom—for a sanctuary it had now become to me, a most welcome refuge in time of trouble.

17.29.oldText: The cavalcade, following the curve of the drive, quickly turned the corner of the house, and I lost sight of it. Adèle now begged to go down; but I took her on my knee and made her understand that she must not on any account think of appearing before the ladies, now or at any other time, unless expressly sent for—that Mr. Rochester would be very angry, and so on. She shed a few natural tears at being told this, but as I began to look very stern, she agreed at last to wipe them.

17.32.oldText: "Chez maman," she said, "quand il y avait du monde, je le suivais partout, au salon et à leurs chambres; souvent je regardais les femmes de chambre coiffer et habiller les dames, et c'était si amusant: comme cela on apprend."

17.40.oldText: She was genuinely hungry, so the chicken and tarts held her attention for a while. It was lucky I had secured this food, or she, Sophie, and I—I brought Sophie a share of our meal—would have risked going without dinner entirely. Everyone downstairs was too busy to think of us. Dessert was not cleared until after nine, and at ten, footmen were still running back and forth with trays and coffee cups. I let Adèle stay up much later than usual, since she declared she could not possibly sleep while doors kept opening and closing below and people hurried about. Besides, she added, a message might still come from Mr. Rochester when she was undressed—"et alors quel dommage!"

17.49.oldText: "Well, I told him that since you were unused to company, I didn't think you would enjoy appearing before so large and fashionable a group, all strangers; and he replied, in his quick way, 'Nonsense! If she objects, tell her it is my particular wish; and if she resists, say I shall come and fetch her personally.'"

17.59.oldText: "You think too much about your appearance, Adèle—but you may have a flower." I took a rose from a vase and fastened it in her sash. She sighed with deep satisfaction, as if her cup of happiness were now full. I turned my face away to hide a smile I could not suppress: there was something both funny and touching in the little Parisian girl's earnest, inborn devotion to matters of dress.

17.63.oldText: First, there was Mrs. Eshton and two of her daughters. She had clearly been a handsome woman and was well preserved still. Of her daughters, the eldest, Amy, was rather small—naive and childlike in face and manner, with a pretty figure. Her white muslin dress and blue sash suited her well. The second, Louisa, was taller and more elegant; with a very pretty face, of the kind the French call a cheeky little face. Both sisters were fair as lilies.

17.68.oldText: As far as her person went, she matched both my picture and Mrs. Fairfax's description point for point. The noble figure, the sloping shoulders, the graceful neck, the dark eyes and black ringlets were all there. But her face? Her face was like her mother's—a youthful, unwrinkled copy: the same low brow, the same strong features, the same pride. It was not, however, quite so oppressive a pride; she laughed constantly, and her laugh was mocking, as was the habitual expression of her arched and haughty lip.

17.72.oldText: You are not to suppose, reader, that Adèle had been sitting motionless on the stool at my feet all this time. No—when the ladies entered, she had risen, walked up to them, made a stately curtsey, and said with gravity—

17.79.oldText: At last coffee was brought in, and the gentlemen were summoned. I sat in the shadows—if there were any shadows in this brilliantly lit room; the window curtain half hid me. Again the arch opened; they came. The gentlemen's collective appearance, like the ladies', was imposing. They were all in black; most were tall, some young. Henry and Frederick Lynn were very dashing indeed, and Colonel Dent a fine soldierly man. Mr. Eshton, the local magistrate, was gentlemanly: his hair quite white, his eyebrows and whiskers still dark, giving him the air of a distinguished stage father. Lord Ingram, like his sisters, was very tall; like them, he was handsome; but he shared Mary's blank, listless look. He seemed to have more length of limb than energy of blood or vigour of mind.

17.81.oldText: He came in last. I was not looking at the arch, yet I saw him enter. I tried to focus on the netting needles, on the meshes of the purse I was making—I wanted to think only of the work in my hands, to see only the silver beads and silk threads in my lap. Yet I saw his figure plainly, and I could not help remembering the last time I had seen it: just after I had done him what he called an essential service, and he, holding my hand and looking down at my face, had gazed at me with eyes that revealed a heart full and ready to overflow—in whose feelings I had a share. How close I had been to him at that moment! What had happened since to change our positions? Yet now, how distant, how far apart we were! So far apart that I did not expect him to come and speak to me. I did not wonder when, without looking my way, he took a seat on the other side of the room and began talking to some of the ladies.

17.85.oldText: Coffee was served. The ladies, since the gentlemen entered, had grown lively as larks; conversation was brisk and merry. Colonel Dent and Mr. Eshton debated politics while their wives listened. The two proud dowagers, Lady Lynn and Lady Ingram, talked together in a corner. Sir George—whom, by the way, I have forgotten to describe: a very large, very ruddy country gentleman—stood before their sofa, coffee cup in hand, occasionally putting in a word. Mr. Frederick Lynn had sat down beside Mary Ingram and was showing her the engravings in a splendid book; she looked, smiled now and then, but said little. The tall, phlegmatic Lord Ingram leaned with folded arms on the back of little, lively Amy Eshton's chair; she glanced up at him and chattered like a wren—she liked him better than Mr. Rochester. Henry Lynn had claimed an ottoman at Louisa's feet; Adèle shared it with him, and he was trying to speak French with her while Louisa laughed at his blunders. With whom would Blanche Ingram pair? She stood alone at a table, bending gracefully over an album. She seemed to be waiting to be approached; but she would not wait long—she would choose her own partner.

17.86.oldText: Mr. Rochester, having left the Eshtons, stood on the hearth as solitary as she stood by the table. She confronted him, taking her position on the opposite side of the mantelpiece.

17.100.oldText: Mrs. Dent here leaned over to the pious lady and whispered something in her ear; I suppose, from the answer it drew, it was a reminder that a member of the hated tribe was present.

17.108.oldText: "We did; and Tedo, you know, I helped you persecute your tutor too—pasty-faced Mr. Vining, 'the parson in the pip' as we called him. He and Miss Wilson took the liberty of falling in love with each other—at least Tedo and I thought so; we caught various tender glances and sighs which we interpreted as tokens of passion, and I assure you the public soon benefited from our discovery. We used it as a lever to hoist those dead weights out of the house. Dear mama, the moment she got wind of it, decided the whole business was immoral. Didn't you, my lady-mother?"

17.125.oldText: Miss Ingram, who had now seated herself with proud grace at the piano, spreading out her white skirts in queenly abundance, launched into a brilliant prelude, talking all the while. She was clearly riding high tonight; both her words and her manner seemed designed to strike her audience as something very dashing and daring indeed.

17.130.oldText: "Commands from Miss Ingram's lips would put spirit into a glass of water."

17.138.oldText: "Now is my chance to slip away," I thought. But the tones that then filled the air stopped me. Mrs. Fairfax had said Mr. Rochester possessed a fine voice, and he did—a mellow, powerful bass into which he poured his own feeling and force, finding a path through the ear to the heart and there stirring something strange and deep. I waited until the last full, resonant vibration had died away—until the tide of talk, briefly checked, had resumed its flow. Then I left my sheltered corner and made my exit by the side door, which was fortunately close. From there a narrow passage led to the hall. Crossing it, I noticed my shoe was loose; I stopped to tie it, kneeling on the mat at the foot of the staircase. I heard the dining room door open; a gentleman came out. Rising quickly, I stood face to face with him: it was Mr. Rochester.

18.2.oldText: I wondered what they would do the first evening a change of entertainment was proposed. They spoke of "playing charades," but in my ignorance I did not know what that meant. The servants were called in, the dining room tables wheeled away, the lights rearranged, and chairs placed in a semicircle facing the arch. While Mr. Rochester and the other gentlemen directed these changes, the ladies ran up and down stairs ringing for their maids. Mrs. Fairfax was called upon to report what the house could supply in the way of shawls, dresses, and draperies of any kind. Certain wardrobes on the third floor were ransacked, and their contents—brocaded and hooped petticoats, satin capes, black silk gowns, lace caps, and the like—were brought down in armloads by the maids. A selection was made, and the chosen items were carried to the boudoir off the drawing room.

18.10.oldText: Seated on the carpet beside this basin was Mr. Rochester, wrapped in shawls, with a turban on his head. His dark eyes, swarthy skin, and exotic features suited the costume perfectly: he looked like an Eastern ruler, an agent or victim of the sultan's justice. Presently Miss Ingram advanced into view. She too was dressed in oriental fashion: a crimson scarf tied like a sash around her waist, an embroidered handkerchief knotted about her temples, her beautifully shaped arms bare, one raised in the act of balancing a pitcher on her head. Her figure and features, her complexion and general air all suggested an Israelite princess from the days of the patriarchs—and that was clearly the character she intended to portray.

18.15.oldText: "Bridewell!" exclaimed Colonel Dent, and the charade was solved.

18.19.oldText: "Alas, yes—the worse for it! Nothing could suit your complexion better than that ruffian's grime."

18.27.oldText: If she had won the victory outright, and he had yielded and sincerely laid his heart at her feet, I would have covered my face, turned to the wall, and (in a manner of speaking) died. If Miss Ingram had been a good and noble woman, gifted with strength, warmth, kindness, and sense, I would have fought one desperate battle with two enemies—jealousy and despair. Then, my heart torn out and devoured, I would have admired her, acknowledged her excellence, and been still for the rest of my days; and the more complete her superiority, the deeper my admiration, the more genuine my peace.
