But as things actually stood, to watch Miss Ingram's efforts at captivating Mr. Rochester, to see them fail again and again—while she remained blind to her failure, imagining each arrow struck home, preening herself on success while her pride and vanity drove further and further away the very thing she wanted to attract—to witness this was to be under constant excitement and ruthless restraint at the same time.

18.34.oldText: It was nearing dusk, and the dressing bell had already sounded, when little Adèle, who was kneeling beside me in the drawing room window seat, suddenly exclaimed—

18.43.oldText: The dressing bell broke up the company. It was not until after dinner that I saw him again; he then seemed perfectly at ease. But I liked his face even less than before: it struck me as being at once restless and lifeless. His eye wandered without purpose: this gave him a strange look unlike any I had seen before. For a handsome and not unpleasant-looking man, he repelled me strongly. There was no force in that smooth-skinned, oval face; no firmness in that straight nose and small, red mouth; no thought on the low, even forehead; no will in that blank, brown eye.

18.45.oldText: He had spoken of Mr. Rochester as an old friend. Theirs must have been a curious friendship—a perfect example of the old saying that opposites attract.

18.54.oldText: "But I can't persuade her to go, my lady," said the footman, "nor can any of the servants. Mrs. Fairfax is with her now, begging her to leave; but she has planted herself in a chair by the kitchen fire and says nothing will shift her until she's allowed to come in here."

18.58.oldText: "A shockingly ugly old creature, miss; almost as black as a crock."

18.61.oldText: "My dear boys, what are you thinking of?" exclaimed Mrs. Lynn.

18.90.oldText: "Now, now, good people," returned Miss Ingram, "don't crowd me. Really, your sense of wonder is easily excited. You seem, judging by the importance you all—my good mama included—attach to this business, actually to believe we have a genuine witch in the house who is in league with the devil. I have seen a gypsy vagrant; she practised the standard tricks of palm reading and told me the usual things. My whim is satisfied; and now I think Mr. Eshton would do well to put the hag in the stocks tomorrow morning, as he threatened."

18.91.oldText: Miss Ingram took up a book, leaned back in her chair, and refused further conversation. I watched her for nearly half an hour: during all that time she never turned a page, and her face grew steadily darker, more dissatisfied, and more sour with disappointment. She had clearly not heard anything to her advantage; and it seemed to me, from her prolonged gloom and silence, that despite her professed indifference she took whatever had been revealed to her far more seriously than she wanted anyone to know.

18.92.oldText: During all that time she never turned a page.

18.93.oldText: Meanwhile, Mary Ingram, Amy, and Louisa Eshton declared they dared not go alone, yet they all wanted to go. A negotiation was opened through the ambassador Sam; and after much going back and forth—until I think poor Sam's legs must have ached with the exercise—permission was at last, with great difficulty, extracted from the stern sibyl for the three to visit her together.

18.94.oldText: Their visit was not so quiet as Miss Ingram's had been. We heard hysterical giggling and little shrieks from the library; and after about twenty minutes they burst through the door, running across the hall as if scared half out of their wits.

18.95.oldText: "I am sure she is something supernatural!" they cried, one and all. "She told us such things! She knows everything about us!" And they sank breathlessly into the various seats the gentlemen hurried to bring them.

18.96.oldText: Pressed for details, they declared she had told them things they had said and done as mere children, described books and ornaments they had in their rooms at home, and keepsakes that various relatives had given them. They swore she had even read their thoughts, and had whispered in each one's ear the name of the person she liked best in the world, and told them what they most wished for.

18.97.oldText: The gentlemen pressed with eager requests to hear more about these last two points; but they got only blushes, exclamations, trembling, and giggles in return. The older ladies meanwhile offered smelling salts and waved fans, and again and again lamented that their warnings had not been heeded. The older gentlemen laughed, and the younger ones offered their services to the agitated young women.

18.98.oldText: In the midst of this commotion, with my eyes and ears fully engaged in the scene before me, I heard a polite cough at my elbow. I turned and saw Sam.

18.99.oldText: "If you please, miss, the gypsy says there is another young single lady in the room who has not been to see her yet, and she vows she will not leave until she has seen everyone. I thought it must be you: there is no one else. What shall I tell her?"

18.100.oldText: "Oh, I will certainly go," I answered. I was glad of the unexpected chance to satisfy my considerable curiosity. I slipped out of the room unnoticed by anyone—for the whole company was clustered around the trembling trio who had just returned—and I closed the door quietly behind me.

18.101.oldText: "If you like, miss," said Sam, "I'll wait in the hall for you; and if she frightens you, just call and I'll come in."

18.102.oldText: "No, Sam, go back to the kitchen. I am not the least bit afraid." Nor was I; but I was very interested and excited.

19.43.oldText: "You do? Do you?" I thought. "So there is something sinister in this after all!"

19.58.oldText: "What a clever dodge! He went to Millcote this morning and will be back tonight or tomorrow. Does that remove him from your acquaintance—erase him from existence?"

19.74.oldText: "Appearances would suggest so. And no doubt (though, with an impudence that deserves correction, you seem to question it) they will make a supremely happy couple. He must love such a handsome, noble, witty, accomplished lady; and she probably loves him—or if not him, at least his purse. I know she considers the Rochester estate highly desirable; though (God forgive me!) I told her something about an hour ago on that subject that made her look very serious: the corners of her mouth dropped half an inch. I would advise her dark-browed suitor to watch out: if another comes along with a larger or clearer income, he is done for—"

19.76.oldText: "Your fortune is still uncertain: when I studied your face, one trait contradicted another. Chance has set aside a measure of happiness for you—that I know. I knew it before I came here this evening. She has laid it carefully aside for you. I watched her do it. It depends on you to reach out your hand and take it. But whether you will—that is the question I am studying. Kneel again on the rug."

19.78.oldText: She did not lean toward me but only gazed, reclining in her chair.

19.79.oldText: I knelt. She did not lean toward me but only gazed, reclining in her chair. She began to murmur—

19.80.oldText: "The flame flickers in the eye; the eye shines like dew; it looks soft and full of feeling; it smiles at my jargon. It is responsive; impression follows impression through its clear depths. Where it stops smiling, it is sad; an unconscious weariness weighs on the lid—that means melancholy born of loneliness. It turns from me; it will not bear further scrutiny; it seems to deny, with a mocking glance, the truth of everything I have already seen—to reject the charge of both tenderness and grief. Its pride and reserve only confirm my opinion. The eye is favourable.

19.81.oldText: "As for the mouth, it delights at times in laughter; it is ready to express all that the brain conceives, though I daresay it would keep silent about much that the heart experiences. Flexible and expressive, it was never meant to be compressed in the eternal silence of solitude. It is a mouth that should speak often and smile often, and have human warmth for its companion. That feature, too, is promising.

19.82.oldText: "I see no obstacle to a happy outcome except in the brow; and that brow seems to say: 'I can live alone, if self-respect and circumstances require it. I need not sell my soul to buy happiness. I have an inner treasure born with me, which can sustain me if all outward joys are withheld—or offered only at a price I cannot afford.' The forehead declares: 'Reason sits firmly in control, and she will not let the feelings bolt and drag her into wild abysses. The passions may rage as furiously as they like; desires may imagine all sorts of impossible things; but judgment shall still have the last word in every argument and the deciding vote in every question. Strong wind, earthquake, and fire may pass; but I shall follow the guidance of that still small voice which speaks the dictates of conscience.'

19.83.oldText: "Well said, forehead; your declaration shall be honoured. I have formed my plans—good plans, I believe them to be—and in them I have respected the claims of conscience and the counsel of reason. I know how quickly youth would fade and joy would perish if, in the cup of happiness offered, a single drop of shame or a single hint of remorse were detected; and I do not want sacrifice, sorrow, ruin—that is not what I seek. I wish to nurture, not to destroy—to earn gratitude, not to wring tears of blood—no, nor of salt. My harvest must be in smiles, in tenderness, in sweet— That will do. I think I am raving in a kind of exquisite delirium. I wish I could stretch this moment out forever; but I dare not. So far I have governed myself completely. I have acted as I inwardly swore I would; but to go further might test me beyond my strength. Rise, Miss Eyre; leave me. 'The play is played out.'"

19.84.oldText: Where was I? Was I awake or asleep? Had I been dreaming? Was I dreaming still? The old woman's voice had changed: her accent, her gesture, everything was as familiar to me as my own face in a mirror—as the sound of my own voice. I got up but did not go. I looked; I stirred the fire and looked again. But she drew her bonnet and bandage closer around her face and again motioned me to leave. The flame lit up her outstretched hand; alert now and watching for clues, I noticed that hand at once. It was no more the withered limb of old age than my own; it was a firm, supple hand with smooth, well-shaped fingers. A broad ring flashed on the little finger, and bending forward, I looked at it and saw a gem I had seen a hundred times before. Again I looked at the face, which was no longer turned away—on the contrary, the bonnet was thrown off, the bandage removed, the head lifted.

19.85.oldText: "Well, Jane, do you know me?" asked the familiar voice.

19.86.oldText: "Just take off the red cloak, sir, and then—"

19.89.oldText: "There, then—'Off, ye trappings!'" And Mr. Rochester stepped out of his disguise.

19.91.oldText: "But well done, wasn't it? Don't you think so?"

19.92.oldText: "With the ladies you must have managed well."

19.94.oldText: "You did not play the gypsy with me."

19.95.oldText: "What character did I play? My own?"

19.96.oldText: "No—some impossible one. In short, I believe you have been trying to draw me out—or trip me up. You have been talking nonsense to make me talk nonsense. It is hardly fair, sir."

19.98.oldText: "I cannot say until I have thought it all over. If, on reflection, I find I have not made a great fool of myself, I shall try to forgive you. But it was not right."

19.99.oldText: "Oh, you were very correct—very careful, very sensible."

19.100.oldText: I thought about it and decided, on the whole, I had been. That was a comfort. But in truth, I had been on my guard almost from the start of the interview. I had suspected some kind of trick. I knew real gypsies and fortune-tellers did not express themselves the way this seeming old woman had; besides, I had noticed her disguised voice and her anxiety to hide her features. But my mind had been running on Grace Poole—that living riddle, that mystery of mysteries, as I considered her. I had never thought of Mr. Rochester.

19.101.oldText: "Well," he said, "what are you musing about? What does that thoughtful smile mean?"

19.102.oldText: "Wonder and self-congratulation, sir. I have your permission to leave now, I suppose?"

19.103.oldText: "No; stay a moment and tell me what the people in the drawing room are doing."

19.105.oldText: "Sit down! Let me hear what they said about me."

19.106.oldText: "I had better not stay long, sir; it must be nearly eleven. Oh, are you aware, Mr. Rochester, that a stranger has arrived since you left this morning?"

19.107.oldText: "A stranger! No—who can it be? I expected no one. Is he gone?"

19.108.oldText: "No; he said he had known you a long time, and that he could take the liberty of making himself at home here until you returned."

19.109.oldText: "The devil he did! Did he give his name?"

19.110.oldText: "His name is Mason, sir; and he comes from the West Indies—from Spanish Town, in Jamaica, I think."

19.111.oldText: Mr. Rochester was standing near me; he had taken my hand, as if to lead me to a chair. As I spoke, he gripped my wrist convulsively. The smile on his lips froze; apparently a spasm seized his breath.

19.112.oldText: "Mason!—the West Indies!" he said, in the tone you might imagine a speaking machine would use to pronounce its words. "Mason!—the West Indies!" he repeated, going over the syllables three times, growing whiter than ash between each utterance. He hardly seemed to know what he was doing.

19.113.oldText: "Do you feel ill, sir?" I asked.

19.114.oldText: "Jane, I've had a blow—I've had a blow, Jane!" He staggered.

19.116.oldText: "Jane, you offered me your shoulder once before; let me have it now."

19.118.oldText: He sat down and made me sit beside him. Holding my hand in both of his, he rubbed warmth into it, gazing at me all the while with the most troubled and desolate look.

19.119.oldText: "My little friend!" he said. "I wish I were on a quiet island with only you, and trouble, and danger, and horrible memories removed from me."

19.120.oldText: "Can I help you, sir? I would give my life to serve you."

19.121.oldText: "Jane, if I need help, I'll seek it from you. I promise."

19.122.oldText: "Thank you, sir. Tell me what to do—I'll try, at least."

19.123.oldText: "Fetch me a glass of wine from the dining room. They will be at supper there. And tell me if Mason is with them, and what he is doing."

19.124.oldText: I went. I found the entire party in the dining room at supper, as Mr. Rochester had said; they were not seated at the table but had helped themselves from the sideboard and stood about in groups with their plates and glasses. Everyone seemed in high spirits; laughter and conversation were general and lively. Mr. Mason stood near the fire, talking to Colonel and Mrs. Dent, and looked as merry as anyone. I filled a wine glass (I saw Miss Ingram watching me with a frown as I did so—she no doubt thought I was taking liberties) and returned to the library.

19.125.oldText: Mr. Rochester's extreme pallor had vanished, and he looked firm and stern once more. He took the glass from my hand.

19.126.oldText: "Here is to your health, guardian spirit!" he said. He drained the glass and gave it back to me. "What are they doing, Jane?"

19.128.oldText: "They don't look grave and mysterious, as if they had heard something strange?"

19.129.oldText: "Not at all: they are full of jokes and good cheer."

19.132.oldText: "If all those people came together and spat at me, what would you do, Jane?"

19.133.oldText: "Throw them out of the room, sir, if I could."

19.134.oldText: He half smiled. "But if I went to them and they only looked at me coldly, and whispered sneeringly among themselves, and then drifted away one by one—what then? Would you go with them?"

19.135.oldText: "I rather think not, sir. I should take more pleasure in staying with you."

19.137.oldText: "Yes, sir, to comfort you as best I could."

19.138.oldText: "And if they condemned you for standing by me?"

19.139.oldText: "I probably would not know of their condemnation; and if I did, I would not care about it."

19.140.oldText: "Then you could bear criticism for my sake?"

19.141.oldText: "I could bear it for the sake of any friend who deserved my loyalty—as you, I am sure, do."

19.142.oldText: "Go back to the room now; walk quietly up to Mason and whisper in his ear that Mr. Rochester has returned and wishes to see him. Bring him here and then leave me."

19.144.oldText: I did as he asked. The whole company stared at me as I walked straight through them. I found Mr. Mason, delivered the message, and led him out of the room. I showed him into the library and then went upstairs.

19.145.oldText: Late that night, after I had been in bed some time, I heard the guests making their way to their rooms. I could distinguish Mr. Rochester's voice, and heard him say, "This way, Mason; this is your room."

19.146.oldText: He spoke cheerfully, and the light tone set my heart at ease. I was soon asleep.

20.9.oldText: I had thrown on some clothes, though horror shook every limb. I came out of my room. The sleepers were all awake: cries of alarm and terrified murmurs sounded in every room. Door after door was flung open; one person looked out, then another; the gallery filled. Gentlemen and ladies alike had left their beds, and "Oh! What is it?" "Who is hurt?" "What has happened?" "Fetch a light!" "Is it fire?" "Are there robbers?" "Where shall we run?" was demanded on all sides. Without the moonlight they would have been in total darkness. They ran back and forth; they crowded together; some sobbed, some stumbled. The confusion was hopeless.

20.20.oldText: No: stillness returned. Every murmur and movement gradually ceased, and within about an hour Thornfield Hall was as hushed as a desert. Sleep and night had resumed their rule. Meanwhile the moon sank; she was about to set. Not wanting to sit in the cold and darkness, I thought I would lie on my bed, dressed as I was. I left the window and crossed the carpet quietly; as I stooped to take off my shoes, a cautious hand tapped softly at the door.

20.49.oldText: Here, then, I was on the third floor, locked into one of its mysterious rooms; night around me; a pale and bloody spectacle under my eyes and hands; a murderess separated from me by a single door. Yes—that was the truly terrifying part—the rest I could endure. But I shuddered at the thought of Grace Poole bursting in on me.

20.54.oldText: And this man I bent over—this commonplace, quiet stranger—how had he become entangled in the web of horror? And why had the Fury attacked him? What brought him to this part of the house at such an hour, when he should have been asleep in bed? I had heard Mr. Rochester assign him a room below—what drew him here? And why, now, was he so meek under the violence done to him? Why did he submit so quietly to the secrecy Mr. Rochester imposed? Why did Mr. Rochester impose it? His guest had been savaged, his own life had been plotted against on a previous occasion; and both attacks he smothered in secrecy and buried in silence! Finally, I could see that Mason was submissive to Mr. Rochester; that the latter's forceful will held complete power over the former's passivity. The few words they had exchanged confirmed this. It was obvious that in their history together, the passive nature of the one had always been ruled by the active energy of the other. Where, then, had Mr. Rochester's terror come from when he heard of Mason's arrival? Why had the mere name of this unresisting man—whom a single word now sufficed to control like a child—struck him, a few hours ago, as a thunderbolt strikes an oak?

20.65.oldText: "Hardly!—courage! Two weeks from now you'll scarcely be the worse for it. You've lost a little blood, that's all. Carter, tell him there's no danger."

20.67.oldText: "She bit me," he murmured. "She savaged me like a tigress, when Rochester got the knife from her."

20.72.oldText: "You thought! You thought! It makes me angry to hear you. But you have suffered, and are likely to suffer enough for not taking my advice; so I'll say no more. Carter—hurry! Hurry! The sun will soon rise, and I must get him away."

20.86.oldText: "We shall get you away quietly, Dick; and it will be better, both for your sake and for the poor creature in there. I have worked hard to avoid exposure, and I should not like it to come now. Here, Carter, help him on with his waistcoat. Where did you leave your fur cloak? You can't travel a mile without it, I know, in this wretched cold climate. In your room?—Jane, run down to Mr. Mason's room, the one next to mine, and fetch a cloak you'll find there."

20.90.oldText: "Good! Now, doctor, I shall take the liberty of administering a dose myself, on my own authority. I got this tonic in Rome, from an Italian quack—a fellow you would have kicked, Carter. It is not something to use carelessly, but it is useful on the right occasion—as now, for example. Jane, a little water."

20.95.oldText: "But will it hurt me? Is it stimulating?"

20.102.oldText: "I'm sure you do. Now, Jane, go ahead of us to the back stairs; unbolt the side door, and tell the driver of the post-chaise you'll see in the yard—or just outside, since I told him not to drive his rattling wheels over the stones—to be ready. We are coming. And Jane, if anyone is about, come to the foot of the stairs and give a signal."

20.103.oldText: It was by now half past five, and the sun was about to rise; but I found the kitchen still dark and quiet. The side door was fastened; I opened it as silently as I could. The yard was empty, but the gates stood wide open, and a post-chaise with horses harnessed and the driver on the box waited just outside. I went to him and said the gentlemen were coming; he nodded. Then I looked carefully around and listened. The stillness of early morning held everything; the curtains were still drawn over the servants' windows; small birds were just beginning to chirp in the blossoming orchard trees, whose branches drooped like white garlands over the wall on one side of the yard; the carriage horses stamped now and then in their stalls. All else was quiet.

20.104.oldText: The gentlemen now appeared. Mason, supported by Mr. Rochester and the surgeon, walked with tolerable ease. They helped him into the chaise; Carter followed.

20.111.oldText: "I do my best; and have done, and will do," was the answer. He shut the chaise door, and the vehicle drove away.

20.113.oldText: This done, he walked slowly and abstractedly toward a door in the wall bordering the orchard. I, thinking he was done with me, turned to go back to the house; but I heard him call "Jane!" He had opened the gate and stood waiting for me.

20.134.oldText: "But Mr. Mason seems an easily led man. Your influence is clearly powerful over him: he will never defy you or deliberately harm you."

20.148.oldText: "Well then, Jane, use your imagination. Suppose you were no longer a well-brought-up, disciplined young woman, but a wild boy spoiled from childhood. Imagine yourself in a remote foreign country. Imagine that there you commit a grave error—never mind what kind or from what motive—but one whose consequences must follow you through life and poison your whole existence. Mind, I don't say a crime; I am not speaking of murder or any guilty act that would bring the law down on you. My word is error. The consequences of what you have done become, in time, utterly unbearable. You take steps to find relief—unusual steps, but neither unlawful nor wicked. Still you are miserable; for hope has left you at the very edge of life. Your noon sun darkens in an eclipse that you feel will last until it sets. Bitter and degrading memories become the only food of your mind. You wander here and there, seeking rest in exile—happiness in pleasure, I mean in mindless, shallow pleasure, the kind that dulls the mind and deadens the heart. Weary in heart and withered in soul, you come home after years of self-imposed exile. You meet someone new—how or where doesn't matter. In this stranger you find the good and bright qualities you have sought for twenty years and never found before; and they are all fresh, healthy, unspoiled and unstained. Such company revives you, regenerates you. You feel better days returning—higher hopes, purer feelings. You want to begin your life again, to spend your remaining days in a way more worthy of an immortal being. To achieve this end, are you justified in leaping over a barrier of custom—a mere conventional obstacle that neither your conscience approves nor your judgment supports?"

20.149.oldText: He paused for an answer: and what was I to say? Oh, for some good spirit to suggest a wise and fitting response! A vain wish! The west wind whispered in the ivy around me; but no gentle angel borrowed its breath to speak through. The birds sang in the treetops; but their song, however sweet, spoke no words.

20.151.oldText: "Is the wandering, sinful, but now rest-seeking and repentant man justified in braving the world's opinion, in order to bind to himself forever this gentle, gracious, generous stranger, thereby securing his own peace of mind and the renewal of his life?"

20.153.oldText: "But the instrument—the instrument! God, who does the work, chooses the instrument. I myself—I tell you plainly—have been a worldly, reckless, restless man; and I believe I have found the instrument for my cure in—"

20.155.oldText: "Little friend," he said, in a completely changed tone—his face changing too, losing all its softness and seriousness, becoming hard and mocking—"you have noticed my tender fondness for Miss Ingram. Don't you think if I married her she would set me right with a vengeance?"

21.0.oldText: Premonitions are strange things! And so are sympathies; and so are signs; and the three combined form one mystery to which humanity has not yet found the key. I never laughed at premonitions in my life, because I have had strange ones of my own. Sympathies, I believe, exist—for instance, between relatives long separated and wholly estranged, who still assert, despite their alienation, the bond of their common origin—and their workings baffle human understanding. And signs, for all we know, may be nothing but Nature's sympathy with humanity.

21.8.oldText: "I'm sorry I can't give you better news of them, Miss. They are very badly off at present—in great trouble."

21.14.oldText: "Well, you see, Miss Eyre, it is not a common misfortune: his life has been very wild. These last three years he gave himself up to terrible ways, and his death was shocking."

21.21.oldText: "Yes; and I will do it now." Having directed him to the servants' hall and recommended him to the care of John's wife and John himself, I went to find Mr. Rochester.

21.40.oldText: "But Reed left children? You must have cousins? Sir George Lynn was talking yesterday about a Reed of Gateshead who, he said, was one of the worst scoundrels in London; and Ingram mentioned a Georgiana Reed from the same place, who was much admired for her beauty a season or two ago."

21.42.oldText: "And what good can you do her? Nonsense, Jane! I would never think of travelling a hundred miles to see an old lady who will perhaps be dead before you arrive—and besides, you say she threw you out."

21.103.oldText: I reached the lodge at Gateshead about five o'clock on the afternoon of May the first. I stopped in there before going up to the hall. It was very clean and neat: the decorative windows hung with little white curtains; the floor spotless; the grate and fire-irons polished bright; the fire burning clear. Bessie sat by the hearth, nursing her youngest child, and Robert and his sister played quietly in a corner.

21.118.oldText: In each sister there was one trait of the mother, and only one: the thin, pale elder daughter had her parent's hard eye; the blooming, ample younger girl had her contour of jaw and chin—perhaps slightly softened, but still giving an indefinable hardness to a face otherwise so full and handsome.

21.125.oldText: "Mama dislikes being disturbed in the evening," Eliza remarked. I soon rose, quietly removed my bonnet and gloves, uninvited, and said I would just step out to Bessie—who was, I imagined, in the kitchen—and ask her to find out whether Mrs. Reed was willing to see me tonight. I went, and having found Bessie and sent her on my errand, I took further steps. It had always been my habit to shrink from rudeness; received as I had been today, a year ago I would have resolved to leave Gateshead the very next morning. Now, it suddenly became clear to me that this would be foolish. I had come a hundred miles to see my aunt, and I must stay until she was better—or dead. As for her daughters' pride or folly, I must set it aside and make myself independent of it. So I spoke to the housekeeper, asked her to show me a room, told her I should probably be a visitor for a week or two, had my trunk taken to my room, and followed it there myself. I met Bessie on the landing.

21.127.oldText: I did not need to be shown to that well-known room, to which I had so often been summoned for punishment or scolding in the old days. I hurried ahead of Bessie; I softly opened the door. A shaded lamp stood on the table, for it was growing dark. There was the great four-poster bed with amber hangings, as before; there the dressing table, the armchair, and the footstool where I had been made to kneel a hundred times to beg pardon for sins I had not committed. I glanced into a certain corner nearby, half expecting to see the thin outline of a cane that used to lurk there, ready to spring out and sting my trembling palm or shrinking neck. I approached the bed; I drew back the curtains and leaned over the high-piled pillows.

21.128.oldText: I remembered Mrs. Reed's face well, and I eagerly looked for the familiar image. It is a good thing that time dampens the thirst for revenge and silences the voice of hatred. I had left this woman in bitterness and anger, and I came back to her now with no feeling except a kind of pity for her great suffering, and a strong desire to forget and forgive all wrongs—to be reconciled and join hands in friendship.

21.129.oldText: The well-known face was there: stern, unyielding as ever—there was that flint-like eye that nothing could melt, and the slightly raised, commanding, tyrannical eyebrow. How often had it lowered on me with menace and hatred! And how the memories of childhood terrors and sorrows revived as I traced its harsh line now! And yet I bent down and kissed her. She looked at me.

21.132.oldText: I had once vowed never to call her aunt again; but I thought it no sin to forget and break that vow now. My fingers had found her hand where it lay outside the sheet. If she had pressed mine kindly, I would at that moment have felt real joy. But cold natures are not so easily softened, nor natural hatreds so quickly erased. Mrs. Reed pulled her hand away, and turning her face from me, remarked that the night was warm. Again she looked at me so icily that I knew at once her opinion of me—her feeling toward me—was unchanged and unchangeable. I could see by her stony eye—impervious to tenderness, unreachable by tears—that she was determined to consider me bad to the last; because to believe me good would give her no pleasure, only a sense of humiliation.

21.143.oldText: "I had a dislike for her mother always; she was my husband's only sister, and a great favourite of his. He opposed the family's disowning her when she made her low marriage; and when news came of her death, he wept like a fool. He would send for the baby, though I begged him to put it out to nurse and pay for its care. I hated it the first time I laid eyes on it—a sickly, whining, pining thing! It would wail in its cradle all night—not screaming heartily like any other child, but whimpering and moaning. Reed pitied it; he used to hold it and fuss over it as if it were his own—more, indeed, than he ever noticed his own children at that age. He tried to make my children friendly to the little beggar; the darlings couldn't stand it, and he was angry with them when they showed their dislike. In his last illness he had it brought constantly to his bedside; and barely an hour before he died, he bound me with a vow to keep the creature. I would as soon have been charged with a pauper's brat from the workhouse—but he was weak, naturally weak. John does not resemble his father at all, and I am glad of it: John is like me and like my brothers—he is a true Gibson. Oh, I wish he would stop tormenting me with letters begging for money! I have no more money to give him: we are growing poor. I must dismiss half the servants and shut up part of the house, or let it. I can never submit to that—yet how are we to manage? Two thirds of my income goes to pay mortgage interest. John gambles terribly, and always loses—poor boy! He is surrounded by swindlers. John is ruined and degraded—his appearance is frightful—I feel ashamed for him when I see him."

21.152.oldText: Eliza still said little: she clearly had no time for talk. I never saw a busier person, yet it was hard to say what she accomplished. She had an alarm clock to wake her early. What she did before breakfast I never discovered, but after that meal she divided her day into precise portions, each hour assigned its task. Three times a day she studied a little book which, on inspection, I found was a Book of Common Prayer. I asked her once what she found so compelling in it, and she said, "The Rubric." Three hours she spent stitching a gold-thread border on a square of crimson cloth, nearly large enough for a carpet. When I asked what it was for, she told me it was a covering for the altar of a new church recently built near Gateshead. Two hours she gave to her diary; two to working alone in the kitchen garden; and one to managing her accounts. She seemed to want no company and no conversation. I believe she was happy in her way: this routine was enough for her, and nothing annoyed her more than any event that forced her to break its clockwork regularity.

21.153.oldText: She told me one evening, in a more communicative mood than usual, that John's behaviour and the threatened ruin of the family had been a source of deep distress to her; but she had now, she said, settled her mind and formed her resolution. Her own fortune she had taken care to protect; and when her mother died—and it was very unlikely, she remarked calmly, that she would either recover or linger long—she would carry out a long-cherished plan: enter a religious retreat where strict habits would be permanently safe from disturbance, and place firm barriers between herself and the frivolous world. I asked if Georgiana would go with her.

21.154.oldText: "Of course not. Georgiana and she had nothing in common; they never had. She would not be burdened with her company for any consideration. Georgiana should go her own way; and she, Eliza, would go hers."

21.155.oldText: Georgiana, when not pouring out her heart to me, spent most of her time lying on the sofa, complaining about the dullness of the house, and wishing again and again that her aunt Gibson would invite her to London. "It would be so much better," she said, "if she could just get away for a month or two, until all was over." I did not ask what she meant by "all being over," but I suppose she referred to her mother's expected death and the gloomy business of the funeral. Eliza generally took no more notice of her sister's laziness and complaints than if no such whining, lounging figure were there at all. One day, however, as she put away her account book and unfolded her embroidery, she suddenly rounded on her—

21.159.oldText: True, generous feeling counts for little with some people; but here were two natures made, the one unbearably bitter and the other contemptibly bland, for the lack of it. Feeling without judgment is a watery drink indeed; but judgment without feeling is too harsh and dry a morsel for anyone to swallow.

21.168.oldText: "Aunt," she repeated. "Who calls me aunt? You are not one of the Gibsons; and yet I know you—that face, and the eyes and forehead are strangely familiar. You look like—why, you look like Jane Eyre!"

21.179.oldText: I am, Madam, &c., &c., JOHN EYRE, Madeira."

21.192.oldText: The nurse came in, and Bessie followed. I stayed another half hour, hoping to see some sign of softening; but she gave none. She was sinking rapidly into stupor; her mind did not rally again. At midnight she died. I was not there to close her eyes, nor were either of her daughters. They came to tell us the next morning that it was over. By then she had been laid out. Eliza and I went to see her; Georgiana, who had burst into loud weeping, said she dared not go. There lay Sarah Reed's once robust and active body, rigid and still: her flint-like eye was shut beneath its cold lid; her brow and strong features still bore the stamp of her unyielding soul. A strange and solemn sight she was to me. I gazed at her with gloom and pain: nothing soft, nothing sweet, nothing merciful or hopeful did the spectacle inspire—only a grating anguish for her woes, not my loss, and a sombre, tearless dread at the fearfulness of death in such a form.

22.16.oldText: Well, he is not a ghost; yet every nerve in my body has come unstrung. For a moment I am beyond my own control. What does this mean? I did not think I would tremble like this when I saw him, or lose my voice or the power of movement in his presence. I will go back as soon as I can move; I need not make an absolute fool of myself. I know another way to the house. It doesn't matter if I knew twenty ways; for he has seen me.

22.17.oldText: "Hello!" he cries, and puts down his book and pencil. "There you are! Come here, if you please."

22.18.oldText: I suppose I do go; though in what manner I cannot tell, since I am barely conscious of my movements, concerned only with appearing calm and, above all, with controlling the muscles of my face—which I feel rebelling against my will, struggling to express what I had resolved to hide. But I have a veil—it is down. I may still manage to behave with some composure.

22.22.oldText: I knew there would be pleasure in seeing my master again, even though it was shadowed by the fear that he would soon cease to be my master, and by the knowledge that I was nothing to him. But there was always in Mr. Rochester (or so it seemed to me) such an abundance of the power to communicate happiness that to taste even the crumbs he scattered to stray birds like me was to feast richly. His last words were balm: they seemed to imply that it mattered to him whether I forgot him or not. And he had spoken of Thornfield as my home—if only it were!

22.35.oldText: That evening I firmly closed my eyes against the future. I stopped my ears against the voice that kept warning me of approaching separation and coming grief. When tea was over and Mrs. Fairfax had taken up her knitting, and I had settled in a low chair near her, and Adèle, kneeling on the carpet, had nestled close to me, and a sense of shared affection seemed to surround us with a ring of golden peace, I offered a silent prayer that we might not be parted far or soon. But when, as we sat like this, Mr. Rochester entered unannounced, and looking at us seemed to take pleasure in the sight of so harmonious a group—when he said he supposed the old lady was all right now that she had her adopted daughter back again, and added that he could see Adèle was "ready to devour her little English mama"—I half dared to hope that even after his marriage he might keep us together somewhere under the shelter of his protection, not entirely banished from the sunshine of his presence.

23.3.oldText: I walked for a while on the paved path; but a subtle, familiar scent—cigar smoke—drifted from a window. I saw the library casement open a few inches; I knew I might be watched from there, so I went apart into the orchard. No corner of the grounds was more sheltered or more like Eden: it was full of trees and blooming with flowers. A very high wall shut it off from the courtyard on one side; on the other, a beech avenue screened it from the lawn. At the far end was a sunken fence—its only boundary with the open fields beyond. A winding path bordered with laurels and ending at a giant horse-chestnut tree, ringed at the base by a bench, led down to the fence. Here one could wander unseen. While such sweet dew fell, such silence reigned, such twilight gathered, I felt as if I could haunt this shade forever. But as I threaded the flower beds at the upper end of the enclosure, drawn there by the light the now-rising moon cast on this more open area, my step was checked—not by any sound or sight, but once again by a warning fragrance.

23.13.oldText: It is one of my flaws that though my tongue can sometimes produce a ready answer, there are times when it fails me badly in framing an excuse—and always at some crisis, when a smooth word or plausible pretext is most needed to save me from painful awkwardness. I did not like walking alone with Mr. Rochester in the shadowy orchard at this hour; but I could not think of a reason to leave him. I followed with dragging steps, my thoughts busy searching for an escape. But he himself looked so composed and so serious that I grew ashamed of my confusion: the danger—if any existed—seemed to be entirely in my own mind; his was calm and undisturbed.

23.16.oldText: "You must have grown somewhat attached to the house—you, with your eye for natural beauty and your strong capacity for attachment?"

23.43.oldText: I said this almost involuntarily, and, with as little exercise of free will, my tears broke free. I did not cry loudly, though; I avoided sobbing. The thought of Mrs. O'Gall and Bitternutt Lodge struck cold to my heart; colder still the thought of all the ocean destined, it seemed, to rush between me and the master at whose side I now walked; and coldest of all the awareness of the wider ocean—wealth, class, custom—that lay between me and the one I naturally and inevitably loved.

23.47.oldText: "And when friends are on the eve of separation, they like to spend the little time that remains close to each other. Come! We'll talk over the voyage and the parting quietly for half an hour or so, while the stars come out up in heaven. Here is the chestnut tree: here is the bench at its old roots. Come, we will sit here in peace tonight, though we may never again be destined to sit here together." He sat down, and I with him.

23.48.oldText: "It is a long way to Ireland, Janet, and I am sorry to send my little friend on such a weary journey. But if I can't do better, what is to be done? Are you anything to me, do you think, Jane?"

23.49.oldText: I could risk no sort of answer now: my heart was full to breaking.

23.53.oldText: In listening, I sobbed convulsively; for I could no longer suppress what I was enduring. I was shaken from head to foot with raw distress. When I did speak, it was only to utter a passionate wish that I had never been born, or never come to Thornfield.

23.56.oldText: "I grieve to leave Thornfield. I love Thornfield—I love it because I have lived here a full and wonderful life, even if only briefly. I have not been trampled on. I have not been turned to stone. I have not been buried among inferior minds, shut out from every glimpse of what is bright and vital and high. I have talked, face to face, with what I revere, with what I delight in—with an original, a powerful, an expansive mind. I have known you, Mr. Rochester; and it strikes me with terror and anguish to feel I absolutely must be torn from you forever. I see the necessity of going; and it is like staring at the necessity of death."

23.93.oldText: "Am I a liar in your eyes?" he asked passionately. "Little sceptic, you shall be convinced. What love have I for Miss Ingram? None—and you know it. What love has she for me? None—as I have taken care to prove. I started a rumour that my fortune was not a third of what people supposed, and then I presented myself to see the result; it was coldness, both from her and her mother. I would not—I could not—marry Miss Ingram. You—you strange, you almost unearthly thing!—I love as my own flesh. You—poor and obscure, and small and plain as you are—I beg to accept me as a husband."

23.103.oldText: "Gratitude!" he exclaimed, and added wildly—"Jane, accept me quickly. Say, Edward—give me my name—Edward—I will marry you."

23.110.oldText: "God pardon me!" he murmured soon after. "And let no one interfere: I have her, and I will hold her."

23.112.oldText: "No—that is the best of it," he said. And if I had loved him less, I might have thought his tone and look of triumph savage. But sitting beside him, woken from the nightmare of separation, called to the paradise of union, I thought only of the bliss given me to drink in such abundant measure. Again and again he asked, "Are you happy, Jane?" And again and again I answered, "Yes." After which he murmured, "It will atone—it will atone. Did I not find her friendless, cold, and comfortless? Will I not guard and cherish and comfort her? Is there not love in my heart, and constancy in my resolve? It will stand justified before God's tribunal. I know my Maker approves what I do. For the world's judgment—I wash my hands of it. For human opinion—I defy it."

23.113.oldText: But what had happened to the night? The moon had not yet set, and we were all in shadow; I could barely see my master's face, near as I was. And what was wrong with the chestnut tree? It writhed and groaned; while wind roared through the laurel walk and swept over us.

24.2.oldText: I was not surprised, when I ran down into the hall, to find that a brilliant June morning had followed the night's storm, and to feel, through the open glass door, the breath of a fresh, fragrant breeze. Nature had to be cheerful when I was so happy. A beggar woman and her little boy — both pale, ragged figures — were coming up the walk. I ran down and gave them all the money I happened to have in my purse, three or four shillings. Whether it brought them good or ill, they had to share in my celebration. The rooks cawed, and brighter birds sang, but nothing was so merry or so musical as my own rejoicing heart.

24.9.oldText: "Jane, you look blooming, and smiling, and pretty," he said. "Truly pretty this morning. Is this my pale little elf? Is this my mustard-seed? This little sunny-faced girl with the dimpled cheek and rosy lips, the satin-smooth hazel hair and the radiant hazel eyes?" (I had green eyes, reader, but you must excuse the mistake. For him they were newly transformed, I suppose.)

24.12.oldText: I did, and I could not quite take it in. It made me dizzy. The feeling his announcement sent through me was something stronger than joy — something that struck and stunned. It was, I think, almost fear.

24.21.oldText: "You are a beauty in my eyes, and a beauty just after the desire of my heart — delicate and ethereal."

24.27.oldText: "You shall stay in Paris, Rome, and Naples — in Florence, Venice, and Vienna. All the ground I have wandered over shall be walked again by you. Wherever I stamped my foot, your light step shall follow. Ten years ago I flew through Europe half mad, with disgust, hate, and rage as my companions. Now I shall revisit it healed and renewed, with an angel at my side as my comfort."

24.37.oldText: "I never met your equal. Jane, you please me and you master me — you seem to submit, and I like the sense of pliancy you give. But while I am winding the soft, silken thread around my finger, it sends a thrill up my arm to my heart. I am influenced — conquered. And the influence is sweeter than I can express, and the conquest I undergo has a power beyond any triumph I can win. Why do you smile, Jane? What does that mysterious, uncanny expression mean?"

24.41.oldText: "Ask me something now, Janet — the smallest thing. I long to be asked, and to say yes."

24.54.oldText: "Is it, sir? You give in very quickly. How stern you look now! Your eyebrows have grown as thick as my finger, and your forehead resembles what I once saw described in some very astonishing poetry as 'a blue-piled thunderloft.' Will that be your married look, sir, I suppose?"

24.67.oldText: "That you may, my good little girl. There is not another being in the world who has the same pure love for me as yourself — for I take that comforting belief to heart, Jane, a faith in your affection."

24.74.oldText: I was soon dressed. When I heard Mr. Rochester leave Mrs. Fairfax's parlour, I hurried down to it. The old lady had been reading her morning portion of Scripture — the lesson for the day. Her Bible lay open before her, and her spectacles were upon it. Her reading, interrupted by Mr. Rochester's announcement, seemed now forgotten. Her eyes, fixed on the blank wall opposite, expressed the surprise of a quiet mind stirred by unexpected news. Seeing me, she roused herself, made a sort of effort to smile, and framed a few words of congratulation. But the smile faded, and the sentence was left unfinished. She put on her spectacles, shut the Bible, and pushed her chair back from the table.

24.89.oldText: "No, you are perfectly fine, and much improved of late. And Mr. Rochester, I daresay, is fond of you. I have always noticed that you were a sort of favourite of his. There are times when, for your sake, I have been a little uneasy at his obvious preference and have wished to warn you. But I did not like to suggest even the possibility of anything wrong. I knew such an idea would shock, perhaps offend you, and you were so sensible, so thoroughly modest and level-headed, that I hoped you could be trusted to look after yourself. Last night I cannot tell you what I suffered when I searched all over the house and could find neither you nor the master anywhere. And then, at midnight, I saw you come in with him."

24.96.oldText: "I told her no. I'll have no children along! I'll have only you."

24.98.oldText: "No, it wouldn't. She will be a nuisance."

24.125.oldText: The hour spent at Millcote was somewhat trying for me. Mr. Rochester made me go to a certain silk warehouse, where I was ordered to choose half a dozen dresses. I hated the business and begged to put it off — but no, it had to be done now. By means of urgent whispers, I reduced the half dozen to two. These, however, he vowed he would select himself. With anxiety I watched his eye roam over the colourful displays. He settled on a rich silk of the most brilliant amethyst and a superb pink satin. I told him in a fresh series of whispers that he might as well buy me a gold gown and a silver bonnet at once — I would certainly never dare to wear his choices. With enormous difficulty, for he was stubborn as a stone, I persuaded him to exchange them for a sober black satin and a pearl-grey silk. "It will do for the present," he said, "but he would yet see me glittering like a flower garden."

24.126.oldText: I was glad to get him out of the silk warehouse, and then out of a jeweller's shop. The more he bought me, the more my cheeks burned with annoyance and humiliation. As we got back into the carriage and I sat back, flushed and worn out, I remembered what, in the rush of events, dark and bright, I had completely forgotten — the letter from my uncle, John Eyre, to Mrs. Reed, about his intention to adopt me and make me his heir. "It would, indeed, be a relief," I thought, "if I had even the smallest independence. I can never bear being dressed like a doll by Mr. Rochester, or sitting like a second Danaë with the golden shower falling daily around me. I will write to Madeira the moment I get home and tell my uncle John I am going to be married, and to whom. If I had even the prospect of one day bringing Mr. Rochester an addition to his fortune, I could better endure being kept by him now." Somewhat comforted by this idea (which I carried out that very day), I ventured once more to meet my master's and lover's eye, which persistently sought mine, though I had been avoiding both his face and his gaze. He smiled, and I thought his smile was the kind a sultan might bestow, in a happy, fond moment, on a slave his gold and gems had enriched. I crushed his hand — which was forever chasing mine — vigorously, and thrust it back to him red from the passionate pressure.

24.127.oldText: "You need not look at me that way," I said. "If you do, I'll wear nothing but my old Lowood dresses to the end of the story. I'll be married in this lilac gingham. You may make a dressing gown for yourself out of the pearl-grey silk and an endless series of waistcoats out of the black satin."

24.129.oldText: The Eastern reference stung me again. "I'll not stand in for a harem," I said, "so don't consider me a substitute for one. If you have a taste for anything in that line, away with you, sir, to the bazaars of Istanbul without delay, and spend some of that spare cash you seem at a loss to use up satisfactorily here."

24.131.oldText: "I'll be preparing myself to go out as a missionary to preach liberty to the enslaved — your harem prisoners among the rest. I'll get admitted there, and I'll start a mutiny. And you, mighty overlord that you are, sir, shall in no time find yourself chained in our hands. Nor will I, for one, agree to cut your bonds until you have signed a charter — the most generous that any tyrant ever granted."

24.137.oldText: "Your love. And if I give you mine in return, that debt will be settled."

24.148.oldText: "I need a smoke, Jane, or a pinch of snuff, to comfort me through all this — to keep my composure, as Adèle would say. Unfortunately I have neither my cigar case nor my snuff box. But listen — come closer. It is your turn now, little tyrant, but mine will come soon. And when once I have fairly seized you, to have and to hold, I'll just — figuratively speaking — attach you to a chain like this" (touching his watch chain). "Yes, bonny wee thing, I'll wear you close to my heart, lest my jewel I should lose."

24.150.oldText: He duly summoned me to his presence that evening. I had prepared an occupation for him, for I was determined not to spend the whole time in private conversation. I remembered his fine voice. I knew he liked to sing — good singers generally do. I was no vocalist myself and, in his exacting judgment, no musician either, but I loved listening when the performance was good. No sooner had twilight begun to lower her blue and starry banner over the window than I rose, opened the piano, and begged him, for the love of heaven, to give me a song. He said I was a fickle witch and that he would rather sing another time, but I insisted that no time was like the present.

24.169.oldText: "That was a strange question to be put by his darling Jane."

24.171.oldText: "Oh, all he longed, all he prayed for, was that I might live with him! Death was not for such as I."

24.172.oldText: "Indeed it was. I had as good a right to die when my time came as he did. But I should wait for that time and not be carried off in some sacrificial ceremony."

24.173.oldText: "Would I forgive him for the selfish idea and prove my pardon by a reconciling kiss?"

24.177.oldText: "Would I be quiet and talk rationally?"

24.181.oldText: The system I had started, I pursued throughout the whole trial period, and with great success. He was kept, to be sure, rather cross and grumpy. But on the whole I could see he was excellently entertained, and that a lamb-like submission and dove-like tenderness, while feeding his tyranny more, would have pleased his judgment, satisfied his common sense, and even suited his taste less.

25.0.oldText: The month of courtship had run its course. Its very last hours were being counted down. There was no putting off the day that was coming — the wedding day — and all preparations for its arrival were complete. I, at least, had nothing more to do. There were my trunks, packed, locked, corded, lined up in a row along the wall of my little room. Tomorrow, at this time, they would be far along the road to London, and so would I (God willing) — or rather, not I, but one Jane Rochester, a person I did not yet know. The address cards alone remained to be attached. They lay, four little squares, in the drawer. Mr. Rochester had himself written the direction, "Mrs. Rochester, —— Hotel, London," on each. I could not bring myself to attach them, or to have them attached. Mrs. Rochester! She did not exist. She would not be born until tomorrow, sometime after eight o'clock in the morning. I would wait to be assured she had come into the world alive before I assigned to her all that property. It was enough that in the closet opposite my dressing table, garments said to be hers had already displaced my black Lowood dress and straw bonnet. For that suit of wedding clothes did not belong to me — the pearl-coloured gown, the filmy veil hanging from the claimed trunk. I shut the closet to conceal the strange, ghost-like clothing it contained, which, at this evening hour — nine o'clock — certainly gave off a most eerie shimmer through the shadows of my room. "I will leave you by yourself, white dream," I said. "I am feverish. I hear the wind blowing. I will go outdoors and feel it."

25.4.oldText: It was not without a certain wild pleasure that I ran before the wind, delivering my troubled mind to the boundless storm thundering through space. Coming down the laurel walk, I faced the wreck of the chestnut tree. It stood black and torn apart, its trunk split down the centre, gaping wide. The two halves were not broken from each other, for the firm base and strong roots kept them joined below. But the shared life was destroyed — the sap could flow no more. Their great boughs on each side were dead, and next winter's storms would surely bring one or both crashing to earth. Yet for now, they could still be called one tree — a ruin, but a complete ruin.

25.22.oldText: He set me down on the pavement. As the groom took his horse and he followed me into the hall, he told me to hurry and put on something dry, then return to him in the library. He stopped me as I headed for the staircase, to extract a promise that I would not be long. Nor was I long — in five minutes I rejoined him. I found him at supper.

25.56.oldText: "All day yesterday I was very busy and very happy in my constant activity. I am not, as you seem to think, troubled by any fears about the new life ahead of me. I think it a glorious thing to have the hope of living with you, because I love you. No, sir, don't caress me now — let me talk undisturbed. Yesterday I trusted in Providence, and believed that events were working together for your good and mine. It was a fine day, if you recall — the calm air and sky forbade worries about your safety or comfort on your journey. I walked a little while on the pavement after tea, thinking of you, and I pictured you so near me in my imagination that I scarcely missed your actual presence. I thought of the life that lay before me — your life, sir — an existence wider and more stirring than my own: as much more so as the depths of the ocean to which a brook runs are wider than the shallows of its own narrow channel. I wondered why moralists call this world a dreary wilderness. For me it blossomed like a rose. Just at sunset, the air turned cold and the sky cloudy. I went in. Sophie called me upstairs to look at my wedding dress, which they had just brought, and under it in the box I found your present — the veil which, in your princely extravagance, you had sent for from London, resolved, I suppose, since I would not have jewels, to trick me into accepting something equally costly. I smiled as I unfolded it, and planned how I would tease you about your aristocratic tastes and your efforts to disguise your common-born bride in the trappings of a noblewoman. I thought how I would carry down to you the square of plain lace I had prepared myself as a covering for my lowly head, and ask if that was not good enough for a woman who could bring her husband neither fortune, beauty, nor connections. I saw plainly how you would look, and heard your impatient protests and your proud dismissal of any need on your part to add to your wealth or raise your standing by marrying either a purse or a title."

25.58.oldText: "No, no, sir. Besides the delicacy and richness of the fabric, I found nothing but Fairfax Rochester's pride. And that did not frighten me, because I am used to seeing that particular demon. But, sir, as it grew dark, the wind rose. It blew yesterday evening, not as it blows now — wild and high — but with a low, moaning sound, far more unsettling. I wished you were home. I came into this room, and the sight of the empty chair and fireless hearth chilled me. For some time after I went to bed, I could not sleep. A sense of anxious excitement plagued me. The rising gale seemed to muffle some mournful under-sound. Whether it came from inside the house or outside I could not at first tell, but it returned, faint yet doleful, at every pause in the wind. At last I made out it must be some dog howling in the distance. I was glad when it stopped. When I fell asleep, I continued in dreams the idea of a dark and gusty night. I continued also the wish to be with you, and I felt a strange, sorrowful awareness of some barrier separating us. During all my first sleep, I was following the twists of an unknown road. Total darkness surrounded me. Rain pelted me. I was burdened with a little child — a very small creature, too young and weak to walk, which shivered in my cold arms and wailed miserably in my ear. I thought, sir, that you were on the road far ahead of me, and I strained every nerve to overtake you, and made effort upon effort to call your name and beg you to stop — but my movements were shackled, and my voice kept dying away, wordless. While you, I felt, drew farther and farther away with every moment."

25.61.oldText: "Well," he said, after some minutes' silence, "it is strange, but that sentence has pierced my heart painfully. Why? I think because you said it with such earnest, almost religious intensity, and because your upward gaze at me now is the very essence of faith, truth, and devotion. It is too much as if some spirit were near me. Look wicked, Jane — as you know well how to look. Show me one of your wild, shy, teasing smiles. Tell me you hate me — tease me, provoke me. Do anything but move me. I would rather be angered than saddened."

25.64.oldText: I shook my head. "What! Is there more? But I will not believe it to be anything important. I warn you of my disbelief beforehand. Go on."

25.83.oldText: It removed my veil from its gaunt head, tore it in two, and flinging both pieces on the floor, trampled on them.

25.85.oldText: "It drew aside the window curtain and looked out. Perhaps it saw dawn approaching, for, taking the candle, it retreated to the door. Just at my bedside, the figure stopped. The fiery eyes glared at me — she thrust the candle close to my face and snuffed it out before my eyes. I was aware her ghastly face hovered over mine, and I lost consciousness. For the second time in my life — only the second time — I fainted from sheer terror."

25.86.oldText: "Who was with you when you came to?"

25.87.oldText: "No one, sir, but the broad daylight. I rose, bathed my head and face in water, drank a long draught. I felt that though I was weak I was not ill, and I decided that to no one but you would I confide this vision. Now, sir, tell me who and what that woman was."

25.88.oldText: "The creation of an overstimulated brain — that is certain. I must be careful with you, my treasure. Nerves like yours were not made for rough handling."

25.89.oldText: "Sir, believe me, my nerves were not at fault. The thing was real. The event actually happened."

25.90.oldText: "And your earlier dreams — were they real too? Is Thornfield Hall a ruin? Am I torn from you by impossible obstacles? Am I leaving you without a tear — without a kiss — without a word?"

25.92.oldText: "Am I about to? Why, the day has already begun which is to bind us forever. And when we are once united, there shall be no return of these mental terrors. I guarantee that."

25.93.oldText: "Mental terrors, sir! I wish I could believe them to be only that. I wish it more now than ever, since even you cannot explain the mystery of that awful visitor."

25.94.oldText: "And since I cannot, Jane, it must have been unreal."

25.95.oldText: "But, sir, when I said as much to myself on rising this morning, and when I looked around the room to gather courage and comfort from the cheerful sight of each familiar object in full daylight, there — on the carpet — I saw what gave the flat lie to my theory: the veil, torn from top to bottom in two halves!"

25.96.oldText: I felt Mr. Rochester flinch and shudder. He hastily flung his arms around me. "Thank God!" he exclaimed. "That if anything evil did come near you last night, it was only the veil that was harmed. Oh, to think what might have happened!"

25.97.oldText: He drew his breath short and strained me so close to him I could scarcely breathe. After some minutes' silence, he continued, more cheerfully —

25.98.oldText: "Now, Janet, I'll explain it all to you. It was half dream, half reality. A woman did, I have no doubt, enter your room. And that woman was — must have been — Grace Poole. You call her a strange creature yourself, and from all you know you have reason to. What did she do to me? What to Mason? In a state between sleeping and waking, you noticed her entrance and her actions. But feverish, almost delirious as you were, you gave her a monstrous appearance different from her own. The long, wild hair, the swollen dark face, the exaggerated height — those were products of nightmare. The spiteful tearing of the veil was real — and that is just like her. I see you would ask why I keep such a woman in my house. When we have been married a year and a day, I will tell you — but not now. Are you satisfied, Jane? Do you accept my explanation?"

25.99.oldText: I thought about it, and in truth it seemed the only possible one. Satisfied I was not, but to please him I tried to appear so — and relieved I certainly did feel. So I answered him with a contented smile. And now, as it was long past one, I prepared to leave him.

25.100.oldText: "Does Sophie not sleep with Adèle in the nursery?" he asked, as I lit my candle.

25.102.oldText: "And there is room enough in Adèle's little bed for you. You must share it with her tonight, Jane. It is no wonder the incident you have described should make you nervous, and I would rather you did not sleep alone. Promise me to go to the nursery."

25.103.oldText: "I shall be very glad to, sir."

25.104.oldText: "And fasten the door securely on the inside. Wake Sophie when you go upstairs, on the pretext of asking her to rouse you in good time tomorrow, for you must be dressed and have finished breakfast before eight. And now, no more dark thoughts. Chase dull care away, Janet. Don't you hear how softly the wind has dropped? And there is no more rain beating against the window-panes. Look here" — he lifted the curtain — "it is a lovely night!"

25.105.oldText: It was. Half the sky was pure and clear. The clouds, now retreating before the wind, which had shifted to the west, were filing off eastward in long, silver columns. The moon shone peacefully.

25.106.oldText: "Well," said Mr. Rochester, gazing searchingly into my eyes, "how is my Janet now?"

25.107.oldText: "The night is serene, sir, and so am I."

25.108.oldText: "And you will not dream of separation and sorrow tonight, but of happy love and blissful union."

25.109.oldText: This prediction was only half fulfilled. I did not indeed dream of sorrow, but neither did I dream of joy — for I never slept at all. With little Adèle in my arms, I watched the slumber of childhood — so peaceful, so calm, so innocent — and waited for the coming day. All my life was awake and stirring in my body. As soon as the sun rose, I rose too. I remember Adèle clung to me as I left her. I remember I kissed her as I loosened her little hands from my neck. And I cried over her with strange emotion, and left her because I feared my sobs would wake her still sound sleep. She seemed the emblem of my past life, and he whom I was now to dress myself to meet, the dread but adored figure of my unknown future day.

26.22.oldText: Our place was taken at the communion rail. Hearing a careful step behind me, I glanced over my shoulder. One of the strangers — a gentleman, clearly — was advancing up the central aisle. The service began. The explanation of the purpose of marriage was read through, and then the clergyman came a step further forward and, bending slightly towards Mr. Rochester, went on.

26.27.oldText: A deep silence fell when he had uttered that word, with quiet but low force. Presently Mr. Wood said —

26.49.oldText: Mr. Rochester, on hearing the name, clenched his teeth. He experienced, too, a sort of violent, convulsive tremor. Near to him as I was, I felt the spasm of fury or despair run through his body. The second stranger, who had until then lingered in the background, now drew near. A pale face looked over the solicitor's shoulder — yes, it was Mason himself. Mr. Rochester turned and glared at him. His eye, as I have often said, was a dark eye. It had now a tawny, even bloody light in its depth. His face flushed — his olive cheek and pale forehead received a glow as from a spreading, rising fire. He stirred, lifted his strong arm — he could have struck Mason, dashed him to the church floor, knocked the breath from his body with one ruthless blow — but Mason shrank away and cried faintly, "Good God!" Contempt fell cold on Mr. Rochester — his passion died as if a blight had withered it. He only asked — "What have you to say?"

26.51.oldText: "The devil take you if you cannot answer clearly. I ask again — what have you to say?"

26.69.oldText: A fierce cry seemed to contradict her favourable report. The clothed creature rose up and stood tall on its hind feet.

26.78.oldText: "Watch out!" cried Grace. The three gentlemen retreated at the same moment. Mr. Rochester flung me behind him. The madwoman sprang and seized his throat savagely, sinking her teeth into his cheek. They struggled. She was a big woman, nearly as tall as her husband, and heavy besides. She showed tremendous force in the fight — more than once she almost throttled him, athletic as he was. He could have brought her down with a single well-placed blow, but he would not strike. He would only wrestle. At last he mastered her arms. Grace Poole gave him a cord, and he tied them behind her. With more rope, which was near at hand, he bound her to a chair. The task was performed amid the fiercest screams and the most violent struggles. Mr. Rochester then turned to the onlookers. He looked at them with a smile both bitter and desolate.

26.79.oldText: "That is my wife," he said. "Such is the only embrace my marriage will ever know — such are the tender moments that will fill my leisure hours! And this is what I wished to have" — laying his hand on my shoulder — "this young girl, who stands so grave and quiet at the mouth of hell, looking calmly at the antics of a demon. I wanted her just as a change after that savage ordeal. Wood and Briggs, look at the difference! Compare these clear eyes with the red ones over there — this face with that mask — this figure with that bulk. Then judge me, priest of the gospel and man of the law, and remember that with what judgment you judge, you shall be judged! Off with you now. I must lock up my prize."

26.83.oldText: "Mr. Mason does. Mr. Eyre has been the Funchal correspondent of his firm for some years. When your uncle received your letter mentioning the planned union between yourself and Mr. Rochester, Mr. Mason, who was staying in Madeira to restore his health on his way back to Jamaica, happened to be with him. Mr. Eyre mentioned the news, for he knew that my client here was acquainted with a gentleman named Rochester. Mr. Mason, as astonished and distressed as you may imagine, revealed the true state of affairs. Your uncle, I am sorry to say, is now on his sickbed — from which, considering the nature of his disease and the stage it has reached, it is unlikely he will ever rise. He could not then hurry to England himself to rescue you from the trap you had fallen into, but he begged Mr. Mason to lose no time in taking steps to prevent the fraudulent marriage. He referred him to me for help. I acted with all speed, and am thankful I was not too late — as you, no doubt, must be also. Were I not morally certain that your uncle will be dead before you reach Madeira, I would advise you to accompany Mr. Mason back. But as it is, I think you had better remain in England until you can hear further, either from or of Mr. Eyre. Have we anything else to stay for?" he asked of Mr. Mason.

26.85.oldText: I heard him go as I stood at the half-open door of my own room, to which I had now retreated. The house emptied, I shut myself in, fastened the bolt so that no one might intrude, and proceeded — not to weep, not to mourn (I was yet too numb for that) — but mechanically to take off the wedding dress and replace it with the plain gown I had worn yesterday, as I thought, for the last time. I then sat down. I felt weak and tired. I leaned my arms on the table and my head dropped onto them. And now I thought. Until now I had only heard, seen, moved — followed up and down where I was led or dragged — watched event rush on event, revelation open beyond revelation. But now, I thought.

26.88.oldText: Jane Eyre, who had been a passionate, expectant woman — almost a bride — was a cold, solitary girl again. Her life was pale. Her prospects were desolate. A Christmas frost had come at midsummer. A white December storm had whirled over June. Ice glazed the ripe apples. Drifts crushed the blooming roses. On hayfield and cornfield lay a frozen shroud. Lanes which last night blushed full of flowers were today pathless with untrodden snow. And the woods, which twelve hours ago waved leafy and fragrant as tropical groves, now spread waste, wild, and white as pine forests in wintry Norway. My hopes were all dead — struck with a sudden doom, such as, in one night, fell on all the firstborn in the land of Egypt. I looked at my cherished wishes, yesterday so blooming and bright. They lay stark, cold, livid corpses that could never revive. I looked at my love — that feeling which was my master's, which he had created. It shivered in my heart like a suffering child in a cold cradle. Sickness and anguish had seized it. It could not seek Mr. Rochester's arms — it could not draw warmth from his breast. Oh, never more could it turn to him, for faith was shattered — trust was destroyed! Mr. Rochester was not to me what he had been, for he was not what I had thought him. I would not call him wicked. I would not say he had betrayed me. But the quality of untarnished truth was gone from my idea of him, and from his presence I must go. That I saw clearly. When — how — where, I could not yet determine. But he himself, I had no doubt, would hurry me from Thornfield. Real affection, it seemed, he could not have for me. It had been only fitful passion — that was thwarted, and he would want me no more. I should fear even to cross his path now. My very sight must be hateful to him. Oh, how blind my eyes had been! How weak my conduct!

26.89.oldText: My eyes were covered and closed. Swirling darkness seemed to swim around me, and thought came in as black and confused a flood. Abandoned by myself, emptied and powerless, I seemed to have lain down in the dried-up bed of a great river. I heard a flood unleashed in remote mountains and felt the torrent coming. To rise I had no will. To flee I had no strength. I lay faint, longing to be dead. One idea only still throbbed with life inside me — a memory of God. It stirred a wordless prayer. These words wandered up and down in my lightless mind, as something that should be whispered, but no energy was found to speak them —

27.5.oldText: I rose up suddenly, terrified by the solitude that so ruthless a judge haunted—by the silence that so awful a voice filled. My head swam as I stood upright. I realized I was growing faint from agitation and hunger; I had eaten and drunk nothing all day, having skipped breakfast. And with a strange pang, I now reflected that, long as I had been shut in here, no one had sent a message to ask how I was or to invite me downstairs. Not even little Adèle had knocked at the door. Not even Mrs. Fairfax had come looking for me. "Friends always forget those whom fortune abandons," I murmured, as I unbolted the door and stepped out. I stumbled over an obstacle—my head was still dizzy, my vision dim, and my limbs feeble. I could not recover myself. I fell, but not to the ground: an outstretched arm caught me. I looked up—I was being held by Mr. Rochester, who sat in a chair across my bedroom threshold.

27.13.oldText: "I cannot. I am tired and sick. I want some water." He let out a sort of shuddering sigh, and taking me in his arms, carried me downstairs. At first I did not know what room he had brought me to; everything was blurred to my glazed sight. Soon I felt the reviving warmth of a fire; for, summer as it was, I had grown ice-cold in my room. He put wine to my lips; I tasted it and revived. Then I ate something he offered me, and was soon myself again. I was in the library—sitting in his chair—he was very close. "If I could leave this life now, without too sharp a pang, it would be well for me," I thought. "Then I would not have to crack my heartstrings in tearing them away from Mr. Rochester. I must leave him, it seems. I do not want to leave him—I cannot leave him."

27.26.oldText: "Oh, Adèle will go to school—I have already settled that. Nor do I mean to torment you with the hideous associations and memories of Thornfield Hall—this accursed place—this tent of Achan—this vault of insolence, offering the ghastliness of living death to the light of the open sky—this narrow stone hell, with its one real demon, worse than a legion of the kind we imagine. Jane, you shall not stay here, and neither will I. I was wrong ever to bring you to Thornfield Hall, knowing as I did how it was haunted. I ordered them to hide from you, before I ever met you, all knowledge of the curse on this place—simply because I feared Adèle would never keep a governess if the woman knew what fellow resident she shared the house with. And my plans would not let me move the madwoman elsewhere—though I own an old house, Ferndean Manor, even more remote and hidden than this, where I could have housed her safely enough, had not a scruple about the unhealthy location, deep in the woods, made my conscience recoil from the arrangement. Probably those damp walls would soon have relieved me of her. But to each villain his own vice; and mine is not a tendency toward indirect murder, even of what I most hate."

27.27.oldText: "However, concealing the madwoman's presence from you was something like covering a child with a cloak and laying it near a poison tree: that demon's proximity is toxic, and always was.
