But I will shut up Thornfield Hall. I will nail up the front door and board the lower windows. I will pay Mrs. Poole two hundred a year to live here with my wife, as you call that fearful creature. Grace will do much for money, and she shall have her son—the keeper at Grimsby Retreat—to bear her company and help her during the fits, when my wife is driven by her demons to burn people in their beds at night, to stab them, to tear the flesh from their bones, and so on—"

27.54.oldText: "Of course: I told you that you would. I'll skip over the madness about parting from me. You mean you must become a part of me. As for the new existence, it's exactly right: you shall still be my wife. I am not married. You shall be Mrs. Rochester—both in reality and in name. I shall be faithful only to you for as long as we both live. You shall go to a place I have in the south of France: a whitewashed villa on the shores of the Mediterranean. There you shall live a happy, protected, and perfectly innocent life. Never fear that I wish to lure you into sin—to make you my mistress. Why did you shake your head? Jane, you must be reasonable, or I swear I shall go mad again."

27.65.oldText: "Well, Jane, being so, he was determined to keep the estate intact. He could not bear the thought of dividing his property and leaving me a fair share: everything, he resolved, should go to my brother Rowland. Yet he could not stand the idea of a son of his being a poor man. I had to be provided for through a wealthy marriage. He found me a match early on. Mr. Mason, a West Indian planter and merchant, was an old acquaintance of his. My father confirmed that his wealth was real and vast; he made inquiries. Mr. Mason, he discovered, had a son and a daughter; and he learned that Mason could and would give the daughter a fortune of thirty thousand pounds. That was enough. When I left university, I was sent to Jamaica to marry a bride who had already been chosen for me. My father said nothing about her money, but he told me Miss Mason was the beauty of Spanish Town—and that was no lie. I found her a striking woman, in the style of Blanche Ingram: tall, dark, and majestic. Her family wanted to secure me because I came from good stock; and so did she. They showed her to me at parties, magnificently dressed. I rarely saw her alone and had very little private conversation with her. She flattered me and lavishly displayed her charms and accomplishments for my pleasure. Every man in her circle seemed to admire her and envy me. I was dazzled, excited. My senses were aroused; and being ignorant, inexperienced, and naive, I thought I loved her. There is no folly so absurd that the stupid rivalries of society, the recklessness and blindness of youth, will not drive a man to commit it. Her relatives encouraged me; rivals goaded me; she seduced me: a marriage was accomplished almost before I knew what had happened. Oh, I have no respect for myself when I think of that act!—an agony of inward shame overwhelms me. I never loved her, I never respected her, I did not even know her. I was not sure of a single virtue in her nature. I had seen neither modesty, nor kindness, nor honesty, nor refinement in her mind or manners—and I married her: gross, groveling, blind fool that I was! With less sin I might have—but let me remember who I am speaking to."

27.71.oldText: "Pity, Jane, from some people is a poisonous and insulting kind of offering—the sort you are justified in hurling back in the faces of those who give it. But that is the pity born of callous, selfish hearts: a self-centered pain at hearing of suffering, mixed with ignorant contempt for those who have endured it. But that is not your pity, Jane. It is not the feeling that fills your whole face at this moment—that brims in your eyes—that heaves in your chest—that trembles through the hand you have placed in mine. Your pity, my darling, is the suffering mother of love: its anguish is the birth-pang of that divine passion. I accept it, Jane; let the child come freely—my arms are ready to receive her."

27.76.oldText: "I said this while I knelt and unlocked a trunk containing a pair of loaded pistols: I meant to shoot myself. I entertained the thought for only a moment; for, not being insane, the crisis of pure and total despair that had given rise to the wish and plan of self-destruction passed in a second."

27.87.oldText: "When you are curious, Jane, you always make me smile. You open your eyes like an eager bird and shift restlessly now and then, as if words in speech don't come fast enough for you and you want to read the very heart itself. But before I go on, tell me what you mean by your 'Well, sir?' It is a little phrase you use constantly, and many a time it has drawn me on and on through endless talk. I am not sure why."

27.91.oldText: "I can tell you whether I found anyone I liked, and whether I asked her to marry me. But what she said is yet to be recorded in the book of Fate. For ten long years I roamed, living first in one capital, then another: sometimes in St. Petersburg, more often in Paris, occasionally in Rome, Naples, and Florence. With plenty of money and the passport of an old family name, I could choose my own company. No circles were closed to me. I looked for my ideal of a woman among English ladies, French countesses, Italian signoras, and German noblewomen. I could not find her. Sometimes, for a fleeting moment, I thought I caught a glance, heard a voice, saw a figure that promised the fulfillment of my dream—but I was soon disappointed. You are not to think I demanded perfection, either of mind or body. I longed only for what suited me—for the opposite of the Creole. And I longed in vain. Among them all I found not one whom, had I been ever so free, I—warned as I was of the risks, the horrors, the revulsion of mismatched unions—would have asked to marry me. Disappointment made me reckless. I tried pleasure-seeking—never debauchery: that I hated, and still hate. That was my wife's nature: a deep-rooted disgust at it and at her restrained me considerably, even in my pleasures. Any enjoyment that bordered on excess seemed to bring me closer to her and her vices, and I avoided it."

27.97.oldText: "On a frosty winter afternoon, I rode within sight of Thornfield Hall. Detested place! I expected no peace there—no pleasure. On a stile in Hay Lane I saw a quiet little figure sitting by itself. I passed it as carelessly as I did the pollarded willow across from it: I had no premonition of what it would be to me. No inner warning that the ruler of my life—my spirit for good or evil—waited there in humble form. I did not know it, even when, after Mesrour's accident, it came up and gravely offered to help me. Childish and slender creature! It seemed as if a sparrow had hopped to my foot and offered to carry me on its tiny wing. I was surly; but the thing would not go away: it stood beside me with a strange persistence, and looked and spoke with a sort of authority. I needed help, and from that hand: and helped I was."

27.100.oldText: "I paid you more attention. There was something glad in your look and warm in your manner when you talked. I saw you had a social heart; it was the silent schoolroom—the tedium of your life—that made you melancholy. I allowed myself the pleasure of being kind to you; kindness stirred emotion quickly. Your face grew soft, your voice gentle. I liked hearing my name spoken by your lips in a grateful, happy tone. I used to enjoy a chance meeting with you, Jane, in those days. There was a charming hesitation in your manner: you glanced at me with a slight unease—a hovering doubt. You did not know what my mood might be—whether I would play the master and be stern, or the friend and be warm. I was now too fond of you to often pretend the first; and when I extended my hand warmly, such color and light and joy rose in your young, hopeful face that I could barely keep myself from pulling you right then and there to my heart."

27.104.oldText: "You see now how things stand—do you not?" he continued. "After a youth and manhood spent half in unspeakable misery and half in dreary solitude, I have for the first time found what I can truly love—I have found you. You are my kindred spirit—my better self—my good angel. I am bound to you with a powerful attachment. I think you good, gifted, and lovely: a deep, solemn passion has taken hold of my heart. It draws me to you, wraps my existence around you, and, burning in a pure, powerful flame, fuses you and me into one."

27.105.oldText: "It was because I felt and knew this that I resolved to marry you. To tell me I already had a wife is meaningless: you know now that I had only a hideous demon. I was wrong to try to deceive you; but I feared a stubbornness in your character. I feared deeply ingrained principles. I wanted to have you safe before risking any confessions. This was cowardly: I should have appealed to your nobility and generosity from the start, as I do now—opened to you plainly my life of agony—described my hunger and thirst for a higher and worthier existence—shown you not my resolution (that word is too weak), but my irresistible drive to love faithfully and well, where I am faithfully and well loved in return. Then I should have asked you to accept my pledge of faithfulness and give me yours. Jane—give it to me now."

27.127.oldText: "Then you snatch love and innocence from me? You fling me back on lust for a passion—vice for an occupation?"

27.130.oldText: This was true. And while he spoke, my very conscience and reason turned traitor against me and accused me of a crime in resisting him. They spoke almost as loudly as Feeling: and Feeling clamored wildly. "Oh, give in!" it said. "Think of his misery; think of his danger—look at the state he will be in when left alone; remember his reckless nature; think about what desperate acts might follow on your refusal—soothe him; save him; love him; tell him you love him and will be his. Who in the world cares for you? or who will be hurt by what you do?"

27.131.oldText: Still, the answer was unyielding—"I care for myself. The more alone, the more friendless, the more without support I am, the more I will respect myself. I will keep the law given by God, sanctioned by man. I will hold to the principles I received when I was sane, not mad—as I am now. Laws and principles are not for the times when there is no temptation: they are for moments like this, when body and soul rise up against their authority. Firm they stand; and I shall not break them. If at my individual convenience I might break them, what would they be worth? They have worth—so I have always believed; and if I cannot believe it now, it is because I am out of my mind, with my blood on fire and my veins churning. I have a prior resolution—that resolution shall stand."

27.132.oldText: I did stand by it. Mr. Rochester, reading my face, saw that I had. His fury reached its peak: he had to yield to it for a moment, whatever came next. He crossed the floor and seized my arm and gripped my waist. He seemed to devour me with his blazing gaze: physically, at that moment, I felt powerless as a reed. But mentally I felt as if I stood somewhere beyond his grasp, above his reach—an essence that neither his fury nor his despair could touch. I looked at his face—and a strange energy ran through me. He had already released my waist and had only my arm—I moved to free myself from that too.

27.133.oldText: "Never," said he through clenched teeth, "never was anything at once so fragile and so unconquerable. She feels like a mere reed in my hand!" (And he shook me with the force of his grip.) "I could bend her with my finger and thumb: and what good would it do if I bent, if I tore up, if I crushed her? Think about this, conscience—and think about the effect on yourself, passion. Think about it—consider it—think about her eye, her face: think about what she is. Look at the look in those eyes. How soft and full of feeling they are! How they still shine with a gentle glow—a glow of devotion and grief for me! Look at the sweet lines of that mouth!" (I was startled, because these last words were said as if to a vision, something unseen by me but apparently visible to him.) "I could bend her" (his voice was tortured), "but would she bend? Would she yield willingly? No—even if I tried, I’d find only tow and splinter in my hands. Forced compliance would give me only what? Only this small frame—this pale face, these delicate features. And the soul? Her soul would escape from my grip like a caged skylark launching upward through shattered bars into the clouds."

27.150.oldText: That night I never expected to sleep; but a slumber fell on me as soon as I lay down. I was carried back in my dreams to childhood: I dreamt I lay in the red room at Gateshead; that the night was dark, and my mind filled with strange fears. The light that long ago had terrified me flashed on the wall. The ghost-like figure of a gleaming moon rose into the sky. I watched it with the panic of a child. As it climbed the dark ceiling and took shape, it spoke to my spirit—unutterably far away, yet so close, whispering through my heart—

27.153.oldText: So I answered after I had woken from the trancelike dream. It was still night, but July nights are short: soon after midnight, dawn comes. "It cannot be too early to start the task I must complete," I thought. I rose. I was dressed; for I had taken off nothing but my shoes. I knew where to find a small silk purse in my drawer: it held twenty shillings—my entire fortune. I picked up my straw bonnet and pinned on my shawl. I took the purse and my slippers, which I would put on later, and stole silently from my room.

27.157.oldText: That kind master, who could not sleep now, was waiting impatiently for morning. He would send for me in the morning; I would be gone. He would have me searched for: in vain. He would feel himself abandoned; his love rejected. He would suffer; perhaps grow desperate. I thought of this too. My hand moved toward the lock. I stopped myself. I forced myself away. I crept on.

27.158.oldText: In a daze I made my way downstairs. I knew what I had to do, and I did it mechanically. I found the key to the side door in the kitchen. I also found a small bottle of oil and a feather. I oiled the key and the lock. I got some water; I got some bread: for I might have to walk far, and my strength, severely tested in the last day, must not fail me completely. I opened the door, stepped through it, and closed it softly. Dim dawn glimmered in the yard. The gate, too, stood open. I slipped through and was gone.

27.159.oldText: A mile off, beyond the fields, lay a road that led in the opposite direction from Millcote; a road I had never traveled but often noticed, wondering where it went. That was where I headed now. No reflection was allowed: not a single glance back, not even one forward. Not one thought of the future could be permitted. The first thing to be done was to move past the moors and beyond the reach of anyone from Thornfield.

27.160.oldText: I skirted fields and hedges and lanes until after sunrise. I believe it was a lovely summer morning: I know my shoes, which I had put on as I left the house, were soon wet with dew. But I looked neither at the rising sun, nor the smiling sky, nor the awakening countryside. A condemned prisoner being led to the scaffold thinks not of the flowers that line the road, but of the block and axe at its end—or rather of the grave that waits beyond. I thought of a drain deep and dark through which a torrent of blood was pouring, from which no dam could stop the flow.

27.161.oldText: When I got there, I was forced to stop and rest under the hedge; and while I sat, I heard wheels and saw a coach approaching. I stood and raised my hand; it stopped. I asked where it was going: the driver named a place far away, where I was sure Mr. Rochester had no connections. I asked the fare: he said thirty shillings. I counted out my purse. It came to twenty. I told him I could pay only that much. He said he would take me for that. I got in—the coach drove on.

28.3.oldText: Some time passed before I felt calm even here. I had a vague dread that wild cattle might be nearby, or that some hunter or poacher might discover me. If a gust of wind swept the wasteland, I looked up, fearing it was the charge of a bull; if a bird whistled, I imagined it a man. Finding my fears groundless, however, and soothed by the deep silence that settled as evening gave way to night, I grew more confident. Until now I had not thought; I had only listened, watched, dreaded. Now I regained the ability to reflect.

28.7.oldText: Beside the crag the heath was very deep: when I lay down my feet were buried in it; rising high on each side, it left only a narrow gap for the night air to enter. I folded my shawl double and spread it over me as a blanket; a low, mossy rise served as my pillow. Lodged like this, I was not, at least at the start of the night, cold.

28.8.oldText: My rest might have been peaceful enough, except that a sad heart kept breaking it. It cried out over its gaping wounds, its inward bleeding, its severed bonds. It trembled for Mr. Rochester and his fate; it mourned him with bitter pity; it called for him with ceaseless longing; and, helpless as a bird with both wings broken, it still fluttered its shattered feathers in useless attempts to reach him.

28.9.oldText: Worn out by this torture of thought, I rose to my knees. Night had come, and her planets had risen: a safe, still night, too serene for the company of fear. We know that God is everywhere; but surely we feel His presence most when His works are spread before us on the grandest scale; and it is in the unclouded night sky, where His worlds wheel their silent course, that we read most clearly His infinity, His power, His presence everywhere. I had risen to my knees to pray for Mr. Rochester. Looking up, I saw through tear-dimmed eyes the mighty Milky Way. Remembering what it was—what countless star systems swept through space like a soft trail of light—I felt the might and strength of God. I was certain of His power to save what He had made: I grew convinced that neither earth would perish, nor any of the souls it held. I turned my prayer to thanksgiving: the Source of Life was also the Savior of spirits. Mr. Rochester was safe: he was God's, and by God he would be guarded. I nestled again against the hillside; and before long, sleep made me forget my sorrow.

28.10.oldText: But the next day, Want came to me—pale and bare. Long after the little birds had left their nests; long after bees had come in the sweet early hours to gather heath honey before the dew had dried—when the long morning shadows had shrunk and the sun filled earth and sky—I got up and looked around me.

28.11.oldText: What a still, hot, perfect day! What a golden desert this spreading moor! Sunshine everywhere. I wished I could live in it and on it. I saw a lizard run over the crag; I saw a bee busy among the sweet bilberries. I would gladly at that moment have become a bee or a lizard, so I might have found proper food and a permanent home here. But I was a human being, with a human being's needs: I could not linger where there was nothing to supply them. I got up; I looked back at the bed I had left. Hopeless about the future, I wished only this—that my Maker had that night seen fit to take my soul while I slept; and that this weary body, freed by death from further struggle against fate, might now simply decay in peace and mingle with the soil of this wilderness. Life, however, was still mine, with all its demands, its pains, and its responsibilities. The burden must be carried; the need provided for; the suffering endured; the duty fulfilled. I set out.

28.12.oldText: Reaching Whitcross again, I followed a road that led away from the sun, now fierce and high. No other factor guided my choice. I walked a long time, and when I thought I had gone far enough and might in good conscience give in to the fatigue that nearly overwhelmed me—might stop this forced march and, sitting on a nearby stone, surrender to the numbness that weighed down my heart and limbs—I heard a bell ring. A church bell.

28.13.oldText: I turned toward the sound, and there, among the picturesque hills whose changes and features I had stopped noticing an hour ago, I saw a hamlet and a spire. The whole valley to my right was full of pasture fields, cornfields, and woods; and a glittering stream ran zigzag through the varied shades of green, the ripening grain, the dark woodland, the clear and sunny meadow. Called back to the road by the rumbling of wheels, I saw a heavily loaded wagon laboring up the hill, and not far beyond were two cows and their drover. Human life and human labor were near. I had to keep going: fight to live and bend to work like the rest.

28.14.oldText: Around two o'clock I entered the village. At the bottom of its single street there was a little shop with some loaves of bread in the window. I wanted a loaf of bread desperately. With that nourishment I could perhaps recover a degree of energy: without it, going on would be nearly impossible. The desire for some strength and vitality returned as soon as I was among other people. I felt it would be degrading to collapse from hunger on the pavement of a hamlet. Did I have anything on me I could trade for one of those rolls? I considered. I had a small silk handkerchief tied around my throat; I had my gloves. I had little idea how men and women in the depths of poverty went about things. I did not know whether either of these items would be accepted: probably they would not; but I had to try.

28.15.oldText: I entered the shop: a woman was there. Seeing a respectably dressed person—a lady, she assumed—she came forward politely. How could she help me? I was seized with shame: my tongue would not form the request I had prepared. I did not dare offer her the half-worn gloves, the creased handkerchief: besides, I felt it would be absurd. I only asked if I might sit down for a moment, as I was tired. Disappointed at not getting a customer, she coolly agreed. She pointed to a seat; I sank into it. I desperately wanted to cry; but knowing how inappropriate that would be, I held it back. Soon I asked her "if there were any dressmakers or seamstresses in the village?"

28.16.oldText: "Yes; two or three. Quite as many as there was work for."

28.17.oldText: I thought it over. I was driven to the breaking point now. I stood face to face with Necessity. I was someone without a resource, without a friend, without a coin. I had to do something. What? I had to apply somewhere. Where?

28.18.oldText: "Did she know of any place in the neighborhood where a servant was needed?"

28.20.oldText: "What was the main trade in this place? What did most of the people do?"

28.21.oldText: "Some were farm workers; a good many worked at Mr. Oliver's needle factory and at the foundry."

28.25.oldText: "I don't know," was the answer. "Some do one thing, and some another. Poor folk have to get by as they can."

28.26.oldText: She seemed tired of my questions: and indeed, what right had I to pester her? A neighbor or two came in; my chair was clearly needed. I left.

28.27.oldText: I walked up the street, looking as I went at all the houses on either side; but I could find no reason or incentive to enter any. I wandered around the hamlet, sometimes going a short distance and returning, for an hour or more. Utterly exhausted, and suffering terribly now for lack of food, I turned down a lane and sat under the hedge. Before many minutes had passed, however, I was on my feet again, searching for something—a resource, or at least some information. A pretty little house stood at the top of the lane, with a garden in front, perfectly neat and brilliantly blooming. I stopped at it. What business did I have approaching the white door or touching the shining knocker? How could the people inside possibly have any interest in helping me? Yet I drew near and knocked. A mild-looking, neatly dressed young woman opened the door. In a voice you would expect from a hopeless heart and a failing body—a voice wretchedly low and unsteady—I asked if a servant was needed here?

28.28.oldText: "No," she said; "we do not keep a servant."

28.29.oldText: "Can you tell me where I could find work of any kind?" I went on. "I am a stranger, without anyone I know in this place. I want some work: no matter what."

28.30.oldText: But it was not her job to think for me, or to find me a place. Besides, in her eyes, how suspicious my character, position, and story must have looked. She shook her head; she "was sorry she could give me no information," and the white door closed, quite gently and politely: but it shut me out. If she had held it open a little longer, I believe I would have begged for a piece of bread; for I was now that desperate.

28.31.oldText: I could not bear to go back to the dreary village, where no prospect of help was in sight. I would have preferred to turn aside to a wood I saw not far off, which seemed in its deep shade to offer inviting shelter; but I was so sick, so weak, so gnawed by nature's cravings, that instinct kept me circling near homes where there was a chance of food. Solitude would be no solitude—rest no rest—while the vulture of hunger sank its beak and talons into my side.

28.32.oldText: I drifted toward houses; I left them, came back again, and wandered away once more: always driven off by the knowledge that I had no claim to ask—no right to expect any interest in my lonely situation. Meanwhile the afternoon wore on, while I roamed about like a lost and starving dog. Crossing a field, I saw the church spire ahead of me: I hurried toward it. Near the churchyard, in the middle of a garden, stood a well-built if small house, which I had no doubt was the parsonage. I remembered that strangers who arrive in a place where they have no friends, and who need work, sometimes ask the clergyman for an introduction and help. It is the clergyman's role to assist—at least with advice—those who want to help themselves. I seemed to have something like a right to seek guidance here. Gathering my courage again and scraping together the last of my strength, I pushed on. I reached the house and knocked at the kitchen door. An old woman opened: I asked if this was the parsonage?

28.39.oldText: "Not so far—about three miles. He had been called away by the sudden death of his father: he was at Marsh End now, and would likely stay there another two weeks."

28.40.oldText: "Was there any lady of the house?"

28.41.oldText: "No, there was just her, and she was the housekeeper;" and of her, reader, I could not bring myself to beg the relief without which I was sinking; I could not yet beg; and again I crawled away.

28.42.oldText: Once more I took off my handkerchief—once more I thought of the loaves in the little shop. Oh, for just a crust! For just one mouthful to ease the pang of hunger! By instinct I turned my face toward the village again; I found the shop again and went in; and though there were others there besides the woman, I risked the request—"Would she give me a roll for this handkerchief?"

28.43.oldText: She looked at me with clear suspicion: "No, she never sold things that way."

28.44.oldText: Almost desperate, I asked for half a loaf; she refused again. "How could she know where I had gotten the handkerchief?" she said.

28.46.oldText: "No! What could she do with them?"

28.47.oldText: Reader, it is not pleasant to dwell on these details. Some say there is satisfaction in looking back on past suffering; but to this day I can barely stand to revisit the times I am describing: the moral humiliation, blended with the physical suffering, forms too painful a memory to willingly revisit. I blamed none of those who turned me away. I felt it was only to be expected, and could not be helped: an ordinary beggar is often regarded with suspicion; a well-dressed beggar, inevitably so. To be sure, what I begged for was work; but whose responsibility was it to give me work? Certainly not the responsibility of people who were seeing me for the first time and knew nothing of my character. And as for the woman who would not take my handkerchief in exchange for bread—well, she was right, if the offer looked suspicious to her or the trade seemed unprofitable. Let me move on. I am sick of the subject.

28.48.oldText: A little before dark I passed a farmhouse, at the open door of which the farmer sat eating his supper of bread and cheese. I stopped and said—

28.49.oldText: "Will you give me a piece of bread? I am very hungry." He glanced at me in surprise; but without answering, he cut a thick slice from his loaf and gave it to me. I imagine he did not take me for a beggar, but only an eccentric sort of lady who had taken a fancy to his brown bread. As soon as I was out of sight of his house, I sat down and ate it.

28.50.oldText: I could not hope to find lodging under a roof, and sought it in the wood I mentioned before. But my night was wretched, my sleep broken: the ground was damp, the air cold; besides, people passed near me more than once, and I had to keep changing my spot: no feeling of safety or peace befriended me. Toward morning it rained; the whole following day was wet. Do not ask me, reader, for a detailed account of that day; as before, I looked for work; as before, I was turned away; as before, I went hungry; only once in that time did food pass my lips. At the door of a cottage I saw a little girl about to throw a bowl of cold porridge into a pig trough. "Will you give me that?" I asked.

28.51.oldText: "Will you give me that?" I asked.

28.52.oldText: She stared at me. "Mother!" she exclaimed, "there is a woman who wants me to give her this porridge."

28.53.oldText: "Well, girl," replied a voice from inside, "give it to her if she's a beggar. The pig doesn't want it."

28.54.oldText: The girl tipped the stiffened mass into my hand, and I devoured it hungrily.

28.55.oldText: As the wet twilight deepened, I stopped on a lonely bridle path I had been following for an hour or more.

28.56.oldText: "My strength is completely failing me," I said aloud. "I feel I cannot go much farther. Shall I be an outcast again tonight? While the rain pours down like this, must I lay my head on the cold, soaked ground? I fear I have no choice: for who will take me in? But it will be terrible, with this feeling of hunger, faintness, chill, and this sense of total abandonment—this complete collapse of hope. Most likely I will die before morning. And why can I not make peace with the prospect of death? Why do I struggle to hold on to a worthless life? Because I know, or believe, that Mr. Rochester is alive: and to die of hunger and cold is a fate that nature cannot passively accept. Oh, Providence! Sustain me a little longer! Help me—guide me!"

28.57.oldText: My glazed eyes wandered over the dim and misty landscape. I saw I had strayed far from the village: it was completely out of sight. Even the farmland surrounding it had disappeared. By crossroads and side paths I had once again drifted near the tract of moorland; and now only a few fields, almost as wild and barren as the heath from which they had barely been reclaimed, lay between me and the dark hill.

28.58.oldText: "Well, I would rather die out there than in a street or on a public road," I reflected. "And far better that crows and ravens—if any ravens there are in these parts—should pick my flesh from my bones, than that they should be shut in a workhouse coffin and rot in a pauper's grave."

28.59.oldText: To the hill, then, I turned. I reached it. It remained now only to find a hollow where I could lie down and feel at least hidden, if not safe. But the entire surface of the wasteland looked level. It showed no variation but in color: green, where rushes and moss covered the marshes; black, where the dry soil bore only heather. Dark as it was becoming, I could still make out these changes, though only as shifts of light and shade; for color had faded with the daylight.

28.60.oldText: My eye still scanned the brooding rise and traced the moor's edge, vanishing into the wildest scenery, when at one dim point, far among the marshes and ridges, a light sprang up. "That is a will-o'-the-wisp," was my first thought; and I expected it would soon vanish. It burned on, however, steady and still, neither receding nor advancing. "Is it a bonfire just lit?" I wondered. I watched to see if it would spread: but no; as it did not shrink, neither did it grow. "It may be a candle in a house," I then guessed; "but if so, I can never reach it. It is much too far away; and even if it were within arm's length, what good would it do? I would only knock at the door to have it shut in my face."

28.61.oldText: And I sank down where I stood and pressed my face against the ground. I lay still for a while: the night wind swept over the hill and over me, and died moaning in the distance; the rain fell hard, soaking me fresh to the skin. If only I could have stiffened into the still frost—the merciful numbness of death—it could have beaten down on me; I would not have felt it. But my still-living flesh shuddered at its chilling touch. Before long I rose.

28.62.oldText: The light was still there, shining faintly but steadily through the rain. I tried to walk again: I dragged my exhausted limbs slowly toward it. It led me at an angle across the hill, through a wide bog that would have been impassable in winter and was splashy and unstable even now, at the height of summer. Here I fell twice; but each time I got up and rallied my strength. That light was my last hope: I had to reach it.

28.63.oldText: Having crossed the marsh, I saw a trace of white across the moor. I approached; it was a road or a track: it led straight up to the light, which now shone from a sort of knoll amid a clump of trees—firs, apparently, from what I could make out of their shapes and foliage through the gloom. My guiding star vanished as I drew close: some obstacle had come between me and it. I put out my hand to feel the dark mass ahead: I made out the rough stones of a low wall—above it, something like fence posts—and beyond, a high, thorny hedge. I groped forward. Again something whitish gleamed ahead: it was a gate—a small wicket; it swung on its hinges as I touched it. On each side stood a dark bush—holly or yew.

28.64.oldText: Passing through the gate and past the bushes, the outline of a house rose into view—black, low, and rather long; but the guiding light shone nowhere. All was dark. Had the people inside gone to bed? I feared so. Looking for the door, I turned a corner: there shot out the friendly glow again, from the diamond panes of a very small window, set within a foot of the ground, made still smaller by the growth of ivy or some other climbing plant whose leaves clustered thickly over the wall around it. The opening was so screened and narrow that no curtain or shutter had been thought necessary; and when I stooped and pushed aside the spray of leaves shooting over it, I could see everything inside. I could see clearly a room with a sanded floor, scrubbed clean; a walnut dresser with pewter plates arranged in rows, reflecting the redness and warmth of a glowing peat fire. I could see a clock, a white deal table, some chairs. The candle whose beam had been my beacon burned on the table; and by its light an elderly woman, somewhat rough-looking but scrupulously clean, like everything around her, was knitting a stocking.

28.65.oldText: I noticed these objects only in passing—there was nothing remarkable about them. A more interesting group sat near the hearth, still and quiet amid the rosy peace and warmth that filled the room. Two young, graceful women—ladies in every respect—sat, one in a low rocking chair, the other on a lower stool; both wore deep mourning of crape and bombazine, which somber clothing set off their very fair necks and faces in striking contrast. A large old pointer dog rested its massive head on the knee of one girl—in the lap of the other lay a curled black cat.

28.66.oldText: A strange place this humble kitchen was for such occupants! Who were they? They could not be the daughters of the elderly woman at the table; she looked like a country woman, and they were all refinement and cultivation. I had never seen faces like theirs: and yet, as I gazed at them, I felt an inexplicable familiarity with every feature. I cannot call them beautiful—they were too pale and serious for that: as each bent over a book, they looked thoughtful almost to severity. A stand between them supported a second candle and two large volumes, which they consulted frequently, comparing them with the smaller books in their hands, like people using a dictionary to help with translation. The scene was as silent as if all the figures had been shadows and the firelit room a painting: so hushed was it that I could hear the cinders falling from the grate, the clock ticking in its corner; I even thought I could distinguish the click-click of the old woman's knitting needles. When, therefore, a voice broke the strange stillness at last, it was perfectly clear to me.

28.67.oldText: "Listen, Diana," said one of the absorbed students; "Franz and old Daniel are together in the nighttime, and Franz is telling a dream from which he has woken in terror—listen!" And in a low voice she read something, of which not one word was intelligible to me; for it was in an unknown language—neither French nor Latin. Whether it was Greek or German I could not tell.

28.68.oldText: "That is powerful," she said when she had finished. "I love it." The other girl, who had lifted her head to listen to her sister, repeated, while she gazed at the fire, a line of what had been read. At a later date I knew the language and the book; so I will quote the line here, though when I first heard it, it was only like a stroke on a gong to me—carrying no meaning:

28.69.oldText: "'Da trat hervor Einer, anzusehen wie die Sternen Nacht.' Good! Good!" she exclaimed, while her dark, deep eyes sparkled. "There you have a dim and mighty archangel perfectly set before you! The line is worth a hundred pages of bombast. 'Ich wäge die Gedanken in der Schale meines Zornes und die Werke mit dem Gewichte meines Grimms.' I love it!"

28.71.oldText: "Is there any country where they talk like that?" asked the old woman, looking up from her knitting.

28.72.oldText: "Yes, Hannah—a far larger country than England, where they talk in no other way."

28.73.oldText: "Well, I'm sure I don't know how they can understand each other: and if either of you went there, you could figure out what they said, I suppose?"

28.74.oldText: "We could probably understand some of what they said, but not all—for we are not as clever as you think us, Hannah. We don't speak German, and we cannot read it without a dictionary to help us."

28.75.oldText: "And what good does it do you?"

28.76.oldText: "We plan to teach it someday—or at least the basics, as they say; and then we shall earn more money than we do now."

28.77.oldText: "Probably so: but stop studying; you've done enough for tonight."

28.78.oldText: "I think we have: at least I'm tired. Mary, are you?"

28.79.oldText: "Completely: after all, it's hard work struggling through a language with nothing but a dictionary for a teacher."

28.80.oldText: "It is, especially a language as difficult but glorious as German. I wonder when St. John will come home."

28.81.oldText: "Surely he won't be long now: it is just ten" (looking at a little gold watch she drew from her belt). "It's raining hard, Hannah: would you be so good as to check the fire in the parlor?"

28.82.oldText: The woman rose: she opened a door through which I dimly saw a passage: soon I heard her stirring a fire in an inner room; she came back shortly.

28.83.oldText: "Ah, children!" she said, "it does trouble me to go into that room now: it looks so lonely with the chair empty and pushed back in a corner."

28.84.oldText: She wiped her eyes with her apron: the two girls, grave before, looked sad now.

28.85.oldText: "But he is in a better place," Hannah continued. "We shouldn't wish him back. And nobody could have had a quieter death than he did."

28.86.oldText: "You say he never mentioned us?" asked one of the ladies.

28.87.oldText: "He didn't have time, child: he was gone in a minute, your father was. He'd been a bit poorly the day before, but nothing serious; and when Mr. St. John asked if he'd like either of you sent for, he actually laughed at him. He felt a bit of heaviness in his head the next day—that is, two weeks ago—and he went to sleep and never woke up. He was nearly cold when your brother went into the room and found him. Ah, children! That's the last of the old line—for you and Mr. St. John are a different sort from those that came before; though your mother was much like you, and nearly as bookish. She was the image of you, Mary: Diana takes more after your father."

28.88.oldText: I thought them so alike I could not see where the old servant (for so I now understood her to be) found the difference. Both were fair-complexioned and slenderly built; both had faces full of distinction and intelligence. One, to be sure, had hair a shade darker than the other, and there was a difference in how they wore it; Mary's pale brown locks were parted and braided smooth: Diana's darker tresses covered her neck with thick curls. The clock struck ten.

28.89.oldText: "You'll be wanting your supper, I'm sure," observed Hannah; "and so will Mr. St. John when he comes in."

28.90.oldText: And she began to prepare the meal. The ladies rose; they seemed about to withdraw to the parlor. Until this moment I had been so absorbed in watching them—their appearance and conversation had stirred such keen interest in me—that I had half-forgotten my own wretched situation. Now it rushed back. More desolate, more desperate than ever, it seemed by contrast. And how impossible it appeared to move the residents of this house to concern on my behalf; to make them believe in the reality of my needs and sufferings—to persuade them to grant me rest from my wandering! As I felt my way to the door and knocked hesitantly, I felt that last hope to be a mere fantasy. Hannah opened.

28.91.oldText: "What do you want?" she asked, in a voice of surprise, studying me by the light of the candle she held.

28.92.oldText: "May I speak to your mistresses?" I said.

28.93.oldText: "You'd better tell me what you have to say to them. Where do you come from?"

28.95.oldText: "What is your business here at this hour?"

28.96.oldText: "I want a night's shelter in an outhouse or anywhere, and a piece of bread to eat."

28.97.oldText: Mistrust—the very reaction I dreaded—appeared in Hannah's face. "I'll give you a piece of bread," she said, after a pause; "but we can't take in a vagrant for the night. That's not happening."

28.98.oldText: "Please let me speak to your mistresses."

28.99.oldText: "No, I won't. What can they do for you? You shouldn't be wandering about at this hour; it looks very bad."

28.100.oldText: "But where shall I go if you turn me away? What shall I do?"

28.101.oldText: "Oh, I'm sure you know where to go and what to do. Just make sure you don't do anything wrong, that's all. Here is a penny; now go—"

28.102.oldText: "A penny cannot feed me, and I have no strength to go farther. Don't shut the door—oh, don't, for God's sake!"

28.103.oldText: "I have to; the rain is blowing in—"

28.104.oldText: "Tell the young ladies. Let me see them—"

28.105.oldText: "I certainly will not. You are not what you should be, or you wouldn't make such a scene. Move along."

28.106.oldText: "But I will die if I am turned away."

28.107.oldText: "No you won't. I suspect you've got some bad scheme in mind, that brings you to people's doors at this time of night. If you've got accomplices—burglars or the like—anywhere near, you can tell them we are not alone in this house; we have a gentleman, and dogs, and guns." Here the honest but unyielding servant slammed the door and bolted it from inside.

28.108.oldText: This was the last straw. A pang of exquisite suffering—a spasm of true despair—tore through my heart. I was utterly spent; I could not take another step. I sank down on the wet doorstep: I groaned—I wrung my hands—I wept in absolute anguish. Oh, this specter of death! Oh, this final hour, approaching in such horror! The isolation—this banishment from humankind! Not only the anchor of hope but the footing of courage was gone—at least for a moment; but I soon tried to regain the latter.

28.109.oldText: "I can only die," I said, "and I believe in God. Let me try to wait for His will in silence."

28.110.oldText: These words I not only thought, but spoke aloud; and forcing all my misery back into my heart, I tried to make it stay there—mute and still.

28.111.oldText: "All people must die," said a voice very close by; "but not all are condemned to meet a slow and premature end, such as yours would be if you perished here of starvation."

28.112.oldText: "Who speaks?" I asked, terrified by the unexpected sound, and no longer capable of drawing hope from anything that happened. A figure was near—what figure, the pitch-dark night and my weakened sight prevented me from making out. With a loud, long knock, the newcomer called at the door.

28.113.oldText: "Is it you, Mr. St. John?" cried Hannah.

28.115.oldText: "Well, how wet and cold you must be, on such a wild night! Come in—your sisters are quite worried about you, and I think there are suspicious people about. There's been a beggar-woman—I swear she's still there!—lying down on the step. Get up! For shame! Move along, I say!"

28.116.oldText: "Hush, Hannah! I have something to say to this woman. You have done your duty in shutting her out; now let me do mine in letting her in. I was nearby and heard both of you. I think this is an unusual case—I must at least look into it. Young woman, stand up and come inside."

28.117.oldText: Hush, Hannah; I have a word to say to the woman.

28.118.oldText: With difficulty I obeyed. Soon I stood inside that clean, bright kitchen—on the very hearth—trembling, sick; aware that my appearance was ghastly, wild, and weatherbeaten in the extreme. The two ladies, their brother Mr. St. John, the old servant—all were staring at me.

28.119.oldText: "St. John, who is it?" I heard one ask.

28.120.oldText: "I cannot tell: I found her at the door," was the reply.

28.122.oldText: "As white as clay or death," came the response. "She will collapse: let her sit."

28.123.oldText: And indeed my head was swimming: I dropped, but a chair caught me. I still had my senses, though at that moment I could not speak.

28.124.oldText: "Perhaps some water would revive her. Hannah, fetch some. But she is wasted to nothing. How terribly thin, and how bloodless!"

28.127.oldText: "Starving, I think. Hannah, is that milk? Give it to me, and a piece of bread."

28.128.oldText: Diana (I knew her by the long curls I saw falling between me and the fire as she bent over me) broke some bread, dipped it in milk, and put it to my lips. Her face was close to mine: I saw pity in it, and I felt sympathy in her hurried breathing. In her simple words, too, the same soothing emotion spoke: "Try to eat."

28.129.oldText: "Yes—try," repeated Mary gently; and Mary's hand removed my soaked bonnet and lifted my head. I tasted what they offered me: feebly at first, then eagerly.

28.130.oldText: "Not too much at first—hold her back," said the brother; "she has had enough." And he took away the cup of milk and the plate of bread.

28.131.oldText: "A little more, St. John—look at the hunger in her eyes."

28.132.oldText: "No more for now, sister. See if she can speak—ask her her name."

28.133.oldText: I felt I could speak, and I answered—"My name is Jane Elliott." Anxious as ever to avoid being found, I had already decided to use a false name.

28.134.oldText: "And where do you live? Where are your friends?"

28.136.oldText: "Can we send for anyone you know?"

28.138.oldText: "What account can you give of yourself?"

28.139.oldText: Somehow, now that I had crossed the threshold of this house and stood face to face with its inhabitants, I no longer felt like an outcast, a vagrant, disowned by the wide world. I dared to shed the beggar's role—to resume my natural manner and character. I began once more to know myself; and when Mr. St. John asked for an explanation—which at present I was far too weak to give—I said, after a short pause—

28.140.oldText: "Sir, I can give you no details tonight."

28.141.oldText: "But what, then," said he, "do you expect me to do for you?"

28.142.oldText: "Nothing," I replied. My strength was enough only for short answers. Diana spoke up—

28.143.oldText: "Do you mean," she asked, "that we have now given you all the help you need? And that we may send you back to the moor and the rainy night?"

28.144.oldText: I looked at her. She had, I thought, a remarkable face—radiating both power and goodness. I took sudden courage. Meeting her compassionate gaze with a smile, I said—"I will trust you. If I were a homeless stray dog, I know you would not turn me from your hearth tonight: as it is, I truly have no fear. Do with me and for me as you see fit; but excuse me from much talking—I am short of breath—I feel a spasm when I speak." All three studied me, and all three were silent.

28.145.oldText: "Hannah," said Mr. St. John at last, "let her sit there for now, and ask her no questions; in ten minutes, give her the rest of that milk and bread. Mary and Diana, let us go into the parlor and discuss the matter."

28.146.oldText: They withdrew. Very soon one of the ladies returned—I could not tell which. A kind of pleasant drowsiness was stealing over me as I sat by the warm fire. In a low voice she gave some instructions to Hannah. Before long, with the servant's help, I managed to climb a staircase; my dripping clothes were removed; soon I was wrapped warm in a dry bed. I thanked God—experienced amid unutterable exhaustion a glow of grateful joy—and slept.

29.5.oldText: "She has a distinctive face; gaunt and hollow as it is, I rather like it; and when she is healthy and animated, I think she would look quite attractive."

29.14.oldText: It was full of the fragrance of fresh bread and the warmth of a generous fire. Hannah was baking. Prejudices, it is well known, are hardest to uproot from a mind that has never been opened by education: they grow there as firmly as weeds among stones. Hannah had been cold and stiff at first: lately she had begun to soften a little; and when she saw me come in tidy and properly dressed, she actually smiled.

29.20.oldText: After a pause she said, "I don't understand that: you've got no house, and no money, I suppose?"

29.21.oldText: "The lack of a house or money does not make a beggar in the way you mean."

29.60.oldText: "But I do think badly of you," I said; "and I'll tell you why—not so much because you refused me shelter, or suspected me of being a fraud, but because you just now treated it as a kind of disgrace that I had no money and no house. Some of the best people who ever lived have been as poor as I am; and if you are a Christian, you ought not to regard poverty as a crime."

29.65.oldText: Old Mr. Rivers, she said, was a simple man, but a gentleman and from as ancient a family as you could find. Marsh End had belonged to the Rivers family for as long as it had been a house: and it was, she declared, over two hundred years old—though it looked just a small, humble place, nothing compared to Mr. Oliver's grand hall down in Morton Vale. But she could remember Bill Oliver's father as a common needlemaker; and the Rivers had been gentry since the days of the Henrys, as anyone could see by looking in the church registers at Morton. Still, she admitted, the old master was like other folk—nothing much out of the ordinary: passionate about shooting, farming, and such things. The mistress was different. She was a great reader and studied a great deal; and the children had taken after her. There was no one like them in these parts, nor had there ever been; they had loved learning, all three, almost from the time they could talk; and they had always been "their own sort." Mr. St. John, when he grew up, would go to university and become a clergyman; and the girls, as soon as they left school, would look for positions as governesses: for they had told her that their father had some years ago lost a great deal of money through a man he trusted going bankrupt; and as he was no longer rich enough to give them inheritances, they would have to provide for themselves. They had lived very little at home for a long while, and were only here now to stay a few weeks on account of their father's death; but they did so love Marsh End and Morton and all these moors and hills. They had been in London and many other great cities; but they always said there was no place like home; and they were so good with each other—never quarreled or argued. She did not know where you could find such a close family.

29.103.oldText: "I do need it, and I seek it to this extent, sir: that some truly kind person will point me toward work that I can do, and for which the pay will keep me in the barest necessities of life."

29.106.oldText: "Mr. Rivers," I said, turning to him and looking at him as directly as he looked at me, "you and your sisters have done me a great service—the greatest one person can do for another: you have rescued me, through your generous hospitality, from death. This gift gives you an unlimited claim on my gratitude, and a claim, to some extent, on my honesty. I will tell you as much of the history of the wanderer you have sheltered as I can tell without compromising my own peace of mind—my own safety, moral and physical, and that of others."

29.121.oldText: "My sisters, you see, take pleasure in keeping you," said Mr. St. John, "as they would take pleasure in keeping and nursing a half-frozen bird that some winter wind might have blown through their window. I feel more inclined to set you on the path to keeping yourself, and shall try to do so; but understand, my world is small. I am merely the minister of a poor country parish: my help must be of the humblest kind. And if you are inclined to look down on modest beginnings, seek more effective aid than I can offer."

30.11.oldText: It began calmly—and indeed, in terms of delivery and tone of voice, it remained calm to the end: but a deeply felt, tightly controlled passion soon breathed through the precise words and drove the powerful language. This grew to force—compressed, concentrated, restrained. The heart was stirred, the mind astonished by the preacher's power: neither was comforted. Throughout there ran a strange bitterness; an absence of gentle consolation; stern references to Calvinist doctrines—election, predestination, damnation—were frequent; and each mention of these ideas sounded like a sentence of doom pronounced. When he finished, instead of feeling better, calmer, more enlightened by his words, I experienced an inexpressible sadness; for it seemed to me—whether equally so to others I cannot say—that the eloquence I had been hearing had sprung from a depth where stirred dark sediments of disappointment, where troubled currents of unsatisfied yearning and restless ambition flowed. I was certain St. John Rivers—clean-living, conscientious, zealous as he was—had not yet found that peace of God which passes all understanding: he had no more found it, I thought, than I had with my hidden, gnawing grief for my shattered idol and lost paradise—grief I have lately avoided mentioning, but which possessed me and tyrannized over me without mercy.

30.22.oldText: "You need not be in any hurry to hear," he said. "Let me be frank: I have nothing attractive or lucrative to suggest. Before I explain, please recall my clear warning that if I helped you, it would be as the blind helping the lame. I am poor; for I find that, when I have paid my father's debts, all the inheritance remaining to me will be this crumbling house, the row of damaged firs behind, and the patch of boggy ground with the yew trees and holly bushes in front. I am obscure: Rivers is an old name; but of the three sole descendants of the line, two earn a dependent's wages among strangers, and the third considers himself an exile from his native land—not only for life but in death. Yes, and deems, and is bound to deem, himself honored by this fate, and aspires only for the day when the cross of separation from earthly ties shall be laid on his shoulders, and when the Head of that Church Militant of whose humblest members he is one shall give the word: 'Rise, follow Me!'"

30.30.oldText: He put the question somewhat hurriedly; he seemed half to expect an indignant, or at least a scornful, rejection of the offer: not knowing all my thoughts and feelings, though guessing some, he could not tell how the prospect would look to me. In truth it was humble—but it was sheltered, and I wanted a safe haven. It was dull—but compared to the life of a governess in a wealthy household, it was independent; and the fear of servitude among strangers cut deep into my soul. It was not ignoble—not unworthy—not intellectually degrading. I made my decision.

30.46.oldText: He startled at the word "ambitious." He repeated, "No. What made you think of ambition? Who is ambitious? I know I am: but how did you find that out?"

30.50.oldText: "I was going to say passionate: but perhaps you would misunderstand the word and be offended. I mean that human bonds and sympathies have a very powerful hold on you. I am sure you cannot long be content to spend your free time in solitude and devote your working hours to monotonous labor completely devoid of stimulation: any more than I can be content," he added with emphasis, "to live here buried in marshland, hemmed in by mountains—my nature, God-given, thwarted; my abilities, heaven-bestowed, paralyzed—rendered useless. You hear how I contradict myself. I, who preached contentment with a humble lot and defended the calling even of woodcutters and water-carriers in God's service—I, His ordained minister, nearly rave in my restlessness. Well, ambitions and principles must somehow be reconciled."

30.55.oldText: At that moment a small event occurred that seemed decreed by fate specifically to confirm the truth of the saying that "misfortunes never come alone," and to add to their troubles the maddening one of a last-minute disappointment. St. John passed the window reading a letter. He came in.

30.61.oldText: "What then, Die?" he replied, maintaining a marble stillness of expression. "What then? Why—nothing. Read."

30.63.oldText: "So be it! We can still survive," said Diana at last.

30.68.oldText: "Jane, you will wonder at us and our mysteries," she said, "and think us hard-hearted for not being more upset at the death of so close a relative as an uncle; but we have never met him or known him. He was my mother's brother. My father and he quarreled long ago. It was on his advice that my father risked most of his money in the speculation that ruined him. Bitter accusations flew between them: they parted in anger and were never reconciled. My uncle went on to more successful ventures: it appears he accumulated a fortune of twenty thousand pounds. He never married and had no close family but ourselves and one other person, no more closely related than we are. My father always clung to the hope that he would make amends for his error by leaving his money to us; that letter informs us that he has left every penny to the other relative, except for thirty guineas to be split between St. John, Diana, and Mary Rivers, for the purchase of three mourning rings. He had every right, of course, to do as he pleased: and yet it dampens the spirits to receive such news. Mary and I would have counted ourselves rich with a thousand pounds each; and to St. John such a sum would have been valuable for the good it would have enabled him to do."

31.7.oldText: While I looked, I thought myself happy, and was surprised to find myself before long weeping—and why? For the fate that had torn me from my master: for him I was never to see again; for the desperate grief and destructive fury—consequences of my departure—that might now, perhaps, be dragging him from the right path, too far to hope for his eventual return. At this thought, I turned my face from the lovely evening sky and the lonely vale of Morton—I say lonely, for in the stretch of it visible to me there was no building except the church and the parsonage, half-hidden in trees, and, at the very far end, the roof of Vale Hall, where the rich Mr. Oliver and his daughter lived. I covered my eyes and leaned my head against the stone doorframe; but soon a slight sound near the little gate that separated my tiny garden from the meadow beyond made me look up. A dog—old Carlo, Mr. Rivers' pointer, as I saw at once—was pushing the gate with his nose, and St. John himself leaned on it with folded arms; his brow furrowed, his gaze stern almost to displeasure, fixed on me. I asked him to come in.

31.20.oldText: "A missionary I resolved to be. From that moment my state of mind changed; the chains dissolved and fell from every faculty, leaving only their painful marks—which only time can heal. My father, it is true, reinforced the decision, but since his death I have no legitimate obstacle left to contend with; some affairs to settle, a successor for Morton to arrange, an attachment or two of the heart to break through or cut away—a last conflict with human weakness, which I know I shall win because I have vowed that I will win—and I leave Europe for the East."

31.23.oldText: It was true. Though Mr. Rivers had started at the first of those musical tones as if lightning had split a cloud over his head, he still stood, at the end of her sentence, in the same position she had caught him in—his arm resting on the gate, his face turned toward the west. He turned at last, with measured deliberation. A vision, it seemed to me, had appeared at his side. There stood, within three feet of him, a figure dressed in pure white—a youthful, graceful form: full yet fine in outline; and when, after stooping to pet Carlo, she raised her head and threw back a long veil, there bloomed under his gaze a face of perfect beauty. Perfect beauty is a bold claim; but I do not take it back or soften it: features as sweet as any ever shaped by England's temperate climate; colors of rose and lily as pure as any her misty skies and damp breezes ever produced—these justified the term in this case. No charm was missing, no flaw was visible; the young woman had regular, delicate features; eyes shaped and colored like those in beautiful paintings—large, dark, and full; the long, shadowy lash that frames a fine eye with such soft allure; the finely drawn brow that gives such clarity; the white, smooth forehead that adds such calm to the livelier beauties of color and light; the cheek, oval, fresh, and smooth; the lips, fresh too, rosy, healthy, sweetly shaped; the even, gleaming teeth without a flaw; the small dimpled chin; the crowning glory of rich, abundant hair—every advantage, in short, which, combined, embodies the ideal of beauty, was fully hers. I gazed at this lovely creature in wonder: I admired her with my whole heart. Nature had surely formed her in a generous mood; and, forgetting her usual stingy allotment of gifts, had showered this favorite child with a grandmother's bounty.

31.24.oldText: What did St. John Rivers think of this earthly angel? I naturally asked myself that question as I saw him turn to her and look at her; and naturally I sought the answer in his expression. He had already withdrawn his eyes from the vision and was staring at a humble tuft of daisies growing by the gate.

31.38.oldText: "I shall come up and help you teach sometimes," she added. "It will be a nice change for me to visit you now and then; and I do like a change. Mr. Rivers, I have been so merry during my stay at S——. Last night, or rather this morning, I was dancing until two o'clock. The ——th regiment is stationed there since the riots; and the officers are the most delightful men in the world: they put all our young knife-grinders and scissor merchants to shame."

31.41.oldText: As she stroked the dog's head, bending with natural grace before his young and severe master, I saw a flush rise to that master's face. I saw his solemn eye soften with sudden fire and flicker with irresistible emotion. Lit up like this, he looked nearly as beautiful as a man can be, as she was as a woman. His chest rose once, as if his large heart, weary of its iron restraint, had swelled in spite of his will and made a powerful leap for freedom. But he checked it, I think, as a determined rider would check a rearing horse. He responded with neither word nor movement to the gentle advances she made.

31.45.oldText: "I forgot!" she exclaimed, shaking her beautiful curled head as if shocked at herself. "I am so giddy and thoughtless! Do excuse me. It slipped my mind that you have good reasons to be in low spirits. Diana and Mary have left you, and Moor House is shut up, and you are so lonely. I am sure I pity you. Do come and see Papa."

32.2.oldText: Rosamond Oliver kept her word about visiting me. She usually called at the school during her morning ride. She would canter up to the door on her pony, followed by a mounted servant in livery. Nothing more exquisite than her appearance could be imagined, in her purple riding habit with her velvet cap set gracefully above the long curls that brushed her cheek and floated to her shoulders: and this is how she would enter the rustic building and glide through the dazzled ranks of village children. She generally came at the hour when Mr. Rivers was giving his daily lesson in religious instruction. Her gaze, I fear, pierced the young clergyman's heart to the quick. A kind of instinct seemed to warn him of her entrance, even when he was not looking; and when his back was to the door, if she appeared, his cheek would glow, and his marble-like features, though they refused to relax, changed in some indescribable way and, in their very stillness, became expressive of a repressed passion stronger than any flexing muscle or darting glance could show.

32.4.oldText: And then she would pout like a disappointed child; a wistful cloud would soften her radiant liveliness; she would snatch her hand from his and turn away in brief irritation from his look, at once so heroic and so martyrlike. St. John, no doubt, would have given the world to follow her, call her back, hold on to her when she left him like this; but he would not give one chance at heaven, nor surrender, for the paradise of her love, one hope of the true, eternal Paradise. Besides, he could not confine everything in his nature—the wanderer, the dreamer, the poet, the priest—within the limits of a single passion. He could not—he would not—trade his wild field of missionary work for the drawing rooms and the peace of Vale Hall. I learned this much from him directly, in an advance I once, despite his reserve, dared to make upon his confidence.

32.5.oldText: Miss Oliver had already honored me with frequent visits to my cottage. I had come to know her whole character, which had no mystery or pretense: she was flirtatious but not heartless; demanding, but not worthlessly selfish. She had been spoiled since birth, but was not ruined by it. She was impulsive but good-natured; vain (she could not help it, when every glance in the mirror showed her such a flood of loveliness) but not affected; generous; free of the arrogance of wealth; straightforward; reasonably intelligent; cheerful, lively, and carefree: she was very charming, in short, even to a cool female observer like me; but she was not deeply interesting or truly impressive. Her mind was of a very different sort from that of St. John's sisters, for instance. Still, I liked her almost as much as I liked my former pupil Adèle; except that for a child we have watched over and taught, a closer affection develops than we can give an equally appealing adult acquaintance.

32.16.oldText: "I have come to see how you are spending your holiday," he said. "Not in gloomy thought, I hope? No, that is good: while you draw you will not feel lonely. You see, I still worry about you, though you have held up wonderfully so far. I have brought you a book for the evening," and he laid on the table a new publication—a poem: one of those genuine masterworks so often granted to the fortunate public of those days—the golden age of modern literature. Alas! the readers of our time are less blessed. But take heart! I will not stop to accuse or lament. I know poetry is not dead, nor genius lost; nor has greed gained power over either, to bind or destroy them: they will both assert their existence, their presence, their freedom and their strength again one day. Mighty angels, safe in heaven! They smile when base souls triumph and timid ones weep over their destruction. Poetry destroyed? Genius banished? No! Mediocrity—no: do not let envy suggest that thought. No; they not only survive but reign and redeem: and without their divine influence everywhere, you would live in hell—the hell of your own smallness.

32.19.oldText: I said first, "Take a seat, Mr. Rivers." But he answered, as he always did, that he could not stay. "Very well," I responded mentally, "stand if you like; but you shall not leave just yet, I am determined. Solitude is at least as harmful for you as it is for me. I will see if I can find the secret spring of your reserve, and an opening in that marble chest through which I can pour one drop of the balm of sympathy."

32.28.oldText: He continued to gaze at the picture: the longer he looked, the more firmly he held it, the more he seemed to want it. "It is like her!" he murmured; "the eye is perfectly done: the color, light, expression are all right. It smiles!"

32.42.oldText: "Now," he said, "that little space was given over to fever and fantasy. I rested my head on the breast of temptation and willingly placed my neck under her garland of flowers; I tasted her cup. The pillow was burning: there is a serpent in the garland: the wine has a bitter taste: her promises are hollow—her offers false. I see and know all this."

32.59.oldText: "No. There is this difference between me and godless philosophers: I believe; and I believe the Gospel. You chose the wrong word. I am not a pagan but a Christian philosopher—a follower of the faith of Jesus. As His disciple I embrace His pure, merciful, generous teachings. I champion them: I am sworn to spread them. Won over to religion in my youth, she has cultivated my original qualities like this: from the tiny seed of natural affection, she has grown the towering tree of love for humanity. From the wild, stringy root of human integrity, she has raised a proper sense of divine justice. The ambition to win power and fame for my wretched self, she has transformed into the ambition to expand my Master's kingdom; to win victories for the banner of the cross. This is what religion has done for me; making the best use of the raw material; pruning and training nature. But she could not root out nature: nor will nature be rooted out until this mortal puts on immortality."

32.66.oldText: "Nothing in the world," was the reply; and, replacing the paper, I saw him deftly tear a narrow strip from the margin. It vanished into his glove; and with one hasty nod and "good afternoon," he was gone.

33.36.oldText: "Half an hour ago," he went on, "I mentioned my impatience to hear the rest of a story. On reflection, I think the matter will be better handled if I take the narrator's part and make you the listener. Before I begin, it is only fair to warn you that the story will sound rather familiar to your ears; but stale details often gain a certain freshness when they pass through new lips. For the rest, whether familiar or new, it is short."

33.48.oldText: I went cold with dread: my worst fears were probably true. He had in all likelihood left England and rushed in reckless desperation to some former haunt on the Continent. And what comfort for his terrible suffering—what outlet for his strong passions—had he sought there? I dared not answer the question. Oh, my poor master—once almost my husband—whom I had so often called "my dear Edward!"

33.64.oldText: "You unbend your forehead at last," said Mr. Rivers. "I thought Medusa had looked at you and you were turning to stone. Perhaps now you will ask how much you are worth?"

33.90.oldText: "But I warned you that I am a stubborn man," he said, "hard to persuade."

33.91.oldText: "And I am a stubborn woman—impossible to put off."

33.92.oldText: And I am a stubborn woman—impossible to put off.

33.93.oldText: "And besides," he went on, "I am cold: no passion touches me."

33.94.oldText: "Whereas I am hot, and fire melts ice. The blaze over there has thawed all the snow from your cloak; and by the same token, it has streamed across my floor and made it look like a trampled street. As you hope ever to be forgiven, Mr. Rivers, the high crime and offense of ruining a sanded kitchen, tell me what I want to know."

33.95.oldText: "Well, then," he said, "I give in; if not to your earnestness, then to your persistence: as stone is worn by constant dripping. Besides, you must find out someday—as well now as later. Your name is Jane Eyre?"

33.96.oldText: "Of course: that was all settled before."

33.97.oldText: "You are not, perhaps, aware that I share your surname?—that I was christened St. John Eyre Rivers?"

33.98.oldText: "No, indeed! I remember now seeing the letter E. included in your initials, written in books you have lent me at various times; but I never asked what name it stood for. But what then? Surely—"

33.99.oldText: I stopped: I could not trust myself to entertain, much less to speak, the thought that rushed upon me—that took shape—that, in a second, stood out as a strong, solid probability. Circumstances linked themselves, fitted together, fell into order: the chain that had been lying in a formless heap of links was drawn out straight—every ring was perfect, the connection complete. I knew, by instinct, how things stood, before St. John had said another word; but I cannot expect the reader to have the same intuitive grasp, so I must repeat his explanation.

33.100.oldText: "My mother's name was Eyre; she had two brothers; one a clergyman, who married Miss Jane Reed of Gateshead; the other, John Eyre, Esquire, merchant, late of Funchal, Madeira. Mr. Briggs, being Mr. Eyre's solicitor, wrote to us last August to inform us of our uncle's death and to say that he had left his property to his brother the clergyman's orphan daughter, bypassing us because of a quarrel, never forgiven, between him and my father. He wrote again a few weeks ago to say that the heiress had disappeared, and to ask if we knew anything about her. A name casually written on a slip of paper has allowed me to find her. You know the rest." Again he was going, but I set my back against the door.

33.101.oldText: "Do let me speak," I said; "give me one moment to catch my breath and think." I paused—he stood before me, hat in hand, looking composed enough. I went on—

33.106.oldText: "My uncle John was your uncle John? You, Diana, and Mary are his sister's children, as I am his brother's child?"

33.108.oldText: "You three, then, are my cousins; half the blood on each side flows from the same source?"

33.110.oldText: I studied him. It seemed I had found a brother: one I could be proud of—one I could love; and two sisters, whose qualities were such that when I knew them only as strangers, they had inspired me with genuine affection and admiration. The two women on whom, kneeling on the wet ground and peering through the low, latticed window of Moor House kitchen, I had gazed with so bitter a mixture of fascination and despair—they were my close relatives; and the young, distinguished gentleman who had found me almost dying on his doorstep was my own blood relation. Glorious discovery for a lonely soul! This was wealth indeed!—wealth for the heart!—a mine of pure, warm affections. This was a blessing, bright, vivid, and exhilarating;—not like the heavy gift of gold: welcome enough in its way, but sobering under its weight. I clapped my hands in sudden joy—my pulse leapt, my blood thrilled.

33.111.oldText: "Oh, I am glad!—I am glad!" I exclaimed.

33.112.oldText: St. John smiled. "Did I not say you neglected the important things to chase after trifles?" he asked. "You were serious when I told you that you had a fortune; and now, for something that hardly matters, you are overjoyed."

33.113.oldText: "What can you mean? It may not matter to you; you have sisters and don't need a cousin; but I had nobody; and now three relatives—or two, if you refuse to be counted—have been born into my world, fully grown. I say again, I am glad!"

33.114.oldText: I paced quickly through the room. I stopped, half suffocating with thoughts that rose faster than I could absorb, understand, or sort them:—thoughts of what might, could, would, and should happen, and soon. I looked at the blank wall: it seemed a sky thick with rising stars—every one lighting me toward a purpose or a joy. Those who had saved my life, whom until this moment I had loved without the power to give anything back, I could now benefit. They were under a yoke—I could free them; they were scattered—I could reunite them. The independence, the abundance that was mine could be theirs too. Were we not four? Twenty thousand pounds divided equally would be five thousand each. Enough and to spare: justice would be done—mutual happiness secured. Now the wealth did not weigh on me: now it was not merely a bequest of coins—it was a gift of life, hope, and joy.

33.115.oldText: How I looked while these ideas were storming through my mind, I cannot say; but I soon noticed that Mr. Rivers had placed a chair behind me and was gently trying to get me to sit down. He also advised me to be calm; I scorned the suggestion that I was helpless and hysterical, shook off his hand, and began pacing again.

33.116.oldText: "Write to Diana and Mary tomorrow," I said, "and tell them to come home at once. Diana said they would both consider themselves rich with a thousand pounds, so with five thousand they will do very well."

33.117.oldText: "Tell me where I can get you a glass of water," said St. John; "you really must try to calm yourself."

33.118.oldText: "Nonsense! And what effect will this bequest have on you? Will it keep you in England, persuade you to marry Miss Oliver, and settle down like an ordinary person?"

33.119.oldText: "You are rambling: your mind is confused. I have been too sudden in breaking the news; it has excited you beyond your strength."

33.120.oldText: "Mr. Rivers! You are driving me mad with frustration: I am perfectly rational; it is you who misunderstand, or pretend to misunderstand."

33.121.oldText: "Perhaps if you explained yourself a little more clearly, I would grasp your meaning better."

33.122.oldText: "Explain! What is there to explain? You must see that twenty thousand pounds, the sum in question, divided equally between the nephew and three nieces of our uncle, gives five thousand to each? What I want is for you to write to your sisters and tell them about the fortune that has come to them."
