33.124.oldText: "I have stated my view of the case: I am incapable of taking any other. I am not brutally selfish, blindly unjust, or monstrously ungrateful. Besides, I am determined to have a home and a family. I like Moor House, and I will live at Moor House; I like Diana and Mary, and I will attach myself to Diana and Mary for life. It would please and benefit me to have five thousand pounds; it would torment and oppress me to have twenty thousand; which, moreover, could never be mine in fairness, though it might be in law. I give up to you, then, what is absolutely surplus to my needs. Let there be no arguments and no debate about it; let us agree among ourselves and settle the matter at once."

33.125.oldText: "This is acting on impulse; you must take days to consider such a thing before your word can be taken seriously."

33.126.oldText: "Oh! If all you doubt is my sincerity, I am at ease: you see the justice of the case?"

33.127.oldText: "I do see a certain justice; but it goes against all custom. Besides, the entire fortune is yours by right: my uncle earned it by his own efforts; he was free to leave it to whomever he wished. He left it to you. After all, justice does permit you to keep it: you may, with a clear conscience, consider it absolutely your own."

33.128.oldText: "With me," I said, "it is fully as much a matter of feeling as of conscience: I must follow my feelings; I so rarely have the chance. If you were to argue, object, and annoy me for a year, I could not give up the delicious pleasure I have glimpsed—that of partly repaying an enormous debt, and gaining lifelong friends."

33.129.oldText: "You think so now," replied St. John, "because you do not know what it means to possess, or consequently to enjoy, wealth: you cannot imagine the importance twenty thousand pounds would give you; the place in society it would allow you; the prospects it would open—you cannot—"

33.130.oldText: "And you," I interrupted, "cannot begin to imagine the hunger I have for family love. I never had a home, I never had brothers or sisters; I must and will have them now: you are not reluctant to acknowledge me and accept me, are you?"

33.131.oldText: "Jane, I will be your brother—my sisters will be your sisters—without requiring this sacrifice of your rightful inheritance."

33.132.oldText: "Brother? Yes; at a distance of a thousand miles! Sisters? Yes; slaving among strangers! I, wealthy—gorged with gold I never earned and do not deserve! You, penniless! Fine equality and brotherhood! Close union! Intimate bond!"

33.133.oldText: "But, Jane, your longing for family ties and domestic happiness may be fulfilled by other means than what you are proposing: you could marry."

33.134.oldText: "Nonsense, again! Marry! I do not want to marry, and never shall."

33.135.oldText: "That is saying too much: such rash claims prove you are speaking under great excitement."

33.136.oldText: "It is not saying too much: I know what I feel, and how completely opposed I am to the very idea of marriage. No one would take me for love; and I refuse to be seen as a mere financial opportunity. And I do not want a stranger—cold, alien, different from me; I want my own family: people with whom I feel a complete bond. Say again you will be my brother: when you spoke those words I was satisfied, happy; repeat them, if you can, and mean them."

33.137.oldText: "I think I can. I know I have always loved my own sisters; and I know what my affection for them rests on—respect for their worth and admiration for their talents. You too have principle and intelligence: your tastes and habits resemble Diana's and Mary's; your company is always agreeable to me; in your conversation I have already for some time found a wholesome comfort. I feel I can easily and naturally make room in my heart for you, as my third and youngest sister."

33.138.oldText: "Thank you: that is enough for tonight. Now you had better go; for if you stay longer, you will probably annoy me again with some mistrustful objection."

33.139.oldText: "And the school, Miss Eyre? It must be closed now, I suppose?"

33.140.oldText: "No. I will keep my post as teacher until you find a replacement."

33.141.oldText: He smiled approvingly: we shook hands, and he left.

33.142.oldText: I need not describe in detail the further battles I fought and arguments I used to get the inheritance settled as I wished. My task was very difficult; but as I was absolutely resolved—as my cousins eventually saw that my mind was truly and unshakably fixed on making a fair division of the property—as they must in their own hearts have felt the justice of the intention, and must, besides, have known instinctively that in my place they would have done exactly what I wished to do—they yielded at last so far as to agree to put the matter to arbitration. The judges chosen were Mr. Oliver and a skilled lawyer: both agreed with my view. I got my way. The legal documents were drawn up: St. John, Diana, Mary, and I each received a competence.

34.1.oldText: Mr. Rivers came up just as I had watched the classes — now numbering sixty girls — file out before me and had locked the door. I stood with the key in my hand, exchanging a few words of special farewell with some half-dozen of my best pupils: as decent, respectable, modest, and well-informed young women as could be found in the ranks of the British peasantry. And that is saying a great deal; for after all, the British peasantry are the best taught, best mannered, and most self-respecting of any in Europe: since those days I have seen paysannes and Bäuerinnen, and the best of them seemed to me ignorant, coarse, and besotted compared with my Morton girls.

34.25.oldText: St. John arrived first. I had begged him to keep quite clear of the house till everything was arranged, and indeed the bare idea of the commotion — at once sordid and trivial — going on within its walls was enough to drive him to stay away. He found me in the kitchen, watching the progress of certain cakes for tea, then baking. Approaching the hearth, he asked, “If I was at last satisfied with housemaid’s work?” I answered by inviting him to accompany me on a general inspection of the result of my labours. With some difficulty, I got him to make the tour of the house. He just looked in at the doors I opened; and when he had wandered upstairs and downstairs, he said I must have gone through a great deal of fatigue and trouble to have effected such considerable changes in so short a time — but not a syllable did he utter to indicate pleasure in the improved appearance of his home.

34.27.oldText: “Not at all; he had, on the contrary, noticed that I had scrupulously respected every association: he feared, indeed, I must have bestowed more thought on the matter than it was worth. How many minutes, for instance, had I devoted to studying the arrangement of this very room? — By the way, could I tell him where such a book was?”

34.30.oldText: “This parlour is not his sphere,” I reflected. “The Himalayan ridge or Caffre bush, even the plague-cursed Guinea Coast swamp would suit him better. Well may he shun the calm of domestic life; it is not his element — there his faculties stagnate, they cannot develop or appear to advantage. It is in scenes of strife and danger — where courage is proved, and energy exercised, and fortitude tested — that he will speak and move, the leader and superior. A merry child would have the advantage of him on this hearth. He is right to choose a missionary’s career — I see it now.”

34.32.oldText: They were stiff from their long and jolting drive from Whitcross, and chilled from the frosty night air; but their pleasant faces brightened in the cheerful firelight. While the driver and Hannah brought in the boxes, they asked for St. John. At that moment he came out from the parlour. They both threw their arms round his neck at once. He gave each one quiet kiss, said in a low tone a few words of welcome, stood a while to be talked to, and then, hinting that he supposed they would soon rejoin him in the parlour, withdrew there as to a place of refuge.

34.34.oldText: Sweet was that evening. My cousins, full of exhilaration, were so eloquent in narrative and comment that their fluency covered St. John’s silence. He was sincerely glad to see his sisters, but in their glow of warmth and flow of joy he could not share. The event of the day — that is, the return of Diana and Mary — pleased him; but the accompaniments of that event — the glad tumult, the garrulous glee of the reception — irked him: I saw he wished the calmer morrow had already come. At the very height of the night’s enjoyment, about an hour after tea, a rap was heard at the door. Hannah entered with word that “a poor lad was come, at this unlikely time, to fetch Mr. Rivers to see his mother, who was drawing away.”

34.61.oldText: “I want you to give up German and learn Hindostanee.”

34.64.oldText: He then went on to explain that Hindostanee was the language he was himself studying at present; that as he advanced, he was apt to forget the beginning; that it would help him greatly to have a pupil with whom he might go over the elements again and again, and so fix them thoroughly in his mind; that his choice had hovered for some time between me and his sisters; but that he had settled on me because he saw I could sit at a task the longest of the three. Would I do him this favour? I should not, perhaps, have to make the sacrifice long, as it now wanted barely three months to his departure.

34.76.oldText: A fine spring shone round me, which I could not enjoy. Summer approached; Diana tried to cheer me: she said I looked ill, and wished to accompany me to the seaside. This St. John opposed; he said I did not need dissipation, I needed employment; my present life was too purposeless, I needed an aim; and, I suppose, by way of supplying deficiencies, he prolonged still further my lessons in Hindostanee, and grew more urgent in demanding their completion: and I, like a fool, never thought of resisting him — I could not resist him.

34.114.oldText: He threw himself down on a swell of heath, and there lay still.

34.115.oldText: “I _can_ do what he wants me to do: I am forced to see and acknowledge that,” I meditated — “that is, if life be spared me. But I feel mine is not the existence to be long protracted under an Indian sun. What then? He does not care for that: when my time came to die, he would resign me, in all serenity and sanctity, to the God who gave me. The case is very plain before me. In leaving England, I should leave a loved but empty land — Mr. Rochester is not there; and if he were, what is, what can that ever be to me? My business is to live without him now: nothing so absurd, so weak as to drag on from day to day, as if I were waiting for some impossible change in circumstances which might reunite me to him. Of course (as St. John once said) I must seek another interest in life to replace the one lost: is not the occupation he now offers me truly the most glorious man can adopt or God assign? Is it not, by its noble cares and sublime results, the one best calculated to fill the void left by uprooted affections and demolished hopes? I believe I must say, Yes — and yet I shudder. Alas! If I join St. John, I abandon half myself: if I go to India, I go to premature death. And how will the interval between leaving England for India, and India for the grave, be filled? Oh, I know well! That, too, is very clear to my vision. By straining to satisfy St. John till my sinews ache, I _shall_ satisfy him — to the finest central point and farthest outward circle of his expectations. If I _do_ go with him — if I _do_ make the sacrifice he urges, I will make it absolutely: I will throw all on the altar — heart, vitals, the entire victim. He will never love me; but he shall approve me; I will show him energies he has not yet seen, resources he has never suspected. Yes, I can work as hard as he can, and with as little grudging.

34.116.oldText: “Consent, then, to his demand is possible: but for one item — one dreadful item. It is — that he asks me to be his wife, and has no more of a husband’s heart for me than that frowning giant of a rock, down which the stream is foaming in yonder gorge. He prizes me as a soldier would a good weapon; and that is all. Unmarried to him, this would never grieve me; but can I let him complete his calculations — coolly put into practice his plans — go through the wedding ceremony? Can I receive from him the bridal ring, endure all the forms of love (which I doubt not he would scrupulously observe) and know that the spirit was quite absent? Can I bear the awareness that every endearment he bestows is a sacrifice made on principle? No: such a martyrdom would be monstrous. I will never undergo it. As his sister, I might accompany him — not as his wife: I will tell him so.”

34.117.oldText: I looked towards the knoll: there he lay, still as a fallen column; his face turned to me: his eye beaming watchful and keen. He started to his feet and approached me.

34.118.oldText: “I am ready to go to India, if I may go free.”

34.119.oldText: “Your answer requires a commentary,” he said; “it is not clear.”

34.120.oldText: “You have until now been my adopted brother — I, your adopted sister: let us continue as such: you and I had better not marry.”

34.121.oldText: He shook his head. “Adopted fraternity will not do in this case. If you were my real sister it would be different: I should take you, and seek no wife. But as it is, either our union must be consecrated and sealed by marriage, or it cannot exist: practical obstacles oppose themselves to any other plan. Do you not see it, Jane? Consider a moment — your strong sense will guide you.”

34.122.oldText: I did consider; and still my sense, such as it was, directed me only to the fact that we did not love each other as man and wife should: and therefore it inferred we ought not to marry. I said so. “St. John,” I returned, “I regard you as a brother — you, me as a sister: so let us continue.”

34.123.oldText: “We cannot — we cannot,” he answered, with short, sharp determination: “it would not do. You have said you will go with me to India: remember — you have said that.”

34.125.oldText: “Well — well. To the main point — the departure with me from England, the co-operation with me in my future labours — you do not object. You have already as good as put your hand to the plough: you are too consistent to withdraw it. You have but one end to keep in view — how the work you have undertaken can best be done. Simplify your complicated interests, feelings, thoughts, wishes, aims; merge all considerations in one purpose: that of fulfilling with effect — with power — the mission of your great Master. To do so, you must have a coadjutor: not a brother — that is a loose tie — but a husband. I, too, do not want a sister: a sister might any day be taken from me. I want a wife: the sole helpmeet I can influence effectively in life, and retain absolutely till death.”

34.126.oldText: I shuddered as he spoke: I felt his influence in my marrow — his hold on my limbs.

34.127.oldText: “Seek one elsewhere than in me, St. John: seek one fitted to you.”

34.128.oldText: “One fitted to my purpose, you mean — fitted to my vocation. Again I tell you it is not the insignificant private individual — the mere man, with the man’s selfish senses — I wish to mate: it is the missionary.”

34.129.oldText: “And I will give the missionary my energies — it is all he wants — but not myself: that would be only adding the husk and shell to the kernel. For them he has no use: I retain them.”

34.130.oldText: “You cannot — you ought not. Do you think God will be satisfied with half an offering? Will He accept a mutilated sacrifice? It is the cause of God I advocate: it is under His standard I enlist you. I cannot accept on His behalf a divided allegiance: it must be entire.”

34.131.oldText: “Oh! I will give my heart to God,” I said. “_You_ do not want it.”

34.132.oldText: I will not swear, reader, that there was not something of repressed sarcasm both in the tone in which I uttered this sentence, and in the feeling that accompanied it. I had silently feared St. John till now, because I had not understood him. He had held me in awe, because he had held me in doubt. How much of him was saint, how much mortal, I could not tell before: but revelations were being made in this conference: the analysis of his nature was proceeding before my eyes. I saw his fallibilities: I understood them. I understood that, sitting there where I did, on the bank of heath, and with that handsome form before me, I sat at the feet of a man, erring as I. The veil fell from his hardness and despotism. Having felt in him the presence of these qualities, I felt his imperfection and took courage. I was with an equal — one with whom I might argue — one whom, if I saw good, I might resist.

34.133.oldText: He was silent after I had uttered the last sentence, and I presently risked an upward glance at his face. His eye, bent on me, expressed at once stern surprise and keen inquiry. “Is she sarcastic, and sarcastic to _me!_” it seemed to say. “What does this signify?”

34.134.oldText: “Do not let us forget that this is a solemn matter,” he said at length; “one of which we may neither think nor talk lightly without sin. I trust, Jane, you are in earnest when you say you will give your heart to God: it is all I want. Once wrench your heart from man, and fix it on your Maker, the advancement of that Maker’s spiritual kingdom on earth will be your chief delight and endeavour; you will be ready to do at once whatever furthers that end. You will see what impetus would be given to your efforts and mine by our physical and mental union in marriage: the only union that gives a character of permanent conformity to the destinies and designs of human beings; and, passing over all minor caprices — all trivial difficulties and delicacies of feeling — all scruple about the degree, kind, strength, or tenderness of mere personal inclination — you will hasten to enter into that union at once.”

34.135.oldText: “Shall I?” I said briefly; and I looked at his features, beautiful in their harmony, but strangely formidable in their still severity; at his brow, commanding but not open; at his eyes, bright and deep and searching, but never soft; at his tall imposing figure; and fancied myself in idea _his wife_. Oh! it would never do! As his curate, his comrade, all would be right: I would cross oceans with him in that capacity; toil under Eastern suns, in Asian deserts with him in that office; admire and emulate his courage and devotion and vigour; accommodate quietly to his masterhood; smile undisturbed at his ineradicable ambition; distinguish the Christian from the man: profoundly esteem the one, and freely forgive the other. I should suffer often, no doubt, attached to him only in this capacity: my body would be under rather a stringent yoke, but my heart and mind would be free. I should still have my unblighted self to turn to: my natural unenslaved feelings with which to commune in moments of loneliness. There would be recesses in my mind which would be only mine, to which he never came, and sentiments growing there fresh and sheltered which his austerity could never blight, nor his measured warrior-march trample down: but as his wife — at his side always, and always restrained, and always checked — forced to keep the fire of my nature continually low, to compel it to burn inwardly and never utter a cry, though the imprisoned flame consumed vital after vital — _this_ would be unendurable.

34.136.oldText: “St. John!” I exclaimed, when I had got so far in my meditation.

34.138.oldText: “I repeat I freely consent to go with you as your fellow-missionary, but not as your wife; I cannot marry you and become part of you.”

34.139.oldText: “A part of me you must become,” he answered steadily; “otherwise the whole bargain is void. How can I, a man not yet thirty, take out with me to India a girl of nineteen, unless she be married to me? How can we be forever together — sometimes in solitudes, sometimes amidst savage tribes — and unwed?”

34.140.oldText: “Very well,” I said shortly; “under the circumstances, quite as well as if I were either your real sister, or a man and a clergyman like yourself.”

34.141.oldText: “It is known that you are not my sister; I cannot introduce you as such: to attempt it would be to fasten harmful suspicions on us both. And for the rest, though you have a man’s vigorous brain, you have a woman’s heart and — it would not do.”

34.142.oldText: “It would do,” I affirmed with some disdain, “perfectly well. I have a woman’s heart, but not where you are concerned; for you I have only a comrade’s constancy; a fellow-soldier’s frankness, fidelity, fraternity, if you like; a neophyte’s respect and submission to his hierophant: nothing more — don’t fear.”

34.143.oldText: “It is what I want,” he said, speaking to himself; “it is just what I want. And there are obstacles in the way: they must be hewn down. Jane, you would not repent marrying me — be certain of that; we _must_ be married. I repeat it: there is no other way; and undoubtedly enough of love would follow upon marriage to render the union right even in your eyes.”

34.144.oldText: “I scorn your idea of love,” I could not help saying, as I rose up and stood before him, leaning my back against the rock. “I scorn the counterfeit sentiment you offer: yes, St. John, and I scorn you when you offer it.”

34.145.oldText: He looked at me fixedly, compressing his well-cut lips while he did so. Whether he was angered or surprised, or what, it was not easy to tell: he could command his countenance thoroughly.

34.146.oldText: “I scarcely expected to hear that expression from you,” he said: “I think I have done and said nothing to deserve scorn.”

34.147.oldText: I was touched by his gentle tone, and overawed by his high, calm mien.

34.148.oldText: “Forgive me the words, St. John; but it is your own fault that I have been roused to speak so unguardedly. You have introduced a topic on which our natures are at variance — a topic we should never discuss: the very name of love is an apple of discord between us. If the reality were required, what should we do? How should we feel? My dear cousin, abandon your scheme of marriage — forget it.”

34.149.oldText: “No,” he said; “it is a long-cherished scheme, and the only one which can secure my great end: but I shall urge you no further at present. Tomorrow, I leave home for Cambridge: I have many friends there to whom I should wish to say farewell. I shall be absent a fortnight — take that space of time to consider my offer: and do not forget that if you reject it, it is not me you deny, but God. Through my means, He opens to you a noble career; as my wife only can you enter upon it. Refuse to be my wife, and you limit yourself forever to a track of selfish ease and barren obscurity. Tremble lest in that case you should be numbered with those who have denied the faith, and are worse than infidels!”

34.150.oldText: He had done. Turning from me, he once more

34.152.oldText: But this time his feelings were all pent in his heart: I was not worthy to hear them uttered. As I walked by his side homeward, I read well in his iron silence all he felt towards me: the disappointment of an austere and despotic nature, which has met resistance where it expected submission — the disapproval of a cool, inflexible judgment, which has detected in another feelings and views in which it has no power to sympathise: in short, as a man, he would have wished to coerce me into obedience: it was only as a sincere Christian that he bore so patiently with my perversity, and allowed so long a space for reflection and repentance.

34.153.oldText: That night, after he had kissed his sisters, he thought proper to forget even to shake hands with me, but left the room in silence. I — who, though I had no love, had much friendship for him — was hurt by the marked omission: so much hurt that tears started to my eyes.

34.154.oldText: “I see you and St. John have been quarrelling, Jane,” said Diana, “during your walk on the moor. But go after him; he is now lingering in the passage expecting you — he will make it up.”

34.155.oldText: I have not much pride under such circumstances: I would always rather be happy than dignified; and I ran after him — he stood at the foot of the stairs.

34.159.oldText: What a cold, loose touch he impressed on my fingers! He was deeply displeased by what had occurred that day; cordiality would not warm him, nor tears move him. No happy reconciliation was to be had with him — no cheering smile or generous word: but still the Christian was patient and placid; and when I asked him if he forgave me, he answered that he was not in the habit of cherishing the remembrance of vexation; that he had nothing to forgive, not having been offended.

34.160.oldText: And with that answer he left me. I would much rather he had knocked me down.

35.1.oldText: Not that St. John harbored any spirit of unchristian revenge—not that he would have harmed a hair on my head if he could. By both nature and principle, he was above petty vengeance. He had forgiven me for saying I scorned him and his love. But he had not forgotten the words. As long as he and I both lived, he never would forget them. I saw by his look, whenever he turned to me, that they hung permanently in the air between us. Whenever I spoke, they sounded in my voice. They colored my every word and action.

35.2.oldText: He didn't stop talking to me. He even called me each morning to join him at his desk as usual. But I fear the imperfect human inside him took a pleasure the pure Christian did not share—pleasure in showing how skillfully he could, while acting and speaking exactly as always, drain every drop of warmth and interest from his words and manner. To me, he had become nothing more than a marble guardian angel. He was still protecting me, still watching over me, but the kindness had turned to ice.

35.3.oldText: All this was torture—refined, lingering torture. It kept up a slow fire of frustration and a trembling grief that wore me down completely. I felt how—if I were his wife—this good man, pure as a deep, sunless spring, could slowly kill me without drawing a single drop of blood, and without staining his crystal conscience with even the faintest mark of crime. I felt this especially when I tried to make peace. No compassion met mine. He felt no suffering in return. He hadn't given himself to me or tried to win me. He stood apart from me as if we were different species. He was quietly confident that he was right, and I was wrong. This conviction showed clearly in everything he said and did.

35.6.oldText: "I hope we are friends," came the unmoved reply. He continued watching the rising moon.

35.11.oldText: This, spoken in a cool, even tone, was both humiliating and baffling. If I'd listened to my pride, I would have walked away at once. But something worked in me more powerfully than pride. I deeply respected my cousin's talent and principles. His friendship meant a great deal to me. Losing it was hard to bear. I wouldn't give up the attempt to regain it so easily.

35.30.oldText: A very long silence followed. What struggle between nature and duty took place in him during that pause, I cannot say. Only strange gleams flickered in his eyes, and dark shadows crossed his face. At last he spoke.

35.38.oldText: "I am. God did not give me my life to throw away. To do as you wish would be nearly the same as suicide. And besides, before I make any final decision about leaving England, I need to know for certain whether I can't do more good by staying than by going."

35.41.oldText: "I know where your heart turns and what it clings to. The attachment you cherish is sinful and unsanctioned. You should have destroyed it long ago. Now you should be ashamed even to mention it. You're thinking of Mr. Rochester."

35.67.oldText: "I must," I said. "Just now, when I repeated my offer to serve as his assistant, he was appalled by my lack of propriety. He seemed to think I'd done something indecent in proposing to travel with him unmarried—as if I hadn't always hoped to find a brother in him and regarded him as one."

35.71.oldText: "And then," I continued, "though I feel only sisterly affection for him now, if forced to be his wife, I can imagine developing an unavoidable, strange, agonizing kind of love for him. Because he is so talented, and there's often a certain heroic grandeur in his look and manner. In that case, my life would become unspeakably wretched. He wouldn't want me to love him. And if I showed my feelings, he'd make me understand they were unwanted and excessive. Superfluous. I know he would."

35.74.oldText: But I was forced to face him again at supper. During the meal he appeared just as composed as usual. I had thought he would barely speak to me, and I was certain he had abandoned his marriage plan. The rest of the evening proved me wrong on both counts. He addressed me exactly in his usual manner—or what had lately become his usual manner—carefully polite. No doubt he had called on the Holy Spirit to subdue the anger I'd provoked, and now believed he had forgiven me. But I saw he had not. It was there in every measured word and controlled gesture. The forgiveness was a performance. Beneath it, the steel remained.

35.75.oldText: For the evening reading before prayers, he chose the twenty-first chapter of Revelation. It was always a pleasure to listen to his voice read the Bible. Never did it sound so sweet and full—never was his manner so impressive in its noble simplicity—as when he delivered the words of God. Tonight that voice took a more solemn tone and his manner a more thrilling quality. He sat amid his household circle—the May moon shining softly through the window—and read of the new heaven and new earth. Of the river of the water of life, and the tree with its twelve kinds of fruit, yielding fruit every month. Of the city with no need of sun or moon, for the glory of God was its light.

35.80.oldText: In the prayer that followed, all his energy gathered and all his stern passion awoke. He was in deep earnest, wrestling with God, determined to prevail. He begged for strength for the fainthearted. He asked for guidance for wanderers from the fold—for a return, even at the last moment, for those being lured from the narrow path. He pleaded for a brand snatched from the burning. Earnestness is always deeply solemn. First, as I listened, I was moved. Then, as the prayer went on, I felt troubled. Was this prayer for me? Was I the one being prayed for? A shiver ran through me.

35.82.oldText: "Thank you, Jane. As I said, I'll return from Cambridge in two weeks. That time is yours for reflection. If I listened to human pride, I would say nothing more about marriage. But I listen to my duty, and I keep my first aim firmly in view—to do all things for the glory of God. My Master was patient, and so will I be. I cannot abandon you to ruin. Repent—decide, while there's still time. Remember, we're told to work while it is day—warned that the night comes when no one can work. Remember the fate of Dives, who had his good things in this life. God give you strength to choose the better part which shall not be taken from you!"

35.83.oldText: He laid his hand on my head as he spoke these last words. He had spoken earnestly, gently. His look was not that of a lover gazing at his beloved, but that of a pastor calling back his wandering sheep—or better, a guardian angel watching over the soul in his care. All men of talent, whether they feel deeply or not—whether they are zealots or despots—if only they are sincere—have their moments of mastery, when they command and rule. I felt reverence for St. John. I felt his power. But the power was not mine to submit to. I would follow him to the ends of the earth. I would not give him my hand.

35.85.oldText: "Could you decide now?" asked the missionary. The question was put gently. He drew me to him, also gently. Oh, that gentleness! How much more powerful it was than force! I could resist St. John's anger. But I grew soft as a reed under his kindness. Yet I knew—if I gave in now, I would still be made to regret my earlier resistance. His nature had not changed in one hour of solemn prayer. It was only lifted up.

35.87.oldText: "My prayers are heard!" St. John exclaimed. He pressed his hand more firmly on my head, as if claiming me. He put his arm around me—almost as if he loved me. I say almost—I knew the difference. I had felt what it was to be loved. But, like him, I had now pushed love aside and thought only of duty. I struggled against the dimness clouding my vision, behind which something still churned. Sincerely, deeply, urgently, I longed to do what was right—and only that. "Show me, show me the path!" I begged of Heaven.

35.88.oldText: The house was completely still. I believe everyone except St. John and me had gone to bed. The single candle was dying out. The room was full of moonlight. My heart beat fast and hard—I could hear its throb. Suddenly it stopped, seized by a feeling beyond description. The feeling was not like an electric shock, but it was just as sharp, strange, and startling. It acted on my senses as if they had been asleep until now, and were suddenly jolted wide awake. They rose, expectant—eye and ear waiting. The flesh trembled on my bones.

35.96.oldText: "Down, superstition!" I told myself, as that phantom rose up dark beside the black yew tree at the gate. "This is not deception, nor witchcraft. It is the work of nature. She was stirred, and she performed—no miracle—but her finest work."

35.97.oldText: I broke away from St. John, who had followed and would have held me back. It was my turn to take command. My powers were awake and active. I told him not to question or comment. I told him to leave me alone. I must and would be alone. He obeyed at once. Where there is energy to command well enough, obedience never fails. I went up to my room, locked myself in, fell on my knees, and prayed in my own way—a different way from St. John's, but effective in its own fashion. I seemed to reach beyond the visible world, as it were—very near a mighty Spirit. And my soul rushed out in gratitude. Not through words. Through something deeper. I rose from my knees. I knew what I had to do.

36.5.oldText: It was still two hours until breakfast. I filled the time walking softly around my room, pondering the experience that had given my plans their new direction. I recalled the sensation I had felt—for I could recall it, with all its indescribable strangeness. I recalled the voice I had heard. Again I asked where it had come from, as uselessly as before. It had seemed to be inside me—not in the external world. I asked myself whether it was just a nervous impression—a hallucination. I couldn't believe so. It seemed more like an inspiration. The extraordinary effect on me confirmed this. I felt as though I had been called—not by mortal voice, but by something higher.

36.12.oldText: I left Moor House at three in the afternoon. Soon after four I stood at the Whitcross signpost, waiting for the coach that would take me to distant Thornfield. In the silence of those lonely roads and empty hills, I heard it approaching from far away. It was the same coach from which, a year ago, I had stepped down on this very spot—utterly lost, hopeless, and purposeless! It stopped at my signal. I climbed in—this time not forced to hand over my last coins for the fare. Once I had been penniless. Now I had means. The coach carried me away.

36.13.oldText: It was a journey of thirty-six hours. I had set out from Whitcross on a Tuesday afternoon. Early Thursday morning the coach stopped to water the horses at a roadside inn, set amid scenery whose green hedges, broad fields, and gentle hills—how mild compared to the stern moors of Morton!—greeted my eyes like the features of a once-familiar face. Yes, I recognized this landscape. I was sure we were near Thornfield. "How far is Thornfield Hall from here?" I asked eagerly.

36.18.oldText: The suggestion was sensible, yet I couldn't force myself to act on it. I so dreaded an answer that would crush me with despair. To prolong doubt was to prolong hope. I might yet see the Hall one more time beneath the morning sky. There was the stile before me—the very fields I had stumbled through, blind, deaf, driven half-mad with anguish, on the morning I fled from Thornfield. Before I fully knew what I'd decided, I was in the midst of them. How fast I walked! How eagerly I strained my eyes toward the familiar landscape!

36.19.oldText: At last the woods rose up. The rookery clustered dark. A loud cawing broke the morning stillness. Strange joy filled me. On I hurried. Another field crossed—a lane threaded—and there were the courtyard walls and the back buildings. The house itself, the rookery still hid. "My first glimpse shall be from the front," I decided, "where the bold battlements will strike my eye at once, and where I can pick out my master's window. Perhaps he'll be standing at it—he rises early. Perhaps he's walking in the orchard, or on the road in front. If so, I could meet him this very minute. Is there not a chance? A possibility?"

36.21.oldText: The crows sailing overhead may have watched me taking this survey. I wonder what they thought. They must have noticed I was very cautious and timid at first, and that gradually I grew bolder. A peek, then a long stare. Then a departure from my hiding place and a drift into the meadow. Then a sudden stop, full in front of the grand house, and a long, hard look straight at it.

36.23.oldText: A lover finds his beloved asleep on a mossy bank. He wants to catch a glimpse of her face without waking her. He creeps softly over the grass, careful to make no sound. He pauses—thinking she's stirred. He retreats. Not for anything would he be seen. All is still. He advances again. He bends over her. A light veil rests on her features. He lifts it, bends lower. His eyes anticipate the vision of beauty—warm, blooming, lovely in sleep. How quick was his first glance! But how it freezes! How he recoils! Not just a veil was lifted—a mask was removed. What he sees is not his beloved's face—but a skeleton. A death's head, cold and grinning where warmth and beauty should have been.

36.26.oldText: And there was the silence of death around it—the solitude of a desolate wasteland. No wonder that letters sent here had never been answered. You might as well have mailed them to a tomb. The black grimness of the stones told how the Hall had fallen—by fire. But how was it started? What story lay behind this disaster? What losses beyond wood and stone and plaster had followed? Had lives been ruined as well as property? If so, whose? Terrible question—one I dreaded having answered, yet felt compelled to ask.

36.27.oldText: Wandering around the shattered walls and through the devastated interior, I gathered evidence that the catastrophe was not recent. Winter snows had drifted through that empty arch. Winter rains had beaten in through hollow windows. Among the soaked piles of rubble, spring had encouraged new growth—grass and weeds sprouted between the stones and fallen beams. And where, in the meantime, was the unfortunate owner of this wreck? In what country? Under what circumstances? My eyes wandered over the grey, neglected ruins. Then they instinctively turned toward the sky above the ruins, as if searching for something more.

36.35.oldText: "I mean the present gentleman, Mr. Edward's father," he explained. I breathed again. My blood flowed once more. Those words fully assured me that Mr. Edward—my Mr. Rochester, God bless him wherever he was!—was at least alive. Was, in fact, "the present gentleman." What comforting words! It seemed I could now bear whatever came next—whatever the revelations might be—with relative calm. Since he was not in the grave, I could endure hearing he was at the other end of the earth.

36.46.oldText: "I'm coming to that, ma'am. Mr. Edward fell in love with her. The servants said they'd never seen anyone so smitten. He followed her everywhere. They used to watch him—servants do, you know, ma'am—and he was devoted to her beyond everything. Though nobody but him thought her all that beautiful. She was a little, small thing, they said—almost like a child. I never saw her myself, but I heard Leah the housemaid talk about her. Leah liked her well enough. Mr. Rochester was about forty, and she was barely twenty. When he proposed to her, you can bet there were plenty of raised eyebrows. But he was determined, and he was the master."

36.48.oldText: "You've hit it, ma'am. It's quite certain it was her—and nobody else—who started it. She had a woman looking after her called Mrs. Poole—an able woman in her line, very trustworthy, except for one weakness. A weakness common to many nurses—she kept a private bottle of gin, and now and then had a drop too much. That's understandable, given the hard life she led. But it was dangerous, because when Mrs. Poole was passed out from the gin, the madwoman would get the keys from her pocket, leave her cell, and wander the house doing whatever wild mischief came into her head. They said she had once set fire to the room next to her husband's bed. But this time she went up to the third floor and set the governess's old room on fire—the room directly above. Then she went down to a lower floor and set fire to the hangings in the room where her husband was sleeping. But he had already woken—the whole floor was blazing. He got up and managed to save the servants. Then he went back for her."

36.50.oldText: "Leave England? God, no! He wouldn't so much as cross the doorstep—except at night, when he'd walk like a ghost around the grounds and through the orchard. As if he'd lost his mind—which, in my opinion, he had. Because before that slip of a governess crossed his path, you'd never have met a more spirited, bolder, keener gentleman. He wasn't a man given to drinking, gambling, or horse racing, as some are, and he wasn't especially handsome. But he had courage and a will of his own, if ever a man did. I knew him from a boy, you see. He was quite fond of me too—I've often thought more should have been done to stop him from going wrong. He was no saint. But he was not the devil people made him out to be either."

36.52.oldText: "Yes, indeed. And he went up to the attics when everything was burning above and below. He got the servants out of their beds and helped them down himself. Then he went back to get his wife out of her room. And then they called up to him that she was on the roof. She was standing there, waving her arms above the battlements, shouting so loud they could hear her a mile away. I saw her and heard her with my own eyes and ears. She was a big woman, with long black hair. We could see it streaming against the flames as she stood there. I heard Mr. Rochester call to her. I saw him climb through the skylight onto the roof. We shouted for him to come down—it was too dangerous. He approached her. Then she yelled, and with one leap she was over the edge—"

36.53.oldText: The next moment she lay smashed on the pavement.

36.55.oldText: "Dead! As dead as the stones her brains and blood were scattered on."

36.57.oldText: "You may well say so, ma'am. It was horrifying!"

36.60.oldText: "Well, ma'am, afterward the house burned to the ground. Only some bits of walls are standing now."

36.62.oldText: "No—perhaps it would have been better if there had."

36.64.oldText: "Poor Mr. Edward!" he burst out. "I never thought I'd see the day! Some say it was God's judgment on him for keeping his first marriage secret and trying to take another wife while she was alive. But I pity him, for my part."

36.66.oldText: "Yes, yes, he's alive. But many think he'd be better off dead."

36.67.oldText: "Why? How?" My blood ran cold again. "Where is he? Is he in England?"

36.68.oldText: "Yes—he's in England. He can't get out of England, I imagine—he's stuck now."

36.69.oldText: What agony! And the man seemed determined to draw it out.

36.70.oldText: "He is stone-blind," he said at last. "Yes—stone-blind is Mr. Edward."

36.71.oldText: I had feared worse. I had feared he was mad. I summoned strength to ask what had caused this.

36.72.oldText: "It was his own courage, and you might say his kindness, in a way, ma'am. He wouldn't leave the house till everyone else was out. As he came down the great staircase after Mrs. Rochester threw herself from the battlements, there was a massive crash—everything collapsed. He was pulled from the ruins alive, but badly injured. A beam had partly protected him, but one eye was destroyed, and one hand was so crushed that the surgeon, Mr. Carter, had to amputate it immediately. He lost the other eye too. He's now helpless—blind and crippled."

36.73.oldText: "Where is he? Where does he live now?"

36.74.oldText: "At Ferndean, a manor house on a farm he owns, about thirty miles away. Quite a desolate place."

36.76.oldText: "Old John and his wife. He wouldn't have anyone else. He's quite broken down, they say."

36.78.oldText: "We have a chaise, ma'am—a very fine chaise."

36.79.oldText: "Have it ready at once. If your driver can get me to Ferndean before dark today, I'll pay you both double the usual rate."

37.0.oldText: Ferndean Manor was a building of considerable age, moderate size, and no architectural ambition, buried deep in a wood. I had heard of it before. Mr. Rochester often spoke of it and sometimes visited. His father had bought the estate for its hunting grounds. He would have rented the house but could find no tenant, because of its remote and unhealthy location. So Ferndean remained empty and unfurnished, except for two or three rooms fitted up for Mr. Rochester's occasional overnight stays.

37.1.oldText: I reached this house just before dark on an evening marked by grey skies, a cold wind, and steady, penetrating rain. The last mile I walked, having dismissed the carriage and driver with the double payment I'd promised. Even when I was very close to the manor, I could see nothing of it—so thick and dark were the trees of the gloomy wood around it. Iron gates between granite pillars showed me where to enter. Passing through them, I found myself among trees. There was no clear drive visible, no smooth lawn or broad walk. The growth of the surrounding woods had crept right up to the very doorstep. They were wild and untrimmed.

37.2.oldText: I thought I had taken a wrong turn and lost my way. The darkness of nature and forest gathered around me. I looked for another path. There was none—only interwoven branches, thick trunks, and dense summer foliage. Not an opening anywhere.

37.3.oldText: I kept going. At last the trees thinned a little. Soon I made out a railing, then the house—barely distinguishable from the trees in the dim light, so damp and green were its decaying walls. I entered through a door fastened only with a latch and stood in an enclosed yard from which the wood curved away in a half circle. There were no flowers, no garden beds—only a broad gravel walk circling a patch of grass, set in the heavy frame of the forest. The house presented two pointed gables in its front. The windows were latticed and narrow. The front door was narrow too—one step led up to it. The whole looked, as the innkeeper had said, "quite a desolate spot."

37.6.oldText: It opened slowly. A figure came out into the twilight and stood on the step—a man without a hat. He stretched out his hand as if to feel whether it was raining. Dark as it was, I recognized his strong shape and features. I nearly revealed myself—but I held back. I was not yet ready to meet him. I had still a thing or two to think through. I needed to prepare myself for the shock—and to prepare him.

37.7.oldText: I stayed where I was, barely breathing, and watched him—studied him, unseen, and sadly invisible to him. It was a meeting in the dark. I held back the tears that threatened and willed my heart to steady itself.

37.8.oldText: His form was the same strong, powerful build as ever. His bearing was still upright. His hair was still raven-black. His features were still sharp and firm. Not in one year's time had decay advanced so far as to alter either. But in his face I saw a change—a look of desperate brooding that reminded me of some wronged and chained wild animal. The sightless eyes were tragic to behold. They were dark, and wild, and hopeless.

37.9.oldText: And, reader, do you think I feared him in his blind fury? If you do, you don't know me. A gentle hope blended with my sorrow. I could feel his heart was still warm, still beating, still mighty. I was sure I could bring him comfort. I just needed to find the right approach.

37.10.oldText: He stepped down from the doorstep and moved slowly, gropingly, toward the grass. Where was his bold stride now? He felt his way cautiously, as one who walks in darkness. He stopped. He stood still. Then he stretched out his right hand—the hand that had no fingers—toward the sky, the trees, the rain. He seemed to gather the elements in that mutilated grasp. He tried to see with those blind eyes. He let his hand fall, then turned and went back inside.

37.11.oldText: "Will you take my arm, sir?" said a voice. It was John. "There's a heavy shower coming on. You'd better go in."

37.13.oldText: John withdrew without noticing me. Mr. Rochester tried again to walk about—in vain. Everything was too uncertain. He groped his way back to the house and re-entered it. I heard him close the door.

37.15.oldText: She started as if she had seen a ghost. I calmed her. To her flustered "Is it really you, miss, come at this late hour to this lonely place?" I answered by taking her hand. Then I followed her into the kitchen, where John now sat by a good fire. I explained in a few words that I had heard everything that had happened since I left Thornfield, and that I had come to see Mr. Rochester. I asked John to go down to the inn at Millcote and fetch my trunk, which I had left there. I then sat down to collect my thoughts and consider how best to approach my master.

37.19.oldText: "You are to send in your name and your business," she replied. She then proceeded to fill a glass with water and place it, with candles, on a tray. I noticed her hand was shaking.

37.23.oldText: I took it from her hand. She pointed me toward the parlour door. The tray shook as I held it. The water sloshed from the glass. My heart pounded. Mary opened the door for me and shut it behind me.

37.24.oldText: The parlour looked grim. A neglected handful of fire burned low in the grate. Leaning over it, with his head propped on his hand, sat the blind tenant of the room. His old dog, Pilot, lay on one side, curled up as if afraid of being accidentally stepped on. Pilot pricked his ears when I came in. Then he jumped up with a yelp and bounded toward me. He almost knocked the tray from my hands. I set it on the table, then patted him and said softly, "Lie down!" Mr. Rochester turned mechanically to see what the commotion was, but since he saw nothing, he returned to his brooding.

37.30.oldText: He put out his hand quickly, but not seeing where I stood, he didn't touch me. "Who is this? Who is this?" he demanded, seeming to try to see with those sightless eyes. An expression of pain and bewilderment crossed his face.

37.48.oldText: "Never will, says the vision? But I always woke and found it an empty mockery. And I was desolate and abandoned—my life dark and lonely—my soul thirsting, and the cup always snatched from my lips."

37.50.oldText: I pressed my lips to his once-brilliant, now sightless eyes. I swept the hair from his brow and kissed that too. He suddenly seemed to trust that I was real. A look of grateful joy broke over his worn face.

37.53.oldText: "And you do not lie dead in some ditch? And you are not a starving outcast among strangers?"

37.57.oldText: "Ah! That is practical—that is real!" he cried. "I should never dream that. Besides, there is your particular voice—I could never mistake that. Jane Eyre—Jane Eyre," he repeated.

37.59.oldText: "But as you're rich, Jane, you must now have friends who will look after you and not let you devote yourself to a blind man like me?"

37.62.oldText: "Certainly—unless you object. I will be your neighbor, your nurse, your housekeeper. I find you lonely. I will be your companion—to read to you, to walk with you, to sit with you, to wait on you, to be eyes and hands to you. Stop looking so gloomy, sir. I will not let you be sad."

37.63.oldText: He didn't answer right away. He seemed deep in thought—withdrawn. He sighed. He half-opened his lips as if to speak, then closed them again. I felt a kind of panic stir in me. I began to wonder if he was going to refuse me.

37.66.oldText: "Yes—but you understand one thing by staying with me, and I understand another. You perhaps could bring yourself to visit the blind man in his cell and sit beside him—to cheer him—and come again tomorrow. But to consent to stay always with this poor, dark, desolate creature—that is another thing entirely."

37.71.oldText: He fell back into gloom. I, on the contrary, grew more cheerful and took fresh courage. These last words gave me an opening. I felt it would not do to let the conversation drift into despair.

37.72.oldText: "It's time someone undertook to bring you back to life," I said, parting his thick, long, uncut hair. "I see you are being turned into a lion, or something of the sort. Your hair reminds me of eagle feathers—whether it has been combed lately I cannot tell."

37.76.oldText: "Did you? Don't tell me that—or I might say something unflattering about your judgment. Now, let me leave you for a moment to find a better fire than this dead pile of ashes."

37.81.oldText: "No, my fairy. But I am grateful enough to hear and feel you."

37.85.oldText: I called for Mary and soon had the room in better order. I prepared him a comfortable meal. My spirits were high, and I was happy to be active and useful. He seemed astonished, even a little overwhelmed, at the rapid change from loneliness to company, from darkness to warmth.

37.86.oldText: After supper, he began asking me many questions—where I had been, what I had been doing, how I had found him. But I gave him only brief answers. It was too late for long stories. Besides, I wanted to keep certain things back until another time.

37.91.oldText: "And there is enchantment in this very hour I am spending with you. Who can tell what a dark, hopeless life I have dragged through since I last saw you? And suddenly, you appear. I stretch my hand and touch what I dreamed would never be real again."

37.92.oldText: A plain, practical reply, cutting against the current of his troubled thoughts, was, I was sure, the best comfort I could offer.

37.93.oldText: "What use is it to do me good, benevolent spirit, when at some moment you will desert me again—passing away like a shadow from my grasp?"

37.96.oldText: "Just to comb out this shaggy black mane. I find you rather alarming at close range. You talk of my being a fairy, but I'm sure you look more like a brownie yourself."

37.100.oldText: "Yet I have been with good people—far better than you. A hundred times better. People with ideas and views you never entertained in your life. Much more refined, and with much better manners."

37.104.oldText: "You won't get it out of me tonight, sir. You must wait until tomorrow. Leaving my tale half-told will, you know, be an excellent way to ensure you let me come back."

37.105.oldText: "You mocking creature—fairy-born and human-raised! You make me feel as I haven't felt in twelve months. If Saul could have had you for his David, the evil spirit would have been exorcised without the need for a harp."

37.109.oldText: Very early the next morning I heard him up and moving about, wandering from one room to another. As soon as Mary came down, I heard the question: "Is Miss Eyre here?" Then: "Which room did you put her in? Is she up? Go and ask if she wants anything. And when she'll come down."

37.110.oldText: I came down as soon as I thought breakfast might be ready. I entered the room very softly. I had a view of him before he discovered my presence. He sat in his chair, his old dog at his feet. Pilot's head rested on the mutilated hand—he was trying to caress the animal, but could not manage it well. The look on his face was one of grief and lonely longing—painful, almost unbearable to witness. Yet I held back my tears. This was not a time for tears. I would be upbeat—relentlessly.

37.111.oldText: "It is a bright, sunny morning, sir," I said. "The rain is over and gone. There is a soft glow after it. You should feel it through the open window. Can you see the light?"

37.112.oldText: His features lit up at once.

37.113.oldText: "Oh, you are really there, my skylark! Come to me. You are not gone—not vanished? I heard one of your kind an hour ago, singing high over the wood. But its song had no music for me, any more than the rising sun had brightness. All the melody on earth comes from one voice. All the sunshine from one presence."

37.114.oldText: The tears stood in my eyes at this confession of his need—just as if a royal eagle, chained to its perch, had been forced to beg a sparrow to be its provider. But I held firm. I would not weep now.

37.115.oldText: Most of the morning was spent outdoors. I led him out of the wet and wild wood into cheerful open fields. I described the sky and the landscape for him. I let him sit on a comfortable seat and feel the sun. I helped him navigate the uneven ground. I was careful and patient. I was also very happy.

37.116.oldText: "Cruel, cruel deserter!" he exclaimed at one point. "Oh, Jane, what did I feel when I discovered you had fled from Thornfield? When I couldn't find you anywhere? When, after searching for hours, I knew you were truly gone?"

37.117.oldText: Prompted by his urgency, I began the story of my experience over the past year. I softened considerably what related to the three days of wandering and starvation—because telling him those things in full would have been torture to him. His loving spirit could not have borne it. The hunger, the cold, the exhaustion—I touched on them lightly, emphasizing instead my rescue.

37.118.oldText: He said I should not have left him that way, without any means of making my way. I should have told him my intentions. I should have trusted him. He would have found a way to set things right without separation. He swore he would never have forced me to remain at Thornfield. He'd have been happy to know I was safe, even far away.

37.126.oldText: "Still young, then. Is he a short, dull, plain man? The kind whose goodness lies more in the absence of vice than in any real strength of character?"

37.143.oldText: "The picture you've just painted suggests a rather overwhelming contrast. Your words have sketched a graceful Apollo—tall, fair, blue-eyed, with a Grecian profile. Your eyes rest on a Vulcan—a real blacksmith, brown, broad-shouldered, and blind and lame into the bargain."

37.144.oldText: "I never thought of it before, but you certainly do resemble Vulcan, sir."

37.188.oldText: "Ah! Now we reach the heart of the matter. He wanted you to marry him."

37.194.oldText: "No, Jane, you are not comfortable—because your heart isn't with me. It's with this cousin—this St. John. Oh, until this moment I thought my little Jane was all mine! I believed she loved me even when she left me. That was a drop of sweetness in the bitterness. For all the time we've been apart, for all the hot tears I've wept over our separation, I never imagined that while I was mourning her, she was loving another! But it's only natural enough. You said he was young, handsome, talented. And I—what am I now?"

37.195.oldText: "Shake me off, then, sir—push me away. I won't leave on my own."

37.201.oldText: "He is not my husband, and never will be. He doesn't love me. I don't love him. He loves—as much as he can love, which is not the way you love—a beautiful young woman called Rosamond. He wanted to marry me only because he thought I'd make a suitable missionary's wife, which she would not. He is good and great, but severe. And for me, cold as an iceberg. He is not like you, sir. I am not happy at his side, nor near him, nor with him. He has no hold on my sympathy or warmth. I do not long for his company. I am not drawn to his approval. No warmth rises in me at his approach."

37.232.oldText: "Sacrifice! What do I sacrifice? Famine for food. Waiting for fulfillment. To be allowed to put my arms around what I treasure—to press my lips to what I love—to rest against what I trust: is that a sacrifice? If so, then yes—I delight in sacrifice."

37.239.oldText: "We must be joined without delay, Jane. There's only the license to get—then we marry."

37.241.oldText: "Fasten it to your belt, Janet, and keep it. I have no use for it."

37.247.oldText: He pursued his own thoughts without hearing me.

37.248.oldText: "Jane! You think me, I'm sure, a godless man. But my heart swells with gratitude to the merciful God of this earth right now. He sees not as man sees, but far more clearly. He judges not as man judges, but far more wisely. I did wrong. I would have stained my innocent flower—breathed guilt on its purity. The Almighty snatched it from me. I, in my stubborn rebellion, nearly cursed the punishment. Instead of bowing to the decree, I defied it. Divine justice followed its course. Disasters came thick upon me. I was forced to pass through the valley of death. His punishments were heavy. I acknowledged their justice. I began to experience remorse, repentance, the wish for reconciliation with my Maker. I began sometimes to pray—brief prayers, but very sincere."

37.249.oldText: "Some days ago—four days, to be exact—last Monday night, a strange mood came over me. Grief replaced frenzy. Sorrow replaced bitterness. I had long been convinced that since I couldn't find you anywhere, you must be dead. Late that night—perhaps between eleven and midnight—before going to my miserable bed, I begged God, if it pleased Him, to take me soon from this life and admit me to the next world, where there was still hope of reunion with Jane."

37.250.oldText: "I was in my room, sitting by the open window. The mild night air soothed me. I could see no stars—only by a faint, luminous haze did I know the moon was out. I longed for you, Janet! Oh, I longed for you with soul and flesh! I asked God, in anguish and humility, whether I had not been desolate and tormented long enough. Whether I might not soon taste peace and happiness again. I admitted I deserved everything I'd endured. I could hardly expect mercy. But I begged for it—urgently. Then I cried out: 'Jane! Jane! Jane!'"

37.256.oldText: "Let me try to describe what those words created in my mind—though it's hard to express. Ferndean is buried, as you see, in heavy woodland where sound falls flat and dies without echo. 'Where are you?' seemed spoken among mountains. I heard a hill-sent echo repeat the words. At that moment the wind felt cooler and fresher on my brow. I could have believed that, in some wild, lonely place, Jane and I were meeting. In spirit, I believe we must have met. You—wherever you were—must have felt it at the same moment."

37.257.oldText: Reader, it was on Monday night—near midnight—that I too had received the mysterious call. Those were the very words with which I had answered it. I listened to Mr. Rochester's account but said nothing in return. The coincidence struck me as too strange and awe-inspiring to discuss. If I told anything, my story would inevitably make a deep impression on his mind—and that mind, already too prone to dark thoughts from suffering, did not need the added weight of supernatural mystery. I kept these things in my heart.

37.258.oldText: "You can't wonder, then," my master continued, "that when you appeared before me so unexpectedly last night, I had difficulty believing you were anything more than a voice and a vision—something that would dissolve into silence, as the midnight whisper and mountain echo had dissolved before. Now, I thank God! I know otherwise. Yes, I thank God!"

38.1.oldText: "Mary, I married Mr. Rochester this morning." The housekeeper and her husband were both the kind of calm, steady people to whom you can safely announce remarkable news without having your ears pierced by a shriek or your head stunned by a flood of amazed chatter. Mary did look up, and she did stare at me. The ladle she was using to baste a pair of roasting chickens did stop in midair for about three minutes. Then, without comment, she resumed her basting. When she had finished and put the ladle down, she said—

38.4.oldText: "I told Mary how it would be," he said. "I knew what Mr. Edward"—John was an old servant who had known his master since boyhood, so he often used his first name—"I knew what Mr. Edward would do. And I was certain he wouldn't wait long either. And he's done right, in my opinion. I wish you joy, Miss!" And he politely touched his forehead.

38.6.oldText: "She'll likely do better for him than any of the grand ladies would have." And again: "If she's not one of the handsomest, she's no fool and very good-natured. And in his eyes she's beautiful—anyone can see that."

38.10.oldText: You haven't quite forgotten little Adele, have you, reader? I hadn't. I soon asked and received permission from Mr. Rochester to visit her at the school where he had placed her. Her wild joy at seeing me again moved me deeply. She looked pale and thin. She said she was unhappy. I found the school's rules were too strict and its coursework too demanding for a child her age. I took her home with me. I had planned to be her governess again, but soon realized that was impractical. So I found a school with a more relaxed approach and placed her there. She settled in well, made good progress, and eventually grew into a pleasant and kind young woman. A good education corrected whatever flaws her French upbringing had given her, and when she left school I found her a faithful and agreeable companion.

38.12.oldText: I have now been married ten years. I know what it is to live entirely for and with the person I love most on earth. I consider myself supremely blessed—blessed beyond what words can express—because I am my husband's life as fully as he is mine. No woman was ever nearer to her husband than I am. We are truly bone of his bone and flesh of his flesh. I never tire of my Edward's company. He never tires of mine, any more than we each tire of the heartbeat in our own chests. We are always together. To be together is for us to be at once as free as if we were alone, and as content as if we were in company. We talk all day long. To talk to each other is only a more animated and audible form of thinking. His presence is all I need. Mine, he says, is all he needs.

38.13.oldText: Mr. Rochester continued to be blind for the first two years of our marriage. Perhaps it was that circumstance that drew us so close—that bound us so tightly. For I was his eyes, as I am still his right hand. Literally, I was—as he often called me—the apple of his eye. He saw nature and books through me. I never tired of gazing on his behalf and putting into words what I saw—field, tree, town, river, cloud, sunbeam. The landscape before us, the weather around us. And impressing by sound on his ear what light could no longer stamp upon his eyes.

38.17.oldText: And have you a pale blue dress on?

38.18.oldText: I had. He told me then that for some time he had thought the darkness clouding one eye was becoming less dense. Now he was sure of it.

38.19.oldText: He and I went to London. He consulted an eminent eye specialist and eventually recovered the sight of that one eye. He cannot see very clearly now. He cannot read or write much. But he can find his way without being led by the hand. The sky is no longer a blank to him—the earth no longer a void. When his firstborn was placed in his arms, he could see that the boy had inherited his own eyes, as they once were—large, brilliant, and dark. On that occasion, he acknowledged once more, with deep gratitude: "God is merciful! He sees that I have earned the right to a little happiness, and He grants it."

38.20.oldText: My Edward and I are happy. And the more so because those we love most are happy too. Diana and Mary Rivers are both married. They visit us once a year, and we visit them. Diana's husband is a captain in the navy—a brave officer and a good man. Mary's is a clergyman, a college friend of her brother's, and worthy of the connection in every respect. Both Captain Fitzjames and Mr. Wharton love their wives and are loved by them.

38.21.oldText: As for St. John Rivers, he left England. He went to India. He entered on the path he had chosen for himself, and he follows it still. A more determined, tireless pioneer never struggled through hardship and danger. Firm, faithful, and devoted, full of energy, zeal, and truth, he works for humanity. He clears their painful way toward progress. He cuts down prejudices of creed and caste like a giant felling trees. He may be stern. He may be demanding. He may be ambitious still. But his is the sternness of the warrior who guards his captain's tent. His is the ambition of the servant laboring in his Master's vineyard. He is a man willing to lay down his life for the truth.

38.22.oldText: St. John is unmarried. He never will marry now. He has been enough, by himself, for the work. And the work draws near its end. His glorious sun is hastening toward its setting. The last letter I received from him drew human tears from my eyes yet filled my heart with divine joy. He anticipated his sure reward—his imperishable crown. I know that a stranger's hand will write to me next, to say that the good and faithful servant has been called at last into the joy of his Lord. And why weep for this? No fear of death will darken St. John's last hour. His mind will be unclouded, his heart will be unshaken, his hope will be sure, his faith will be steadfast. His own words are a pledge of this—

38.23.oldText: "My Master," he says, "has forewarned me. Daily He announces more distinctly—'Surely I come quickly!' and hourly I more eagerly respond—'Amen; even so, come, Lord Jesus!'"
